Paper Title: Co-Creating Accessibility-Centred Mobility Strategies in Low-Density Suburban Contexts: Evidence from Coimbra, Portugal
Study type / basis for inclusion: Primary fieldwork. Three deliberative focus groups the authors ran themselves; a case where the design process deliberately equalised institutional and citizen input.
Case setting: Sao Martinho do Bispo, a low-density suburban parish on Coimbra's southwestern periphery, Portugal (about 13,000 residents, 21 square km, ageing traditional cores plus newer housing, steep topography, one operator SMTUC with roughly one hundred stops). Run inside the ENTROPY project. Citizen participants were predominantly older adults, average ages above 60 (p. 7).
Method(s), session by session: Three focus groups in Sao Martinho do Bispo, March to April 2025, 18 participants (institutional, technical, citizen), recruited via local associations, municipal contacts, and institutional partnerships. Institutional/technical and citizen participants met in separate groups to reduce power asymmetries (p. 7). Each session about 90 minutes, four phases: (1) trust building (not analysed), (2) open debate on six predefined strategies plus a green/yellow/red visual vote, (3) individual proposals worked up collaboratively on detailed maps of the study area, then colour-coded assessment, (4) an autonomous individual prioritisation via digital scoring (Slido, 1 to 5 Likert) of a separate proposal set introduced by the research team (p. 5 to 6). Sessions recorded and transcribed, then coded in Atlas.ti 25 with a hybrid inductive-deductive scheme, single coder, co-occurrence coefficient threshold c at least 0.20 (p. 8). A final co-creation phase consolidated eight strategies, each cross-checked against the co-occurrence results (p. 21 to 22).
Tools and artifacts: Six predefined strategy prompts as a shared reference; green/yellow/red visual voting cards; detailed printed maps of the study area for spatial diagnosis; Slido online polling with a five-point Likert scale; Atlas.ti 25 for coding and co-occurrence analysis; session recordings and transcripts triangulated with field observation and documentary sources (p. 4). The 15-Minute City, Transit-Oriented Development, and Mobility as a Service were carried in as analytical lenses, not templates (p. 2).
Underlying principle of the method: Grounded in collaborative and communicative planning (Healey; Innes and Booher; Forester), aiming to bridge expert and experiential knowledge (p. 4, p. 16). Group separation to mitigate power asymmetries and foster open deliberation (p. 7). In the synthesis phase, outputs from all groups were treated as analytically equivalent with no hierarchical weighting between institutional, technical, or citizen inputs (p. 24). Mobility framed as a social right rather than solely a matter of efficiency (p. 2).
Provocation used to generate new ideas: Yes. Six predefined strategies were used as a shared conceptual framework to stimulate reflection and identify structural barriers and opportunities (p. 5). Detailed maps prompted participants to locate spatial inequalities and formulate territorial proposals (p. 5). Global proximity models (15-Minute City, TOD, MaaS) were reframed as things to reinterpret rather than adopt (p. 2, p. 23). The phase-four proposal set was introduced by the research team specifically to test preferences (p. 15).
Who holds design authority: Shared but framed by the research team (ENTROPY project, TRANSyT at UPM Madrid, University of Extremadura, University of Coimbra), which set the predefined strategies and proposal set and did all coding (single coder, p. 8). Institutional, technical, and citizen stakeholders co-created the eight strategies; the synthesis applied no hierarchical weighting (p. 24). Implementation authority is split: infrastructure strategies depend on municipal authorities and transport operators, awareness and behavioural strategies on schools, local associations, and community organisations (p. 23 to 24). Object is the mobility service, network, and street redesign, not statutory policy.
What is being designed: Eight co-created sustainable mobility strategies for Sao Martinho do Bispo: pedestrian infrastructure and public-space redesign; cycling infrastructure and services; regulation of private transport and parking; education, awareness, and a culture of sustainable mobility; public transport frequency, reliability, and real-time information; mobility plans for schools and workplaces; road-space reallocation toward pedestrians and cyclists with an equity and safety focus; integrated spatial planning (Table 5, p. 22). Framed as an initial deliberative step; the study does not evaluate long-term implementation feasibility (p. 24).
Values surfaced in the case: Institutional and technical actors emphasised efficiency, coordination, system rationality, and long-term planning, and were cautious about new investment citing efficiency and maintenance (p. 6, p. 13, p. 16). Citizens emphasised everyday accessibility, walkability, reliability, comfort, and safety, with usability and reliability taking precedence over systemic innovation (p. 15, p. 16). Shared across groups: accessibility, connectivity, safe continuous pedestrian networks. Relational trust recurs: acceptance of restrictive measures and of multimodal projects was said to rely on trust, fairness, and transparent communication more than technical design (p. 14, p. 19). Flexibility for variable need appears as a warning that digital-only systems risk excluding older and digitally vulnerable users, requiring analogue alternatives (p. 18, p. 23).
Ideal traveler per decision-makers: Not named as an ideal traveler construct. Institutional and technical actors' priorities imply a traveler served by diversified modal options and integrated digital services: their top scores went to cycling infrastructure, shared mobility, and pedestrian zones, reflecting an understanding of mobility as dependent on multimodality and digitalisation and a shift toward integrated mobility ecosystems and MaaS (p. 15). A municipal representative benchmarked transit against the private car: 'It is inconceivable that a public transport route takes 50 min when the same trip by car takes 15' (p. 13). A health-sector participant framed the rational traveler as one who weighs cost and time: 'Many young people call an Uber, not realising that if they wait five minutes, they spend 10 times less and take 15 min longer' (p. 18).
Actual travelers encountered: Citizen participants were mostly older adults, retired residents and active workers relying on walking, public transport, and private vehicles, in an area whose steep slopes constrain active travel for older residents and people with reduced mobility (p. 7, p. 9). Their stated needs: continuous pavements (currently 'forced to walk along drainage ditches', p. 13), reliable and frequent buses, real-time information, safe crossings. Cautious interest in shared mobility, influenced by limited familiarity with these emerging systems (p. 15). People with disabilities, migrants, and younger low-income residents were largely absent from the room (p. 24 to 25).
Gap between the two: Institutional actors emphasised efficiency, coordination, long-term planning, and technological or MaaS solutions and were wary of new spending; citizens wanted concrete daily improvements, walkability, and reliability, and were wary of digital-only systems. On new facilities the split was sharp: institutional and technical participants (n equals 13) voted mostly red (8 negative), citizens (n equals 5) mostly green (3 positive) (p. 13). The paper reads this as complementarity between institutional rationality and citizen pragmatism rather than open conflict, and credits the deliberative design and no-weighting synthesis with partly reconciling it (p. 15, p. 24).
Quotable moment: "The divergence reflects differing priorities: institutional actors emphasised efficiency and maintenance, whereas citizens focused on everyday accessibility." (p. 13). On the process itself: "outputs from all groups were treated as analytically equivalent and systematically compared, with no hierarchical weighting between institutional, technical, or citizen inputs" (p. 24).
Cross-comparison note (our synthesis): A rare documented case where the process design itself refused to let technical actors set the terms: the no-hierarchical-weighting synthesis (p. 24) is close to a working model of the participation our paper argues AV deployment skips. The institutional-versus-citizen split it surfaces (efficiency, coordination, and system rationality on one side; walkability, reliability, and everyday access on the other) maps directly onto our efficiency-versus-community-values axis, and here it was visible in the room rather than only in outcomes. Useful as a counter-model. Caveats: the citizen sample skewed to older adults with no people with disabilities or younger low-income residents, so flexibility for variable need is only partly represented; this is strategy co-creation, not vehicle or service design, and it stops before implementation.

Paper Title: Transportation barriers and equity: Values and experiences of elected officials
Study type / basis for inclusion: Primary fieldwork and a decision-maker paper. A national survey plus 38 interviews the authors ran with elected officials; supplies the decision-maker side of the ideal-traveler contrast with direct evidence.
Case setting: Canadian municipal and regional elected officials (mayors and councilors) in jurisdictions that have some form of public transit. 165 survey respondents across seven provinces and one territory; 38 follow-up interviewees. Sample skews senior (41 percent) and to smaller communities; under 10 percent identify as racialized, disabled, Indigenous, LGBTQ+, or immigrant (p. 7 to 8).
Method(s), session by session: Mixed method. (1) National online survey, open June to September 2022 (note 3), sent to 2,148 mayors and councilors via a university survey centre with two follow-up emails, 165 completed responses, 8.2 percent response rate, about 25 minutes each. Three themes: personal experience with transportation barriers; sources of knowledge; equity values via forced-choice paired statements; plus demographics and travel behaviour. Instrument developed in consultation with the Mobilizing Justice research partnership (academics, practitioners, community advocates) and grounded in Linovski et al. 2021 (p. 6 to 7). (2) 38 key-informant interviews, January to March 2023, 20 minutes to 1 hour, with survey respondents who opted in; transcribed and coded in Dedoose using the framework method, codes tested on a sample and reviewed by multiple team members (p. 6). (3) Preliminary findings presented to the Community and Equity Advisory Table affiliated with Mobilizing Justice (note 15).
Tools and artifacts: Six forced-choice value pairs (Table 7): procedural fairness, mode-choice fairness, geographic fairness, utilitarian versus targeted, maintenance of existing conditions, willingness to pay; respondent picks one of two statements. A barrier ranking exercise for self and for constituents (Table 5). A deliberately unprimed interview question, 'What populations or groups of people do you think of when considering transportation barriers?', with no option list (p. 12). Census-aligned mode-of-travel questions. Dedoose qualitative software.
Underlying principle of the method: Policy-learning theory: decision-making as a mix of personal experience, network exposure, and evidence (p. 4 to 5). The study deliberately treats elected officials as endogenous to transportation decision-making, against a technical-rational tradition that treats politicians as exogenous to the process (Marsden and Reardon, cited p. 2). Centering the decision-maker's own values and lived experience as the object of study, on the premise that who decides shapes distribution. Uses the category approach to equity groups while noting its limits (Church et al., cited p. 3).
Provocation used to generate new ideas: Limited and not a design provocation. The forced-choice value pairs act as elicitation devices, each forcing a choice between a mainstream-equity statement and a competing utilitarian, geographic, or status-quo statement to surface latent values (p. 13 to 14). The unprimed interview question was designed so respondents would develop their own responses rather than be primed with a list of options (p. 12). No prototypes, scenarios, or ideation exercises; the instrument provokes articulation of existing values, not generation of new mobility ideas.
Who holds design authority: The research team (planning academics at the University of Manitoba and University of Waterloo, and United Way Greater Toronto), with the survey instrument co-developed with the Mobilizing Justice partnership and reviewed by named advisors. The study's subjects, elected officials, hold real decision authority over long-range planning, infrastructure, services, and resource allocation (p. 6), but as participants they design nothing here. Scope: this is about who sets transportation investment priorities; it does not itself design a service, vehicle, or network.
What is being designed: Nothing designed. Diagnostic study of decision-makers' values. Its practical recommendation is that planning staff and advocates engage elected officials in policy learning early, before officials are charged with making decisions (p. 17).
Values surfaced in the case: Utilitarian greatest-good dominates: 63 percent chose transportation policies that 'provide benefits to the greatest number of people' over prioritising marginalised people and communities (37 percent) (Table 7, Q4). Procedural fairness endorsed in the abstract: 73 percent agreed consultation is only fair if people from different identities and communities can fully participate (Q1, p. 13). 84 percent accept that existing costs or infrastructure sometimes need to change for fairness (Q5); 77 percent say car users should pay the full costs of driving (Q6). Geographic fairness near evenly split, 56 percent prioritise historically underinvested areas versus 44 percent equal investment everywhere (Q3). Mode-choice equity endorsed in principle by 66 percent (Q2). Support for equity-targeted values rises with personal or close-relation experience of barriers, with being a woman (60 percent of those prioritising marginalised groups), and with larger community size (p. 14 to 15). Officials rely most on staff reports (81 percent regularly) and least on advocacy groups (40 percent) and constituent associations (47 percent) (p. 12 to 13).
Ideal traveler per decision-makers: The paper does not use the term. Its value data imply a traveler who is a member of the general public counted in 'the greatest number' (63 percent, Q4), for whom transportation investment is a community-wide good rather than targeted redress, and who most likely owns a car: 90 percent of officials have at least one household car and 71 percent drive to work, no respondent used paratransit or ride-hailing for any trip (p. 8). Officials reported little direct experience of the barriers under discussion: 5 percent a mobility-limiting disability, 6 percent inability to afford transit, 7 percent harassment (p. 9). A councilor named the mental model directly (p. 12, quoted below).
Actual travelers encountered: Surfaced second-hand through officials' interview accounts, not collected from travelers. Examples officials gave: a 96-year-old living with her son in a mobile home, out of food, with no transportation (Interview 38, p. 12); a growing newcomer and refugee population who do not feel comfortable 'due to the racism or the sexism, and exhibited violence on transit' (Interview 23, p. 12); residents pushed 'further and further from the core' into cheap suburban housing with infrequent transit (Interview 26, p. 12). Officials most often named people with disabilities (66 percent), low income (58 percent), and seniors (45 percent) as facing barriers; immigrants, women, and racialized people were rarely named (Table 6, p. 11 to 12).
Gap between the two: 73 percent endorse fully inclusive consultation but only 37 percent would prioritise marginalised communities in investment (p. 13 to 14). The paper names this 'a significant disconnect between academic and professional understandings of equity and the values of many elected officials' (p. 16) and opens with the nested quote 'a fundamental mismatch between who is making key transit decisions . . . and who is most affected by those decisions' (p. 2, quoting TransitCenter, 2022, p. 5). Officials' thin direct experience of affordability, disability, and harassment barriers tracks with their lower support for equity-targeted values (p. 16).
Quotable moment: ". . . those people are in the habit of thinking, you know, that everybody has a house and a car. Well, not everybody has both, and not everybody has either." (p. 12, councilor, Interview 19).
Cross-comparison note (our synthesis): This paper supplies the decision-maker side of our contrast with direct evidence rather than inference: a majority of Canadian local elected officials hold a utilitarian, community-wide-benefit view of transportation investment (63 percent), own cars (90 percent), and have little first-hand experience of the barriers under discussion, while endorsing inclusive process in the abstract (73 percent). That profile is the implicit ideal traveler our fieldwork participants are measured against. The paper's own framing, an academic and professional versus political values gap, parallels our engineering-efficiency versus community-values axis and shows the mismatch sits upstream of any particular technology, already present in who sets priorities. Caveats: 8.2 percent response rate with self-selection toward officials with strong transportation views; the traveler evidence here is second-hand through officials' accounts.

Paper Title: "The bus is accessible, but how do you get to the bus": First and last mile experiences of disabled transit riders
Study type / basis for inclusion: Primary fieldwork. Its central claim is directly about the ideal traveler: access measures assume riders who can complete first and last mile trips with ease.
Case setting: 16 disabled transit riders who rely on public transit, greater Austin, Texas (10) and Seattle, Washington (6), interviewed September to December 2022 by Zoom. Vision (5), mobility (6), cognitive (1), and multiple (4) disabilities; 9 women, 7 men. Recruited through disability and transit advocacy organizations and agency advisory committees. Comparative case: Seattle as an exceptional case with a 2017 citywide sidewalk assessment and accessibility focus, Austin as a typical mid-to-large US city (p. 3).
Method(s), session by session: Single method, comparative case study. 16 semi-structured virtual interviews, 30 to 60 minutes, September to December 2022, using an approved protocol. Participants introduced themselves, their disability, and their typical travel, then discussed first and last mile experiences; the conversation was deliberately not pre-structured around mobility disability so participants could self-identify their relationship to disability and travel (p. 4). Purposive and snowball sampling via professional networks, community-based organizations, civil rights organizations, university student groups, community centers, and transit agency advisory groups. Manually transcribed and inductively coded (descriptive codes plus a priori codes from the first and last mile literature), codebook refined iteratively into 8 categories and 5 themes, validated through peer review with colleagues in transportation planning, social justice, and critical disability studies (p. 4). Part of the author's dissertation research.
Tools and artifacts: Semi-structured interview protocol (Appendix A), which includes design-imagination prompts: 'What would an accessible public transit system look like to you?', 'How would you design the built environment to be more accessible and inclusive?', 'What types of goals and investments do you think public transit agencies should prioritize?'. Zoom; Calendly self-scheduling; manual transcription; a codebook; a hierarchy-of-codes diagram (Fig. 1).
Underlying principle of the method: Mobility justice framework (Sheller; The Untokening's Principles of Mobility Justice), treating disability as constructed by the built and social environment rather than as an individual deficit (Jackson). Lived experience as necessary and currently missing knowledge: 'The lived experience of disability is largely missing from transportation planning practices that are based on meeting minimum standards for accessibility set by the ADA' (p. 3). 'Advancing mobility justice in practice can only be achieved if affected communities co-lead the planning process' (p. 2). Intersectional rather than additive analysis. The author uses 'access' rather than 'accessibility' to respect disability studies scholarship (p. 1).
Provocation used to generate new ideas: Limited. The protocol carried speculative design questions asking participants to describe an accessible neighborhood and transit system and to say how they would redesign the built environment (Appendix A). No prototypes, scenarios, maps, or workshop; elicitation was mainly retrospective account of experience.
Who holds design authority: In the systems studied: transit agencies and local jurisdictions design routes, stop placement, pedestrian infrastructure, wayfinding and information formats, and even service names (a participant's screen reader misreads the 'LINK' light rail name, and the agency 'were set on LINK', p. 6). Agency advisory committees for accessibility exist but are consultative; disabled travelers 'are seldom in the room when transportation decisions are made' (p. 6). The researcher holds analytic and authorial authority. Scope: transit service, stops, pedestrian infrastructure, wayfinding, and digital interfaces, not statutory policy.
What is being designed: Nothing designed. Diagnostic interview study. Recommends participatory data gathering, providing door-to-door transportation to engagement events so first and last mile barriers do not deter participation, and accessibility improvements beyond physical ones (wayfinding, communication, information) (p. 7).
Values surfaced in the case: Engineering and efficiency values named by the paper: transit systems 'inherently prioritize the travel needs of non-disabled commuters' and make 'assumptions about average users' (p. 1); ADA compliance treated as adequate through 'minimum standards' and 'compliance-based approaches' (p. 2); microtransit framed as eliminating 'the need for first and last mile improvements' (p. 2), a system-efficiency logic. Community values from riders: dignity (an operator's annoyance 'just made me feel really horrible'), confidence (a rider 'would feel too uncomfortable to ask' the operator to lower the bus), relational trust (agencies 'have all this energy in the beginning ... But then when it comes to the end, it's crickets', p. 6), and flexibility for variable need (riders add time, distance, and cost to route around missing sidewalks and full bike racks). Maps to equitable access (foreclosed), relational trust, and flexibility for variable need.
Ideal traveler per decision-makers: Not named as an ideal traveler construct, but the paper repeatedly characterizes the traveler planning assumes: a non-disabled commuter who can walk or roll the first and last mile with ease, hear audio cues, read visual signage, use a smartphone app, and lift a bike onto a rack. 'Public transit systems inherently prioritizes the travel needs of non-disabled commuters and makes assumptions about how transit riders complete first and last mile trip segments' (p. 1). 'Assumptions about average users and their travel behavior in common transportation planning measures leave out many transportation system users' (p. 1). A participant: 'I feel like people who don't rely on transit are coming up with these plans. You know they're just talking about the commute that's already outdated' (p. 6).
Actual travelers encountered: 16 disabled riders who cannot afford to live near accessible infrastructure ('Seattle is so ... expensive ... basically the entire city is unaffordable', p. 4); cross streets slower than the 'allotted time' at an unmaintained crosswalk; push a wheelchair over cracked or absent sidewalks; cannot hear audio announcements 'when you got seven lanes of cars going back and forth' (p. 6); are excluded by a screen-reader-hostile service name; and, with one usable hand, cannot lift a bike when the front rack is full and wait for the next bus rather than ask the driver for help. Women reported compounded social and safety burdens along the first and last mile.
Gap between the two: Planning assumes an average non-disabled commuter completing the first and last mile with ease; the riders interviewed face disproportionate and intersectional barriers, reshape their trips to cope, and are 'seldom in the room' when decisions are made (p. 6). Seattle, the exceptional case with a citywide sidewalk assessment, produced first and last mile experiences similar to typical-case Austin, so the gap is not closed by data investment alone (p. 7). Engagement that invites co-creation during a pilot then goes silent afterward is named as a distinct trust failure ('it's crickets', p. 6).
Quotable moment: "The bus is accessible, but how do you get to the bus?" (p. 5). And on who designs: "I feel like people who don't rely on transit are coming up with these plans. You know they're just talking about the commute that's already outdated." (p. 6).
Cross-comparison note (our synthesis): Direct support for our claim that the ideal traveler is set by non-users: the paper's central move, that access measures 'assume that transit riders can complete first and last mile trips with ease' (p. 1), is the efficiency assumption our argument targets, and the interviews show its cost in changed trips, lost dignity, and abandoned attempts to ask for help. The 'crickets' pattern (rich engagement during a pilot, silence after) is a concrete instance of the relational-trust foreclosure we describe. Caveat for our own fieldwork: the sample was recruited through advisory committees and by email, so it over-represents disabled riders already active in first and last mile advocacy and misses those without internet access (p. 4).

Paper Title: Moving Towards Mobility Justice: Challenges and Considerations for Supporting Advocacy
Study type / basis for inclusion: Primary fieldwork. Interviews with advocates, not travelers, but names the planners' assumed traveler and the expert-public divide directly.
Case setting: 16 mobility justice advocates across Canada, most in the Greater Toronto Area (9 GTA, 6 in national organizations working in Montreal, GTA, and Vancouver, 1 in London, Ontario), interviewed June to September 2022. Senior figures: program managers, principal coordinators, and CEOs; 8 from explicitly mobility justice organizations, 8 from adjacent sustainability or environmental justice organizations (Table 1). Supported by the Toronto Climate Observatory. An HCI and CSCW paper.
Method(s), session by session: Single method. 16 semi-structured interviews, 45 to 60 minutes, over Zoom, video recorded, transcribed with Otter and verified by the first two authors (p. 6 to 7). Recruited through civic technology interest groups, snowball sampling, Google searches, and personal connections. Interviews were broad: day-to-day activities, primary projects, technical tools and resources used and produced, how organizations run planning sessions, stakeholders, and outreach. Reflexive thematic analysis (Braun and Clarke): two authors coded independently on the Otter transcripts, built preliminary themes separately, then iteratively merged codes into hierarchies across several discussion meetings, converging on an eight-code codebook (Information accessibility; Lack of holistic transportation planning; Challenges with data and digitization; Need for tracking impact; Increased focus on innovation; Changes required in people's behaviour; Increased focus on business impact; Fear of backlash) (p. 7).
Tools and artifacts: Studied, mostly not built by the authors: transit maps, highly technical planning proposals, city and municipal websites, Twitter as a channel for expert transit knowledge, learning management systems and a 'Data Trust' concept for advocacy data. Advocates' own tools: personas or avatars built from neighbourhood demographic data for 'empathy exercises', Google Mind Maps for collaborative asset mapping, physical 'pop-ups' (small-scale demonstrations of mobility solutions before implementation), storytelling and fixed key messages emphasizing 'temporary' and 'pilot', visuals borrowed from groups in other cities, research reports such as Mixed Signals (2018), and co-presentations with city councilors in their own wards. Authors' own tools: Zoom, Otter, reflexive thematic analysis.
Underlying principle of the method: Mobility justice (Sheller) as a relational, multi-scalar frame, combined with path-dependence and lock-in (MacKenzie and Wajcman; Foxon) as the systemic explanation. HCI and CSCW concepts: 'publics' formed through shared conditions, data infrastructure literacy (Gray et al.), infrastructuring (Ludwig et al.), Scott's 'panoptic legibility' contrasted with a bottom-up 'local legibility', friction as a design frame, and relational rather than transactional civic interaction. Data treated as authority, as evidence, and as ambivalent (Le Dantec).
Provocation used to generate new ideas: Yes, used by the advocates and reported rather than run by the authors. Personas and avatars built from neighbourhood demographics let youth 'relate better' to different needs (P6). Google Mind Maps support collaborative asset mapping. Pop-ups are 'smaller scale demonstrations of mobility solutions aimed at gathering support prior to implementation' (p. 12), messaged deliberately as 'it's a test, it's a pilot' to lower resistance (P5). Borrowed visuals and story-driven framing are used to move debate away from novelty toward tried-and-tested solutions. The authors' interview method itself was not provocation-based.
Who holds design authority: Urban planners and municipalities design mobility infrastructure, transit maps, planning proposals, and public-participation formats, and hold near-total authority: a participant describes decisions 'being imposed' after 'a conversation that only some people are allowed to be in' (P7). Elected officials shape priorities and 'prefer to cater to automobility needs based on the neighbourhoods they represent', fearing 'political backlash' (p. 13). Advocates work outside this, translating and contesting. HCI and CSCW researchers and designers are the paper's addressee for future tool design. Scope: mobility information systems, maps, planning tools, participation processes, and street-redesign pilots.
What is being designed: Nothing designed by the study. It is diagnostic plus a design agenda for HCI and CSCW: situated mapping tools, visual, video, and social-media-forward digital artifacts, story-driven games, data infrastructure literacy programs, tools that build relationships between planners and multiple publics, designed-in 'friction' moments, and adaptable infrastructuring systems (p. 15 to 17). The advocates themselves design pop-ups, personas, asset maps, and research reports.
Values surfaced in the case: Engineering and efficiency values named by participants: planners' 'focus on innovation', new solutions 'designed for this region only', over well-known solutions (p. 11); 'highly technical proposals' that 'limit who can participate in an informed manner' (p. 7); safety judged 'based on the number of cars' rather than 'perceptions of safety, and comfort and belonging' (P2); 'prioritization of financial impact assessments, sometimes even over other human safety assessments' (p. 13), with 'business impact' the deciding data even when 'separated bike lanes save lives' (P2); Scott's 'panoptic legibility' serving 'bureaucratic structures'. Community values at stake: relational trust (the expert-public divide, decisions imposed), flexibility for variable need (maps only in English in a city with 'like 50 languages', every street treated the same when 'every street is not the same'), and equitable access (assumptions imposed on marginalized and immigrant suburban populations).
Ideal traveler per decision-makers: Not named as an ideal traveler construct. Evidence of the assumed traveler: planners and government 'rely on assumptions in the design of suburban residential areas' where marginalized and immigrant populations live, specifically 'There is this perception that automatically in the suburbs, trips are going to be longer, we just assume that things are further apart' (P11), even though 'fully 1/3rd of all trips in the GTHA are five kilometers or less'. Municipalities 'count car traffic counts, seriously injured incidences, emergency services and nearby major institutions' and read safety off car numbers (P2). 'Elected officials prefer to cater to these automobility needs' (p. 13). The imagined traveler is a car driver making long suburban trips, legible through traffic counts and business metrics.
Actual travelers encountered: Surfaced second-hand through advocates. Non-English-speaking riders confused by maps and by unexpected turns ('What if you don't speak English? It's very, very confusing to you', P3); cross-boundary commuters ('Folks will travel to Brampton to go work in a warehouse') failed by single-system maps (P9); suburban residents a third of whose trips are within a 20-minute bike ride but who lack the infrastructure (P11); and 'the poor, disabled, women, and children, who ultimately bear the brunt' of carbon-intensive systems (p. 15). Advocates themselves are resource-constrained, doing unpaid data labor for funder reports.
Gap between the two: Planning tools and proposals are 'top-down, expert-driven and divorced from the situated particularities of place' (p. 15); the format of participation and the technical language make it 'a conversation that only some people are allowed to be in ... things ... being imposed' (P7). Planners assume long suburban car trips while a third of GTHA trips are under 5 km (P11). Safety and investment are decided by car counts and business impact even when a measure 'save[s] lives' (P2). Path-dependence makes this pattern hard to even recognize, let alone change (p. 14 to 15).
Quotable moment: "that barrier to entry, turns it into, you know, a conversation that only some people are allowed to be in, and you know that you end up with a lot of people very frustrated by decisions [transit-related], because they weren't in that conversation and feeling like things [mobility infrastructure-related policies] are being imposed." (p. 8, participant P7).
Cross-comparison note (our synthesis): Strong support for the arrives-without-participation half of our argument, at the level of tools and knowledge infrastructure rather than one deployment. 'Path-dependence' is a useful named mechanism for why efficiency values persist across technology generations. The bike-lane example, where business-impact data outweighed a life-safety finding, is a clean case of an efficiency metric foreclosing a community value. The pop-up tactic, messaged as 'temporary' to lower resistance, is worth noting for our own recommendations. Caveats: GTA-specific and, by the authors' own statement, interpretive and not generalizable; participants are advocates, so both the ideal-traveler and the traveler evidence are second-hand; the HCI framing points some recommendations at tool design rather than governance.

Paper Title: Toward Structured Public Involvement: Justice, Geography and Collaborative Geospatial/Geovisual Decision Support Systems
Study type / basis for inclusion: Primary fieldwork. Reviews the authors' own Structured Public Involvement deployments (AMIS, CAVE) in real infrastructure meetings, plus their Arnstein Ladder surveys of professionals and the public.
Case setting: US transportation infrastructure planning. Arnstein Ladder polling at real project meetings and professional conferences: 600 plus public responses from forums in Kentucky, Indiana, Arizona, and Alaska; 59 transportation professionals at the 2006 Transportation Research Board Annual Meeting (mean 7.2 years of public involvement experience); 28 local planners at the 2006 Bridging Boundaries conference in Louisville; 63 at the 2007 American Planning Association Annual Conference. SPI deployments: a highway corridor evaluation in southern Kentucky (AMIS, involving a caving and recreation group), noise wall and berm design in humid eastern and arid western landscapes (CAVE), a transit-oriented development study in a low-income minority neighborhood, and large-scale bridge evaluation. Sponsors: Kentucky Transportation Cabinet, Indiana DOT, Woodford County Planning, Jeffersonville, Indiana.
Method(s), session by session: (1) Arnstein Ladder polling: the eight-step ladder is shown at real infrastructure meetings and professional conferences; participants answer how they would characterize public participation now and where it should be, via anonymous real-time radio-frequency electronic polling, coded 1 to 8 (p. 6 to 7). (2) AMIS protocol: 69 landscape elements identified in facilitated meetings with a state highway agency; impedance (net social cost) values elicited element by element in facilitated focus groups; participants aggregate elements into affinity groupings; a three-level analytic hierarchy process weights classes and elements; ArcView generates a raster decision landscape and least-cost routing scripts produce candidate corridors; AMIS is then featured at public meetings as a dialogic element (p. 16 to 18). (3) CAVE protocol: landscape architects parameterize an image palette into a design vocabulary via literature survey and a brainstorming session with stock images, then remove overlapping parameters; a pilot scoring session with focus groups checks that community values are not neglected; wider outreach follows; the public scores 20 to 30 parameterized visualizations on a Likert scale via anonymous real-time polling in two-hour facilitated meetings; a fuzzy-set neural network maps community preference to design elements and estimates preference for untested combinations (p. 19 to 20). (4) Process satisfaction: a final anonymous real-time vote, 'Evaluate your satisfaction with this process,' scored 1 to 10 (p. 21).
Tools and artifacts: The Arnstein Ladder diagram; radio-frequency electronic polling keypads (SharpeDecisions and Fleetwood); multiple display computers; ArcView GIS; an analytic hierarchy process model; AMIS impedance and decision-landscape raster maps; CAVE design-vocabulary matrices; parameterized visualizations of noise walls, berms, and bridges; fuzzy-set-theoretic neural network models; facilitated focus groups.
Underlying principle of the method: A geographical justice framework from Rawls's A Theory of Justice: because perfectly equitable distributional justice is 'not attainable' at large scale in a pluralist democracy, maximize procedural justice and access to justice instead. The Arnstein Gap, the roughly 2.5-rung gap between the public's perceived and desired level of involvement, is the deficit to close, and doing so requires 'a redistribution of decision authority.' Habermasian consensus is rejected as infeasible for large heterogeneous groups in favour of Mouffe's 'conflictual consensus.' Geovisual and geospatial technologies are 'dialogic media,' not decision engines, and a process should never be 'organized exclusively around a particular technology in such a way that the operators of the technology are excessively privileged.' 'All public inputs should be incorporated into the analytic model, regardless of professional conceit' (p. 16). Rawls's Veil of Ignorance is invoked to structure fairness. Respect for participants' time is treated as a principle.
Provocation used to generate new ideas: Yes. AMIS's 'core premise is to move routing questions away from immediate contestation over specific landscape features and into a more analytic framework about cultural values and aims' (p. 16 to 17). CAVE shows 20 to 30 parameterized visualizations to be scored and estimates preference for untested design combinations, locating preference 'plateaus' and 'sinkholes' (p. 20). Brainstorming sessions with stock images set the design vocabulary. The Arnstein Ladder is itself used as a provocation with professionals: 'showing the professionals the Arnstein Gap findings was one way of illustrating the problem' (p. 22).
Who holds design authority: Explicitly negotiated and partitioned. 'SPI repositions the planner or designer as a consultant and facilitator to the design process. Professionals do not attempt to appropriate complete control' (p. 16). But the 'framework within which participation takes place is determined by transportation agencies according to legislative remit' (p. 16); CAVE 'input parameters are determined by professionals' and the design vocabulary is negotiated in facilitated meetings with design experts (p. 20); the 'decision envelope is partitioned into public and professional domains that accord with preferred Arnstein Ladder levels' (p. 20). Project sponsors' 'preferred Arnstein Ladder positions' cap how far authority moves, the research team 'has not possessed the direct power to ensure that designs are built,' and citizens' advisory boards are 'constrained by their actual limited political power' (p. 23). Scope: highway corridors, noise walls and berms, bridges, and a transit-oriented development.
What is being designed: Transportation infrastructure: highway corridor alignments (AMIS), highway noise wall and berm aesthetics (CAVE), large bridge structures, and a transit-oriented development. The SPI framework itself is the authors' methodological design contribution.
Values surfaced in the case: Engineering and expert-authority values: professionals hold a 'professional conceit', believing 'public involvement is more effective than the public does' (p. 7); many 'assume that the public prefers, and will demand, full participation' and so 'fear loss of autonomy or project control, or even their own obsolescence' (p. 7); some expressed 'unease with the idea that the public, or uninformed stakeholders, would be exercising design authority' and impulses 'to tell the public they were wrong' (p. 22); a US literature that frames public involvement as something to be 'managing, controlling, or containing' or a route to 'voter approval' (p. 6). Engineers assumed 'engineering variables would strongly control the route', which the authors call a 'false but pernicious assumption' (p. 18). Community values: procedural justice and relational trust (persistent 'public skepticism and mistrust of TI designers, planners, and other professionals', p. 6; 'in exchange for participation in a fair and open process, citizens often are willing to support the outcome ... even if their preferred alternative is not selected', p. 20), respect for participants' time, and the caving group's need for a 'secure geospatial information-sharing system' built 'in an initial environment of incomplete trust' (p. 18). Maps to relational trust and procedural or equitable access.
Ideal traveler per decision-makers: No traveler construct appears; the paper is about who participates in infrastructure decisions. The nearest analogue is the public that professionals imagine: either 'uninformed' and therefore not to 'be permitted to participate' at a partnership level, or a public that will 'demand' citizen control and threaten professional autonomy. In fact 'in no case so far do we find that the public prefers citizen control', and the public's desired position is 'partnership', which shows it 'clearly recognizes the expert domain of engineers and planners' (p. 7). State agencies otherwise gauge design quality 'informally ... based on number and intensity of complaints' (p. 20), so the implicitly preferred public is one that is quiet, defers to expertise, and does not litigate.
Actual travelers encountered: The publics encountered: a caving and recreation group holding proprietary geospatial data on cave locations that state engineers did not know existed (p. 18); up to 300 attendees per public meeting participating 'fully and equally' (p. 23); a low-income minority neighbourhood in a transit-oriented development study whose participants 'had never seen this level of public involvement before in a similar project' (p. 21); and publics across four states who consistently rate current involvement at 3.6, between informing and consultation, and want partnership (p. 7).
Gap between the two: The Arnstein Gap: the public rates current infrastructure participation at 3.6 (informing to consultation) and wants partnership, about 2.5 rungs higher, while professionals show a 'professional conceit', rating the process as more effective than the public does (unpaired t test, p value 0.0271) (p. 7). US practice frames public involvement as something to 'manage' or 'contain' or a path to 'voter approval' (p. 6) rather than a redistribution of authority. Even under SPI, the 'decision envelope' and CAVE parameters stay professionally and legislatively bounded, and sponsors' 'preferred Arnstein Ladder positions' cap how far authority actually shifts (p. 23).
Quotable moment: "All public inputs should be incorporated into the analytic model, regardless of professional conceit (i.e., judgment on the suitability of specific inputs into the design on the part of the designers)." (p. 16). On the surrounding literature: it addresses public involvement in terms of "managing," "controlling," or "containing" what are seen as its negative aspects (p. 6).
Cross-comparison note (our synthesis): The Arnstein Gap is a quantified version of the participation deficit our paper argues about, measured directly with transportation professionals and the public. Key nuance for us: the public here wants partnership, not control, and 'clearly recognizes the expert domain of engineers and planners' (p. 7), which sharpens our claim, the problem is not that communities want to run the engineering, it is that they are placed below consultation. The 'professional conceit', professionals rating the process better than the public does, is a clean mechanism for why deficits persist unnoticed. SPI shows a partial remedy is possible within existing mandates and with no extra meetings, and also shows its ceiling: sponsors' preferred Arnstein level and legislatively fixed decision envelopes bound how much authority moves. Caveats: a 2010 paper, pre-AV; the case evidence is the authors' own deployments and the satisfaction scores they collected; the authors concede their participation sample 'could be considered biased, stratified, or numerically inadequate' (p. 23).

Paper Title: Centering disability justice in active transportation transitions: A conceptual counter-cartography
Study type / basis for inclusion: Primary fieldwork, explicitly participatory. Names the able-bodied template and universal user directly, so it also carries strong ideal-traveler evidence.
Case setting: Montreal, Quebec (metro population over four million, roughly 16 percent of residents have a disability). 20 in-depth interviews with people with disabilities (10 men, 8 women, 2 non-binary; ages 25 to 70; 10 francophone, 10 anglophone; 14 White European, 6 Asian, Black, or Hispanic; wheelchair 9, cane or walker 7, mobility scooter 4; 17 post-secondary; living across 11 of Montreal's 19 boroughs), plus 47 local policy documents narrowed to 15 in effect 2022 to 2025. A follow-up study led by and with Montrealers with intellectual disabilities is underway.
Method(s), session by session: Conceptual counter-cartography (Fig. 1), a five-step procedure. (1) Search for local policy documents on active travel, active transportation systems, and disability inclusion from city and transport authorities (n equals 47). (2) Apply inclusion and exclusion criteria, keeping only policies on active travel or disability inclusion in effect 2022 to 2025 (n equals 15). (3) Conduct 20 semi-structured in-depth interviews, one to two hours, run separately by three researchers, stratified purposeful sampling, recruited through partner disability organizations' listservs and social media; the guide covered experiences of local transportation systems and planning, including public-consultation processes. (4) Deductively code policy and interview data against three conceptual-cartography analytical axes: Notion, Application, and Social linkages and barriers. (5) Comparative analysis juxtaposing dominant policy understandings with divergent interview findings, quoting participants verbatim to prioritize underrepresented voices. An earlier inductive pass surfaced the injustice themes pursued here.
Tools and artifacts: A semi-structured interview guide; three analytical axes with guiding questions ('Who is included and excluded from these conceptual frameworks?'); a comparison table (Table 2) setting dominant policy understandings against divergent interview findings; elucidatory photos of Montreal infrastructure (a plowed bike lane beside an unplowed sidewalk); the counter-cartography process diagram. Quebec disability scholars, community members, and organizations took part in method selection, research-tool design, recruitment, and analysis.
Underlying principle of the method: Disability justice (Sins Invalid; Hamraie), crip theory, and epistemic justice (Fricker). Four disability justice principles: ableism and disablism as pervasive forces; collective access and the leadership of people with disabilities; interdependence and cross-disability solidarity; reimagining wholeness beyond productivity. 'Knowledge should be co-created with a diversity of voices from the disability community and oriented toward their priorities' (p. 3). Concepts are treated as 'semiotic technologies' that enable or disable; the counter-cartography adds interviews and policy to a documentary method to center marginalized knowledge. Crip time (Kafer): bend the clock to meet disabled bodies and minds, not the reverse. Anti-ableism moves 'beyond special accommodations towards ... a culture of co-leadership'.
Provocation used to generate new ideas: Modest and conceptual. The three analytical axes and the comparison table are the device: guiding questions about inclusion and exclusion are applied to both policy text and lived accounts to make the mismatch visible. The conclusion poses four open redesign questions (for example, 'How can we work to redesign cycling infrastructure that is not only planned and labelled for standard (two-wheeled) bikes ...?') offered 'as a starting place for communities'. No workshop, prototype, or co-design session.
Who holds design authority: The City of Montreal and its transport authority (ARTM) define active travel and design cycling and pedestrian infrastructure, bike racks, signage, snow-clearing priority, and public consultations. Mainstream universal design guidelines 'rest on a linear, technocratic process meant to accommodate a universal user' (p. 12). Disability organizations have 'a long history of fighting for accessible transportation services, including through litigation' (p. 5). The researchers hold analytic authority and involved disability communities in the research design. The paper argues authority should shift toward 'the leadership of people with disabilities in urban planning and policymaking' and toward 'collective access as an iterative, value-explicit process of co-creation'. Scope: active transportation infrastructure (wheeling and cycling facilities, sidewalks, crossings, rest spaces, signage) and the policy definitions that shape it.
What is being designed: Nothing designed by the study. It reconceptualizes 'active travel' and poses four redesign questions: wheeling infrastructure for non-standard cycles and mobility aids; pedestrian and multi-use infrastructure for diverse disabilities; spaces of rest and conviviality as integral to journeys; and continual engagement with disability justice principles. It points to existing recommendations (Wheels for Wellbeing design guidelines, Project Sidewalk data tools, community adaptive-cycling centers).
Values surfaced in the case: Techno-managerial and efficiency values: active travel defined as travel 'by bike' and 'on foot' or 'travelling using your own energy' (ARTM); a 'linear, technocratic process meant to accommodate a universal user'; universal design guidelines that 'may meet minimum requirements in select areas, but fail to elicit meaningful change' (p. 12); walkability metrics that 'largely ignore accessibility barriers'; the city's framing of protected bike lanes as travel 'in a safe, efficient and pleasant way' and of active travel as universal 'me-time' (Fig. 7). Community values: flexibility for variable need (crip time, low-speed travel, rest and refuge as 'integral components of active journeys'), relational trust (consultations that fail: 'hitting a brick wall every time. We give recommendations, and they don't listen'; 'participation fatigue'; having to 'walk on eggshells' when advocating), and equitable access (exclusion from the very definition of the traveler, snow cleared from bike lanes but not sidewalks, bike racks that do not fit adapted cycles).
Ideal traveler per decision-makers: Near-explicit. Urban planning concepts 'often center on an able-bodied template, which can implicitly infer or reinforce the notion that disabled people are out of place' (p. 3). Montreal defines active travel as travel 'by bike' and 'on foot' (Ville de Montreal) or 'travelling using your own energy' (ARTM), and many respondents' mobility practices 'would not fit within the confines of' these definitions (Table 2). Mainstream universal design accommodates a 'universal user' (p. 12). A critiqued academic definition, quoted from Cook et al. via Larrington-Spencer, is active travel as that in which 'physical exertion of the traveler directly contributes to their motion' (p. 2). The city frames bike lanes as 'safe, efficient and pleasant' and active travel as 'me-time' (Fig. 7). The imagined traveler is able-bodied, moving on two feet or a standard two-wheeled bike, self-exerting, at pedestrian speed or faster, needing no rest.
Actual travelers encountered: 20 disabled Montrealers using wheelchairs (9), canes or walkers (7), mobility scooters (4), tricycles, tandem cycles, and service animals. They move at low speed: electric wheelchairs and scooters 'go at least 50 percent faster than the average pedestrian' (p. 6), so both sidewalks and cycle lanes misfit; a cyclist tells a wheelchair user to 'get on the sidewalk' (p. 9); a blind interviewee waits 'ad vitam aeternam' to cross a cycle path (p. 9); adapted cycles are larger and costlier, do not fit bike racks, and are sometimes given up for lack of storage (p. 6 to 7); sidewalks go unplowed while bike lanes are cleared (Fig. 2); and interviewees report 'participation fatigue' from consultations that ignore them.
Gap between the two: Policy and design center an able-bodied 'universal user' moving on two feet or two wheels under their own exertion; the disabled travelers interviewed do not fit that definition, are excluded from the concept itself, face infrastructure not built for their speed or devices, and find consultations 'fail to result in meaningful change' (p. 9). The city's universalizing 'me-time' and 'safe, efficient and pleasant' framings erase differential impacts. The proposed remedy is to 'bend infrastructure to meet disabled bodies and minds, rather than trying to bend disabled bodies and minds to meet normative infrastructure standards' (p. 11).
Quotable moment: "A lot of us are tired of doing this. I know we shouldn't be. But it's like hitting a brick wall every time. We give recommendations, and they don't listen." (p. 9, Interview 19). On the underlying principle, quoting Kafer: "rather than bend disabled bodies and minds to meet the clock, crip time bends the clock to meet disabled bodies and minds" (p. 11).
Cross-comparison note (our synthesis): One of the clearest statements in the set of the ideal traveler as an implicit value: the paper names the 'able-bodied template' and 'universal user' directly and shows, through Table 2, the mismatch with 20 lived accounts. 'Crip time' gives us a precise vocabulary for the flexibility-for-variable-need value. The consultation-fatigue findings ('brick wall', 'walk on eggshells') are direct evidence of relational-trust foreclosure inside the very processes meant to build it. Transferable to AVs: a service optimized for predictable, standard trips reproduces the same template. Caveats: 20 interviews in one city, over-representing post-secondary-educated participants and physical disabilities, with only one participant reporting an intellectual disability (a separate participatory study is underway); the paper is conceptual and proposes questions rather than tested designs.

Paper Title: Performative versus Authentic Equity Work: An Assessment of Current Practices in Transportation Planning
Study type / basis for inclusion: Primary fieldwork. Not a traveler study, but an insider account of the acultural planning frame ('auto throughput') and who sits in the boardroom versus who is served.
Case setting: California transportation professionals who also identify as Black or people of color. 28 interviewed (36 percent Latinx, 21 percent Black, 14 percent Asian or Pacific Islander, 25 percent mixed race, 3 percent Middle Eastern; 64 percent female, 25 percent male, 11 percent non-binary; 85 percent under 40; 42 percent in advocacy, 25 percent policy, 25 percent government or planning, 8 percent research or education). Recruitment and interviews April to August 2020, during the onset of COVID-19 and the uprisings following the murder of George Floyd. Efforts to recruit Indigenous and tribal-nation professionals were unsuccessful, so the authors use BPOC rather than BIPOC.
Method(s), session by session: (1) Purposive expert sampling through transportation planning networks (Caltrans, APA California Chapter, Young Planners in Transportation, ASLA Transportation Division, Women in Transportation, Urban Land Institute) plus the authors' own contacts, then snowball referrals. (2) Screening: over 18, works in transportation, and identifies as BIPOC or works primarily with BIPOC communities or works in transportation equity. (3) Round-one interviews, 1 to 1.5 hours, via Zoom, recorded and transcribed; the guide covered professional trajectory, how the participant defines equity, DEI involvement, communities and stakeholders served, whether new mobility technologies can address equity, research needs, examples of successful and unsuccessful equity projects, and a closing vision for equitable transportation. (4) The guide was revised mid-study to add questions on how COVID-19 and the Floyd uprisings changed the participant's work and sense of what feels possible (Appendix 2). (5) After round one the sample was assessed for diversity and round two targeted late-career, Central Valley or Northern California, Indigenous, and male-identified professionals. (6) Coding in Dedoose: coded first to question-aligned themes, refined with emergent codes after half the interviews, remaining interviews coded under the new rubric and earlier ones recoded, then contextualized against the transportation-equity literature. Data saturation at 28 (p. 3 to 4).
Tools and artifacts: Two interview guides, original and COVID and Floyd-revised (Appendices 1 to 2); two code rubrics (Appendices 3 to 4); Dedoose coding software; Zoom; a performative-versus-authentic-equity typology (Table 1) mapped onto Patricia Hill Collins's matrix of domination (individual and interpersonal, cultural, institutional). A feminist science studies 'accounting for bias' framework guides the analysis; the lead author co-authored the Untokening's Principles of Mobility Justice.
Underlying principle of the method: Standpoint epistemology and the ethnic-studies notion of 'double vision': being Black or a person of color plus transportation expertise gives 'a unique and highly valuable lens' on what equity work is impactful. Feminist science studies' rejection of 'the god trick' of view-from-nowhere objectivity, and the claim that 'all knowledge is partial'. Mobility justice (Untokening) and design justice on how design processes 'unequally distribute risks, harms, and benefits'. The study explicitly presumes that 'traditional transportation practices emerged from practices of discrimination and racism' and that operating from the status quo perpetuates them (p. 4).
Provocation used to generate new ideas: The closing question, asking participants to envision an equitable and just transportation system, works as a speculative provocation and produced the Future Vision section (for example 'Streets with No Police'). The COVID and Floyd revision added prompts about 'what feels possible'. Otherwise retrospective interview elicitation, not a design workshop or prototype.
Who holds design authority: Transportation agencies (US DOT, Caltrans, CalSTA, the California Transportation Commission), their leadership and boards, and funders. A participant: 'Many of the people are older, able-bodied, straight white men. And so maybe the bigger problem there is just that the people that we're theoretically all serving are not the people leading those decisions' (p. 12). Funders 'dictate what money can be used for rather than consulting with the community' (p. 12). Equity hires are given responsibility 'but not giving them any of the real decision-making power'. The recommended shift is 'redistribution of decision-making power to communities' and 'from White-led to Community-led' (Table 1). Scope: transportation planning, resource allocation, infrastructure, and the integration of new mobility technologies.
What is being designed: Nothing designed. A diagnostic study producing a typology (performative versus authentic equity work) and recommendations: action-oriented equity work, resource redistribution to disinvested communities, redistribution of decision-making power, flexibility in how funds can be spent, dignity-infused engagement, and community-led agendas. It points to models: the Thrivance Group's Dignity-Infused Community Engagement training, People for Mobility Justice's 'Five Ds', and a Central Valley group that builds 'equity-led agendas at monthly meetings with community members' (p. 11).
Values surfaced in the case: Status-quo and efficiency values, named as 'performative equity': it 'privileges the comfort and perspective of dominant groups, reinforces the status quo, stays in the realm of the rhetoric' (abstract); a 'checklist approach'; 'retrofitting equity' and 'downscaling equity efforts to just outreach' (Table 1, p. 11); a wish to 'quickly solve equity so that their colleagues could get on with the things they really cared about'; 'Maybe we don't need to do 100 percent equity. Maybe we do 50 percent equity, because ... I'm not willing to sacrifice what I want to give you what you deserve' (p. 11); grant restrictions that 'prevent them from addressing community needs' (p. 12). The acultural planning frame: 'You are numbers, you are auto throughput, you are cars on the road, you are not a person with identity and history and culture' (p. 8). Community and authentic values: dignity ('Equity includes dignity. So me not having to explain or make anyone privy to my trauma in order to qualify for equity', p. 5), relational trust (engagement where 'residents can benefit from the time that they spend sharing their feedback', versus being brought in 'after all the decisions are made'), and flexibility for variable need ('Equity is not one-size-fits-all', 'give everyone their shoe size and what they need', flexibility in fund use). Maps to relational trust, equitable access, and flexibility for variable need.
Ideal traveler per decision-makers: Not a traveler study, but strong adjacent evidence. Planning is described as 'acultural': 'You are numbers, you are auto throughput, you are cars on the road, you are not a person with identity and history and culture' (p. 8). Decision-making bodies are 'older, able-bodied, straight white men' and 'the people that we're theoretically all serving are not the people leading those decisions' (p. 12). Performative equity 'privileges the comfort and perspective of dominant groups' (abstract). So the implicit subject of planning is an abstract throughput unit, and the implicit constituency whose comfort is protected is the white, able-bodied dominant group. The paper does not use the phrase 'ideal traveler'.
Actual travelers encountered: The 28 BPOC professionals carry 'emotional labor', code-switch, craft messaging so colleagues are not upset, and do 'emotional work at home'; they are hired but not retained ('get these folks of color in the door so we can say we did it'); given 'lofty goals ... but no decision-making power'; and bring the aftermath of a police shooting 'to work'. The communities they describe want funding parity, funds 'spent in ways that the community wishes', and engagement that leads to benefit; unhoused people whose exclusion is recast as 'public safety'; and Black people subject to what Charles Brown calls 'arrested mobility' (p. 12).
Gap between the two: Agencies 'state that equity is a value' and are 'increasingly dedicating time and resources to hiring equity experts', but 'organizational structures or policies often become barriers' and equity is 'performed' while 'meaningful action remains undone'. Professionals of color are hired but not retained and given responsibility without power. Planning treats people as 'auto throughput' rather than 'a person with identity and history and culture'. Decision-makers are demographically unlike those served. Community engagement is often post-hoc: 'after all the decisions are made and you can't really impact much' (p. 11).
Quotable moment: "You are numbers, you are auto throughput, you are cars on the road, you are not a person with identity and history and culture." (p. 8, interviewee). And on who decides: "a truly equitable transportation system would not only look different in the street, it would look different in the boardroom" (p. 5).
Cross-comparison note (our synthesis): This paper locates the efficiency-versus-community-values clash inside the agency: 'performative equity' is efficiency values ('checklist', 'outreach box', 'quickly solve equity') displacing the slower relational work. The 'auto throughput' quote is a compact statement of the engineering frame our paper critiques, spoken by an insider. The retention findings show that bringing community-aligned expertise into the agency does not shift outcomes without a transfer of decision-making power, which supports our claim that representation is not participation. Counter-models worth citing: the Thrivance Group's dignity-infused engagement and the Central Valley 'equity-led agendas'. Caveats: 28 professionals, California only, recruited through the authors' networks and skewing young and early-career; interviews in mid-2020, a moment of unusual salience for racial-equity discourse; the authors write from an explicit standpoint and the lead author co-authored the Principles of Mobility Justice.

Paper Title: Is the medium the message? Exploring the intersection of social media and collective action in the San José Bike Party
Study type / basis for inclusion: Primary fieldwork. Weakest fit in the fieldwork set: a leisure-studies study of social media and collective action, contributing one vivid ideal-traveler quote and the prefigurative-politics frame.
Case setting: The San José Bike Party (SJBP), a monthly mass ride of 2,000 to 4,000 cyclists on a pre-announced 15 to 30 mile route through San José, California (city population about one million, roughly 40 percent White and 36 percent Asian). Self-defined as 'one-half political party, one-half street party'. Incorporated in 2014, a 501(c)(3) since 2016, run by volunteer organizers working with local partners including law enforcement, government entities, and advocacy organizations. Modeled and copied by Bike Parties in cities worldwide. Fieldwork was pre-COVID, part of a larger multi-year study.
Method(s), session by session: Interpretivist qualitative inquiry. Semi-structured one-on-one interviews with 21 men and women of varying Bike Party experience, about one to one and a half hours, digitally recorded and transcribed verbatim, conducted in varied settings including on bicycles, at party and regroup stops during rides, in rooms, by phone, and over email. Two focus groups (5 and 6 participants). 'Moving methodologies': researchers joined several rides as participants and interviewed others 'on the move'. Structured field notes and video recordings of events and of the moving interviews were analyzed. Open-ended questions covered social and political space, social media and the internet, activism and collective action, and physically active space. Thematic analysis produced three themes: Critical Analysis of Social Media's Influence, Political Expressions in the SJBP, and Prefigurative Politics in the SJBP (p. 8).
Tools and artifacts: Semi-structured and focus-group interview guides; moving or on-bike interviewing; field notes; video of events and moving interviews; the SJBP website, Facebook page, and night-before social-media route and theme announcements as objects of study. Framing texts and concepts: McLuhan and Fiore's The Medium is the Message, connective-action theory (Bennett and Segerberg), and prefigurative politics (Yates).
Underlying principle of the method: Qualitative inquiry as understanding how people 'interpret and make sense of their experiences' (Sparkes and Smith). Prefigurative politics: expressing political 'ends' through 'means' and partially actualizing a movement's goals. Connective action: participation 'highly flexible and personalized', able to proceed without 'collective identity framing'. The authors 'steer away from the over-optimistic assumption that the internet can serve as a democratizing force for activism where no digital divide exists' (p. 6). A mobilities and geography lens treats the street as contested space.
Provocation used to generate new ideas: The ride itself is a prefigurative provocation: 'In the attempt to norm the act of bicycling in the midst of a sedentary and car-dependent society, Bike Party does just that ... it suggests that road spaces should be shared and celebrated' (p. 13), with monthly themes and costumes. This is the movement's tactic, not a research method; the authors observed and rode rather than staging anything.
Who holds design authority: City planners and traffic engineers design the streets: 'Streets assume that there will not be people riding bikes around there' (Speaker 2, p. 12), and 'the argument of planners remains that because there are few cyclists, infrastructure is not needed' (p. 14). The SJBP's volunteer organizers design the monthly route, theme, rest stops, and rules (many 'lifted from the Midnight Ridazz website') and coordinate with law enforcement and city entities. Participants 'agree on our tactics but ... don't agree on our goals' (Nick, p. 13). The paper notes it is 'unclear ... if and how the SJBP movement is actually creating a tangible (call for) change in infrastructure, planning and development' (p. 14). Scope: street space, cycling infrastructure, and an event and organizational template, not infrastructure delivery or policy.
What is being designed: By the SJBP: a monthly ride (route, theme, rules, rest stops) and a replicable website, philosophy, and organizational template that other cities copy 'nearly verbatim'. By the study: nothing; it analyzes the movement and proposes future research into SJBP's power to advocate for a 'safe cycling foundation' for the 'interested but concerned', especially 'equity-seeking groups' (p. 14).
Values surfaced in the case: Automobility and efficiency values in the built environment: streets that 'privilege motor vehicles'; 'cycling takes place in opposition to the normative meanings and practices of the road' (p. 14); and the planners' circular logic that low cycling rates justify not building cycling infrastructure, when 'a small percentage of cyclists are due to infrastructure that does not allow for safe or effective cycling' (p. 14). The SJBP's stated values: 'sustainable, empowering and inclusive, collaborative and transparent and local', 'building community through cycling', and to 'demonstrate a tangible alternative to car-based transportation' freeing 'people from costly fees, stuffy cars, sedentary lifestyles, and dreadful commutes' (p. 6). Community values at stake: relational trust and community (a participant 'stopped going because it got so big', finding 'a meaningful community was unattainable', p. 10), pluralism (the ride 'represents something different for everyone', 'we all agree on our tactics but we don't agree on our goals'), and equitable access (the route is 'exclusively posted on electronic platforms', p. 10).
Ideal traveler per decision-makers: One strong data point. 'Streets assume that there will not be people riding bikes around there' (Speaker 2, p. 12), that is, street design assumes a motorist. 'The argument of planners remains that because there are few cyclists, infrastructure is not needed' (p. 14), a self-fulfilling assumption that treats the cyclist as a negligible edge case. Less than 1 percent of Americans bike to work (FHWA 2011), and planning takes that as the design population. The paper does not use the phrase 'ideal traveler'.
Actual travelers encountered: 2,000 to 4,000 monthly riders 'represented across ages ... of all genders and representative of the population demographics of San José', on decorated bikes and in costume; people who ride partly because of 'the cost of cars'; participants for whom the ride 'represents something different for everyone', from party to protest to community to a 'silent war on oil'; some who left as it grew because 'with more people comes more issues'; and friends who after attending 'now ride to the store, and everywhere they go'. Excluded: people without 'a digital device', since the route is posted only electronically.
Gap between the two: Streets are designed on the assumption that 'there will not be people riding bikes', and planners justify not building cycling infrastructure by pointing to low ridership, which the missing infrastructure itself produces. The SJBP puts thousands of cyclists on the street monthly, but the paper is candid that whether this 'moving collective action' translates into 'a tangible (call for) change in infrastructure, planning and development' is unresolved (p. 14), and its reliance on electronically posted routes reproduces a digital divide.
Quotable moment: "Streets assume that there will not be people riding bikes around there." (p. 12, participant, Speaker 2). On the planner logic: "the argument of planners remains that because there are few cyclists, infrastructure is not needed. Still, cyclists argue that a small percentage of cyclists are due to infrastructure that does not allow for safe or effective cycling" (p. 14).
Cross-comparison note (our synthesis): A compact statement of the ideal-traveler-as-assumption problem: street design 'assume[s] that there will not be people riding bikes', and the planner's ridership-justifies-infrastructure logic is a self-fulfilling loop, exactly the circularity our argument names when a system optimized for the assumed user makes the non-assumed user rarer. The SJBP is a prefigurative counter-move that makes the un-assumed traveler visible en masse. The paper's honesty about not knowing whether the ride changes planning, and about its own digital divide, is a useful caution against treating grassroots visibility as participation. This is the thinnest contributor in the fieldwork set.

Paper Title: Achieving transportation equity: Meaningful public involvement to meet the needs of underserved communities
Study type / basis for inclusion: Literature review plus two California case studies, not the authors' own fieldwork. Contributes strongly: states plainly that community-prioritized needs and agency optimization criteria are different objects.
Case setting: US regional transportation planning by metropolitan planning organizations, focused on California. Two cases: (1) California's SB 535 (2012), a 25 percent set-aside of cap-and-trade auction revenue (over 2 billion dollars in FY2016) for disadvantaged communities, implemented via CARB's December 2015 funding guidelines, with a late-2015 convening of nearly 100 community-based organizations on implementation. (2) Plan Bay Area (2013), the region's first RTP under SB 375; the Metropolitan Transportation Commission concentrated 80 percent of projected housing growth in Priority Development Areas, and the '6 Wins for Social Equity' network of over 20 advocacy groups built an alternative 'Equity, Environment and Jobs' scenario outside official channels.
Method(s), session by session: A review of the public-involvement effectiveness literature, then two case studies of California policy and planning practice, from which the authors synthesize a three-step model. Not the authors' own fieldwork: they draw on published accounts, advocacy documents, prior modeling (MTC's environmental impact report comparing five scenarios; Marcantonio and Karner 2014), and regulatory text (SB 535, CARB 2015 guidance, Executive Order 12898). One author (Marcantonio, Public Advocates Inc.) was a participant in the Bay Area advocacy and litigation, so the second case is partly participant-authored.
Tools and artifacts: The four eligibility questions EJ and civil rights advocates wrote for SB 535 funding ('Does the investment meet an important need identified by a disadvantaged community?', 'Is the benefit a significant one, rather than incidental?', 'Are the benefits targeted to low-income residents?', 'Does the investment avoid substantial harms?'); CARB's example table of commonly identified community needs (Table 1: public health and safety, economic, environmental); the 6 Wins Network's EEJ alternative transportation and land use scenario; MTC's travel demand and land use modeling. Reference frames: participatory budgeting, Arnstein's ladder, Webler's 'fairness and competence', Rowe and Frewer's acceptance and process criteria.
Underlying principle of the method: 'A particular plan or program can only be judged to be equitable to the extent that it is responsive to the needs of low-income and minority residents' (p. 3 of the preprint). An operational approach: identify and address the 'priority unmet needs experienced by underserved populations today' rather than an abstract definition of just outcomes. Meaningful involvement means participants can 'shape decisions and achieve just outcomes'; process justice and outcome justice are inseparable. Participatory-budgeting logic: tie participation to a dedicated revenue stream so the benefits of participating outweigh the costs.
