Community-based organizations 'that have trusting relationships with low-income, transit dependent, senior, and limited English proficiency constituencies' should be resourced to lead (p. 12 of the preprint).
Provocation used to generate new ideas: The SB 535 process surfaced a table of community-identified needs; the 6 Wins Network built a full counter-scenario (EEJ) as a provocation to the MPO's preferred plan, which the agency was then required to model. Participatory budgeting is offered as a transferable device. These were run by advocates and agencies, not by the authors.
Who holds design authority: MPOs such as MTC design regional transportation plans and select projects, and their boards are 'almost never democratically elected nor are they representative of their regional constituents' (note 5 of the preprint). 'Best practices' have participants 'choose between alternative transportation and land use scenarios pre-defined by the agency' (p. 7 of the preprint). The paper argues authority should shift so 'interested parties ... become engaged in shaping the very process', with CBOs co-designing project selection criteria (SB 535) or 'the broad contours of transportation and land use plans' (EEJ). In the cases, advocates wrote the SB 535 eligibility questions (CARB adopted three of four) and the 6 Wins wrote the EEJ scenario (MTC modeled it, named it environmentally superior, adopted several amendments, but 'did not adopt the community's plan', p. 12 of the preprint). Scope: regional transportation and land use plans, project selection, and revenue allocation.
What is being designed: The authors design a three-step model for transportation equity: identify current priority unmet needs through a resourced, community-led, participatory-budgeting-like process; allocate a dedicated near-term revenue stream to meet them; tailor metrics and measure progress year by year. The cases designed SB 535 project eligibility criteria and the EEJ alternative scenario (shift transit capital to operating funds, some housing growth from Priority Development Areas to suburban job centers, condition One Bay Area grants on anti-displacement protections).
Values surfaced in the case: Agency and efficiency values, stated explicitly: community priority needs 'deviate markedly from those typically pursued by public agencies (e.g., cost-effectiveness, positive benefits in a cost-benefit framework, or Pareto optimality)' (p. 10 of the preprint). A 'decide, announce, defend' engineering mentality; equity analysis fixated on 'distant forecast year conditions' over present need; agencies focused on 'legal compliance' 'without adequately considering the other four' purposes; proximity mistaken for benefit (the 500 million dollar Oakland Airport Connector 'traversing a heavily minority and low-income corridor' with 'no intermediate stations'). Community values: equitable access (the whole priority-unmet-needs frame, and Table 1 items like reduced transit costs, service reliability on high-use routes, anti-displacement), relational trust (resourcing CBOs with existing trust; PB tying participation to real allocation), and flexibility for variable need (needs 'self-identified' by communities, 'not one-size-fits-all', metrics 'tailored to quantify the specific changes the community desires'). Maps to equitable access, relational trust, and flexibility for variable need.
Ideal traveler per decision-makers: Not a traveler study, but clear adjacent evidence. Agencies 'typically pursue ... cost-effectiveness, positive benefits in a cost-benefit framework, or Pareto optimality' (p. 10 of the preprint), and equity analysis fixates on forecast-horizon conditions rather than present need. Proximity is treated as benefit: the Oakland Airport Connector 'primarily benefits those traveling between the Oakland International Airport and the regional rail system, not the people of color living along the alignment' (p. 10 of the preprint). MPO boards are 'almost never democratically elected nor ... representative of their regional constituents' (note 5). The implicit subject is an aggregate captured by cost-benefit and travel-demand models at a forecast horizon; in the Airport Connector case the implicit beneficiary is an airport-to-rail traveler, not the corridor's residents. No 'ideal traveler' phrase.
Actual travelers encountered: Community-based organizations representing 'low-income, transit dependent, senior, and limited English proficiency constituencies'; nearly 100 CBOs at the SB 535 convening; the 20-plus groups of the 6 Wins Network seeking 'high quality transit service, affordable housing, healthy and safe communities, protection against displacement, and quality job creation' (p. 11 of the preprint); the residents of the heavily minority, low-income corridor the Airport Connector skipped; and Black Bay Area residents dispersed by displacement between 2000 and 2010, so that 'poorer populations more likely to use transit are displaced from areas where it is most effective'.
Gap between the two: Federal EJ and civil rights law requires 'full and fair participation' and to 'seek out and consider the needs of ... low-income and minority households', but 'traditional public involvement does not work well' (Innes and Booher) and California agencies 'emphasize process-related factors like inclusion but provide no guarantee of substantive effects on outcomes' (p. 7 of the preprint). The needs communities prioritize 'deviate markedly' from agencies' cost-effectiveness, CBA, and Pareto criteria. When a community built a superior alternative (EEJ), the agency modeled it, called it environmentally superior, and still 'did not adopt the community's plan' (p. 12 of the preprint). Even the well-run SB 535 guideline process raised 'issues with transparency and potential digital divides' in project selection (p. 10 of the preprint).
Quotable moment: "Table 1 vividly illustrates that the priority needs of underserved communities deviate markedly from those typically pursued by public agencies (e.g., cost-effectiveness, positive benefits in a cost-benefit framework, or Pareto optimality)" (p. 10 of the author preprint). And, quoting Innes and Booher: "Legally required methods of public participation in government decision making in the US ... do not work" (p. 8 of the preprint).
Cross-comparison note (our synthesis): This paper gives the clearest published statement that community-prioritized needs and agency optimization criteria are different objects: cost-effectiveness, CBA, and Pareto optimality on one side, a concrete list of lived needs on the other. The EEJ case is a strong data point: a community coalition working outside official channels produced a plan the agency's own models rated superior, and it was still not adopted, which shows a demonstrably better community alternative does not override the agency's authority to set the plan. The three-step model (a dedicated revenue stream tied to community-identified needs) is a concrete participation mechanism worth citing as a contrast to how AV infrastructure arrives. Caveats: this is the author's manuscript version, so page numbers do not match the published Public Works Management and Policy article; the cases are from California, 'a state with a unique history of EJ activism'; one author was a participant in the Bay Area advocacy; the model is proposed, not evaluated.

Paper Title: Limitations of Technical Approaches to Transport Planning Practice in Two Cases: Social Issues as a Critical Component of Urban Projects
Study type / basis for inclusion: Primary fieldwork. Two rail megaproject case studies with the authors' own roughly 30 interviews and an expert focus group; strong on the engineering-values-versus-social-needs contrast.
Case setting: Two urban rail megaprojects evaluated with technical modelling. The North-South Metro Line (Noord-Zuid MetroLijn) under central Amsterdam, first proposed in a 1968 metro plan and opened July 2018 after a 16-year build; a 2008 construction incident damaged homes on the Vijzelgracht, halting the project and triggering the year-long Veerman Committee investigation and a total loss of social licence. And the Parramatta Rail Link in Sydney, from the NSW 1998 Action for Transport 2010 plan, meant to link Parramatta to Epping, later shortened to the Epping to Chatswood Rail Link and folded into Sydney Metro North West (opened 2019).
Method(s), session by session: Multi-methods qualitative. Document analysis of primary and secondary sources (Dutch and English for Amsterdam). About 30 semi-structured interviews with key informants who 'had directed or influenced the social impact evaluation, project management, and/or governance' of the projects: regulators, politicians, impact-assessment practitioners, construction personnel, local transport authorities, municipal and national government representatives, consultants, aldermen, and a citizens' representative. Australian desktop review and interviews in 2016; Dutch interviews in 2017 to 2018, mostly in person. Interviews recorded (transcribed for Amsterdam, replayed with extensive notes for Sydney), plus field diary notes and reflexive memos. One focus group with five impact-assessment experts at the May 2018 IAIA annual conference in Durban. Data analysed thematically. Eight project-management and SIA stages (Lessard and Miller; Vanclay et al.) grouped into three phases (Strategic Planning; Project Planning and Construction; Operations, Maintenance and Closure) structure the analysis (journal pp. 44 to 45).
Tools and artifacts: Semi-structured interview guides; a focus-group discussion protocol; a synthesis table (Table 1) mapping eight project stages to project-management descriptions, SIA descriptions, and key activities; document corpora; the International Guidelines for SIA (Vanclay et al. 2015); the 'social licence to operate' concept; and a Social Impact Management Plan as the good-practice deliverable.
Underlying principle of the method: Social Impact Assessment: 'a more integrated and people-centred approach to social policy and transport development' based 'around social need'. SIA should start 'early in the shaping stages of projects', engage and 'empower impacted people, especially vulnerable and marginalised groups', 'prior to a decision (to inform that decision)', and run across 'the whole project lifecycle' with adaptive management and follow-up. 'Technical quantitative approaches are inadequate in capturing distributional issues and can misrepresent complex social problems'. Mobility justice (Sheller): participation, deliberation, recognition, and procedural fairness. 'Social licence to operate' is the risk metric.
Provocation used to generate new ideas: Not a provocation study. The framework device is the eight-stage, three-phase model used to locate where in each project's timeline social issues were dropped. No prototypes, scenarios, or community workshops; the expert focus group was diagnostic.
Who holds design authority: Transport engineers, project-management teams, and government departments. 'The decision about the public need for the NZL had been made many years earlier in the metro plan', so 'technical planning for the NZL only focused on geotechnical risks and construction challenges' (journal p. 50). A focus-group participant: decision-making 'does tend to get dominated by a few people who want the large concrete entity between A and B' built 'as quickly as possible' (journal p. 51). A citizens' representative: 'when most of the time governments come with plans, the plan is already ready ... we cannot change it anymore' (journal p. 48). Consultation 'is formally required' but there is 'no requirement to actually modify the project', and SIA practitioners have too little role in early project planning. Scope: rail alignment, stations, construction method, and mitigation.
What is being designed: Two heavy or metro rail lines (alignment, stations, tunnelling method) plus construction-impact mitigation and compensation. The authors design an analytic model: an eight-stage, three-phase framework for when and how to assess and manage social impacts across a megaproject lifecycle, and a recommendation that SIA be 'mandatory and embedded within integrated urban spatial planning' (journal p. 53).
Values surfaced in the case: Engineering and economic values: 'an overemphasis on economic and engineering considerations' (abstract, journal p. 39); 'predict and provide', 'point to point', and 'line-oriented' design approaches that 'ignore wider social contexts'; 'emphasis on cost-benefit analysis as the standard decision-making tool'; assessments that 'rely on the modelled capability of the transport system, rather than ... the actual behaviour of the system' (journal p. 41); a project 'focussed on safety and technical possibilities: can it be made?, can it be constructed?' while 'nobody ever wondered whether the people around it get enough sleep, or if children living there would be happy' (journal p. 50); 'physical engineers ... think about transport from the physical perspective ... Some of them will clearly lose, that's a fact' (journal p. 50); an NZL communication strategy that 'deliberately focussed on the temporary short-term impacts during construction, rather than on the long-term social impacts or needs' (journal p. 50). Community values: relational trust and social licence (the NZL's 'complete loss of social licence' after the Vijzelgracht incident; the PRL's 'loss of public trust and confidence in the government'; 'So why then do you ask us?'), flexibility for variable need ('changing values within the enclaves of the city ... managing that is the biggest challenge'; plans 'made to last for too long'), and equitable access (the PRL's shortening 'resulted in reduced social benefit (less accessibility for Sydney's Western Suburbs) and a less equitable social outcome', journal p. 51). Maps to relational trust, flexibility for variable need, and equitable access.
Ideal traveler per decision-makers: Not a traveler construct as such, but clear evidence of the traveler model embedded in technical planning. Assessments measure 'accessibility and system performance' from 'the modelled capability of the transport system, rather than ... the actual behaviour of the system' (journal p. 41). Engineers 'do look into needs and demands, because they need to have a market for what they are going to be proposing, but that's the extent' (journal p. 50). 'Project advocates promote economic benefits over the alleged social benefits' (journal p. 42), and models' solutions 'systematically ignore how people are differentially affected' (Martens, journal p. 42). The imagined traveler is an aggregate demand figure whose accessibility gain appears in the model at project completion; the residents living beside a 10-to-16-year build, and the groups who 'clearly lose', are outside the frame.
Actual travelers encountered: Residents along the NZL alignment whose homes were damaged and whose sleep and children's wellbeing were never 'part of the project'; Sydney's Western Suburbs residents whose 'accessibility challenges ... have not been adequately addressed' and who lost service when the PRL was shortened; a public that opposed the PRL's preferred bridge alternative through a national park and forced a route change ('the route had to be changed', journal p. 49); citizens told the plan 'cannot be changed anymore'; and the groups who 'clearly lose' in a technical planning process.
Gap between the two: Technical planning fixed 'the public need' years before design, so the work became 'very technical', about whether the tunnel 'can ... be made', while 'nobody ever wondered' about residents' sleep or children (journal p. 50). Consultation is 'formally required' but with 'no requirement to actually modify the project', and comes 'too late in the project life-cycle', so its 'insights ... do not necessarily get transferred into the assessment and management of social issues' (journal p. 52). Both projects lost social licence. When the PRL was re-scoped for 'technical and economic reasons', the lost accessibility for Western Sydney 'was not captured in the second EIA' (journal p. 51).
Quotable moment: "when most of the time governments come with plans, the plan is already ready. They say 'What do you think of our plan?' ... They say, 'Yeah okay, we've already discussed that and we cannot change it anymore'. So we think, 'So why then do you ask us?'" (journal p. 48, Citizens' Representative Interview). And the engineer's frame: "Nobody ever wondered whether the people around it get enough sleep, or if children living there would be happy, that wasn't part of the project." (journal p. 50, Government representative Interview).
Cross-comparison note (our synthesis): The NZL government representative's account, 'everything was focussed on safety and technical possibilities: can it be made?', is a near-verbatim statement of the engineering value-set our paper attributes to AV development, from inside a major transit project. 'So why then do you ask us?' is a clean statement of consultation-without-influence, the exact failure mode our argument names. The paper's mechanism, that 'the decision about the public need ... had been made many years earlier' so all later engagement is downstream of a fixed concept, transfers directly to how AV pilots arrive, and 'social licence to operate' names what is lost. Table 1 even lists 'switch to autonomous vehicles' as a decommissioning-stage upgrade opportunity (journal p. 47), a small tell that AV substitution is imagined as a technical swap. Caveats: 2020, pre-widespread-AV; two rail megaprojects in wealthy cities with mandatory or quasi-mandatory EIA; the roughly 30 informants are project and governance insiders plus five IA experts, with one citizens' representative quoted, so the community voice here is largely secondhand.

Paper Title: Lived expertise of the structurally disadvantaged: towards a more just participatory transport planning process
Study type / basis for inclusion: Primary fieldwork. Three rounds of focus groups following a real street-reallocation participatory process; directly about who is left out of participatory design and the young, healthy template.
Case setting: The Graefekiez neighbourhood, Friedrichshain-Kreuzberg, Berlin (about 19,000 residents, dense and diverse: 27 percent foreign citizenship, 47 percent migration background, average age 38.7, roughly 10 percent over 65). In 2023 the district municipality ran a six-month project repurposing about 400 car parking spaces into resident-managed green spaces and parklets, plus car, scooter, and bike-sharing stations and delivery zones, with objectives of school-route safety and Berlin's 2045 climate neutrality. The Berlin Social Science Center and partners monitored and evaluated it; a participation consultancy facilitated resident engagement; results went to the district councillors' assembly (BVV), which evaluated the project positively. The Werner-Duttmann Siedlung, a social-housing settlement (62 percent on state support, 75 percent migration background), sits in the neighbourhood but outside the core project area.
Method(s), session by session: In-depth qualitative analysis of focus groups following the Graefekiez participatory process, using Verba, Schlozman, and Brady's Civic Voluntarism Model (resources, psychological engagement, recruitment network) as a heuristic held open for relational dimensions. Two target groups, chosen for vulnerability, political underrepresentation, and observed absence from Graefekiez participation: (FG1) mobility-disabled people (self-assessed movement, vision, behaviour, or orientation disability; German-speaking), and (FG2) women from the Werner-Duttmann Siedlung. Recruitment from February 2023 by engaging locals active in neighbourhood life to identify underrepresented groups, then targeted outreach via social media, an August 2023 flyer campaign, and visiting existing community spaces such as a weekly women's breakfast; recruiting disabled participants was 'swift', the women's group 'required more time and relational work'. Three focus-group rounds per group, August to December 2023, two hours each, with a 50 euro expense allowance for the first two. Round one was semi-structured on the CVM but left space for participants to shape it; feedback was asked at the end of each session; round three presented the findings back for 'collective evaluation of the research process'. Venues were in the neighbourhood to reduce barriers (a drop-in centre, an elderly home's community room, a church room). Moderation was outsourced at first, then taken over by the authors 'to create a space with fewer people and reduce perceived hierarchies'. FG1: 17 attendees in round one (over-recruitment), 8 in round two, plus 3 follow-up interviews. FG2: 9 participants aged 20 to 50, mostly with a migration background, bilingual and translating for each other. Recordings transcribed, anonymised, and coded in MAXQDA with inductive-deductive qualitative content analysis (Glaser and Laudel).
Tools and artifacts: A semi-structured focus-group guide built on the CVM's three factors; the CVM as a coding scheme; MAXQDA; a round-three findings presentation for participant validation; a 50 euro expense allowance; accessible neighbourhood venues; a neighbourhood flyer campaign; Arnstein's ladder used to classify the project's own formats (mostly 'informative' or 'deliberative', that is 'tokenism'; only the parklet redesign was 'collaborative', and not the sharing or delivery stations). The Graefekiez project's own formats: a 2021 representative online and street survey presenting street-space scenarios (the preferred one BVV-voted in June 2022), websites, flyers, information events, and neighbourhood consultation hours.
Underlying principle of the method: Mobility justice (Sheller) as distributional plus procedural plus recognitional justice, plus epistemic justice. 'Lived expertise' (Vigar; Lowe, Barajas, and Coren) as a distinct, undervalued knowledge form alongside technical, practice, and political knowledge: 'it encompasses what people value as well as what they know'. 'Who is (not) in the room' (Klaever and Verlinghieri). Transport research is 'heavily influenced by engineering and economics, often emphasising technical and descriptive, quantitative knowledge', and the 'old, linear planning paradigm' considered 'solely these types of knowledge' (journal p. 557). Invited spaces (municipality-initiated) versus claimed spaces (civil-society-initiated) (Gaventa); society-centric planning (Karner et al.) requiring 'discourse between planners and the public'; crip time (Kafer).
Provocation used to generate new ideas: The Graefekiez project's 2021 survey 'presented various scenarios for the future of public street space' as a provocation, and the preferred scenario was BVV-voted. The researchers' focus-group format was not provocation-based; it is analysed as an unintended participation instrument. No prototypes or speculative artifacts in the focus groups; the round-three findings presentation is a reflexive device.
Who holds design authority: The Friedrichshain-Kreuzberg district municipality initiated and owns the project, and the district councillors' assembly votes on continuation and can dismantle it. A participation consultancy facilitated engagement; scientific institutions monitored and evaluated. Residents were 'given power and control' only over the parklet redesign (a collaborative rung on Arnstein's ladder), not the sharing or delivery stations or the core decision (BVV-voted from survey scenarios). Participants' verdict: invited spaces are a 'friendly side offer' where 'nothing fundamental could be decided' (journal p. 565). Scope: street-space reallocation, parklets, sharing stations, and delivery zones.
What is being designed: The Graefekiez street-space reallocation: about 400 repurposed parking spaces, resident-managed parklets and green spaces, car, scooter, and bike-sharing stations, and delivery zones. The researchers design a participation-format recommendation: diversify the teams running participation and complement invited spaces with 'outreach participatory formats that meet people in their individual and everyday lives' (journal p. 567), such as schools, bars, elderly homes, the women's breakfast, and WhatsApp groups.
Values surfaced in the case: Technical-knowledge dominance: transport research 'heavily influenced by engineering and economics, often emphasising technical and descriptive, quantitative knowledge', with the 'old, linear planning paradigm' considering 'solely' those forms (journal p. 557). Invited-space design values: 'favouring a loud, priviliged minority' (abstract); processes that 'reproduce existing power asymmetries and rely heavily on expert knowledge, with a focus on consensus and negotiation logic' (journal p. 556); 'academic vocabulary used by the actors'; formats classified as mostly 'tokenism' on Arnstein's ladder; a redesign oriented to 'young, healthy, tourists'. Community values: recognition and lived expertise (interests 'actually reflected in the design', not 'just somehow on paper'), relational trust ('Nothing is harder to get back than lost trust'; 'I've been talking to and against walls for years'; a 'friendly side offer'), flexibility for variable need (crip time; health-driven time constraints; caregiving; 'some people use their car every fortnight ... but for other groups it can jeopardize their livelihoods'), and belonging ('Without them, the word neighbourhood doesn't come into its own for me'). Maps to relational trust and recognition or epistemic justice, plus flexibility for variable need and equitable access.
Ideal traveler per decision-makers: Near-explicit. A participant on the redesign: 'It [the redesign] is all about young, healthy people, everything is oriented towards young healthy, tourists, young healthy, everything is young healthy, and the others fall behind' (journal p. 564, FG1). Invited spaces are described as places where 'only the physically-able and socio-economically privileged voices and needs are acknowledged', favouring 'a loud, priviliged minority' and requiring an assumed 'language and knowledge' and 'intellectual performance'. The imagined participant and beneficiary is a young, healthy, socio-economically secure, German-fluent, politically articulate resident (or a tourist) with flexible time. The paper does not use the phrase 'ideal traveler'.
Actual travelers encountered: Mobility-disabled residents who 'have been trying for years to have a say when a building is being built ... so that it is perhaps built a bit more inclusively', met by a mayor who said 'If you don't like it, why don't you move to Zehlendorf?' (journal p. 564); women from the social-housing settlement, on state support, bilingual, translating for each other, who 'do not actively seek to engage in political processes (other than voting)' but 'are interested in contributing' when reached; a resident whose health meant they 'put a lot of post aside' and missed the project; families who received only 'the petition against the project, issued by the opposition party' and no municipal information; and people with caregiving duties or public-benefit appointments clashing with events.
Gap between the two: The municipality ran a participation process framed as inclusive, but observation showed attendees were 'predominantly white or-white passing, middle-aged and non-disabled' (journal p. 561). Structurally disadvantaged residents felt 'excluded and ignored': information did not reach their recruitment networks, events assumed an academic vocabulary and time flexibility they lacked, and prior attempts to contribute lived expertise had been rebuffed ('talking to and against walls for years'), producing 'negative political self-efficacy' and lost trust. The redesign is experienced as 'all about young, healthy people'. The same residents experienced the researchers' smaller, in-neighbourhood, similar-peers focus groups as genuine participation and felt 'recognised and acknowledged' (journal p. 566).
Quotable moment: "It [the redesign] is all about young, healthy people, everything is oriented towards young healthy, tourists, young healthy, everything is young healthy, and the others fall behind." (journal p. 564, Dominique, FG1). On trust: "I've been talking to and against walls for years. [...] in the meantime, I no longer speak." (journal p. 564, Dominique, FG1).
Cross-comparison note (our synthesis): A rare case that both documents a participatory design process failing its most-affected residents and shows what a better format looked like, within one study. The 'young, healthy, tourists' quote is a direct statement of the ideal-user template from someone excluded by it, and it maps onto the AV rider our paper describes (able-bodied, smartphone-equipped, predictable trips, flexible time). The 'invited versus claimed spaces' and 'outreach versus invited' distinctions give us concrete vocabulary, and 'negative political self-efficacy' names the accumulated cost of consultation without influence. The finding that the research focus groups were experienced as more real participation than the official process is a useful, slightly uncomfortable data point about method. Caveats: one Berlin neighbourhood and a small experimental parking project, not infrastructure at AV-deployment scale; FG1 excluded people with intellectual disabilities and non-German-speakers by design; FG2 was a single social-housing women's group; and the better format was researcher-run with a 50 euro incentive, not a scalable municipal process.

Paper Title: Mobility justice and accessible public transport networks for people with intellectual disability
Study type / basis for inclusion: Primary fieldwork. A one-day multi-stakeholder focus group deliberately run as 'performative research' to craft, not just record, an industry-wide approach. Strong on the competent-commuter template.
Case setting: Melbourne and Victoria, Australia, and Melbourne's privatised, franchised, 'splintered' public transport network (rail infrastructure state-owned, tram, train, and bus operation privatised in 1999, operators 'compete for patrons rather than strategically plan and coordinate'). About 3 percent of Victoria's population has an intellectual disability (a broad ABS definition covering developmental disability, acquired brain injury, and dementia); close to 60 percent of people with intellectual disability have severe communication limitations. Victoria is 'considered a world leader in accessible public transport'. Institutional actors: the Minister of Public Transport, Public Transport Victoria (statutory authority running the network and the electronic ticketing system), the Minister-appointed Public Transport Access Committee (people with professional or lived experience of sensory or physical disability), and the individualised NDIS funding model (people with intellectual disability its largest participant group).
Method(s), session by session: One focus group run as a one-day event with three structured sessions, 16 participants. Recruitment: a list of the largest PT providers and stakeholders (including the Public Transport Users' Association), then accessibility and inclusion specialists sought via internet searches and author contacts, plus snowballing (adding a volunteer travel-assistance not-for-profit and the transport staff union). Participants: two inclusion or accessibility officers and a general manager from the three largest bus and rail operators; a regional rail inclusion officer; PTV's inclusion officer and a wayfinding expert; a Transport Bus Rail Union representative; the PTUA president; the manager of a trained-volunteer travel-assistance not-for-profit; two representatives of an intellectual-disability advocacy organisation, one contributing his lived expertise of ID. Scope experts presented on communication accessibility before the roundtables. Three structured questions (current initiatives; barriers and opportunities; whether inclusive participation mechanisms exist and how to create them) posed by Wiesel and Legacy across three collective sessions; participants answered individually first, then a moderated open conversation, with facilitators ensuring equal airtime when disagreement arose (for example union versus providers on workloads). A notetaker recorded; the authors analysed the notes thematically. Designed as a 'performative research initiative' (Cameron, Manhood, and Pomfrett), 'geared towards crafting rather than capturing realities' (journal p. 13).
Tools and artifacts: Three structured discussion questions; a pre-session Scope presentation on communication accessibility; notetaking and thematic analysis. Initiatives and artifacts discussed: PTV colour-coded wayfinding, PTV style guidelines, the PTV journey-planner app, the electronic travelcard, a proposed low-tech disability travelcard to present to ground staff during disruption, 'Try Before You Ride' familiarisation events, virtual-reality journey familiarisation, beacon-technology trials for low-vision directional advice, a 'no wrong door' staff approach, the PTV 'Traveling in the Shoes of Others' staff empathy program, the Public Transport Access Committee and provider customer-reference groups, and a provider database of people with access needs.
Underlying principle of the method: Mobility justice (Sheller): mobility injustices 'emerge beyond the confines of transport infrastructure' and are 'shaped by unequal power relationships in wider society', so marginalised groups must be in decision-making, and 'the expertise of non-traditional transport users such as poor people and people with disability, allows the introduction of new problems and ideas'. 'Splintered urbanism' (Graham and Marvin) as the diagnosis of privatised fragmentation. 'Communication access' (Scope): people communicate 'through symbols, routine, gestures, facial expressions, verbal communication and written word', but services rely on written and verbal. 'Distributed responsibility' across a network. Structural accessibility over individualised support: individual solutions 'reduce incentives to make transport systems structurally accessible' (Martens, journal p. 4).
Provocation used to generate new ideas: Yes. The focus group was 'designed as a performative research initiative ... geared towards crafting rather than capturing realities' (journal pp. 6 and 13), aiming to 'record current initiatives' while it 'promoted stakeholder awareness and encouraged collaboration'. The third question, on how inclusive participation mechanisms 'might be created', is a generative provocation and directly produced commitments: a disability advocate 'offered to help find suitable candidates for reference groups', and participants 'recognised the need to pro-actively include people with ID'. The Scope presentation seeded the frame; 'Traveling in the Shoes of Others' and 'Try Before You Ride' are embodied provocation devices discussed within.
Who holds design authority: Public Transport Victoria designs wayfinding, style guidelines, the app, and electronic ticketing; the Minister appoints the Public Transport Access Committee and carries state responsibility; private franchisees operate and maintain assets and 'compete for patrons rather than strategically plan and coordinate ... a poor service for all' (journal p. 7); federal policy sets the Disability Standards for Accessible Public Transport (2002), which dictate 'very specific accessibility requirements such as the width of ramps ... the font size of printed information'. Existing reference groups and the Access Committee 'tend to focus on sensory and physical disabilities, and often do not include people with ID' (journal p. 12) and 'favour the most skilled and vocal'. The researchers convened and facilitated the focus group. Scope: network design, wayfinding, information, staffing, ticketing, and participation mechanisms.
What is being designed: Nothing physically designed by the study. The focus group scoped 'an industry wide approach to inclusive public transport for people with ID' and produced concrete proposals: shared communication standards and style guidelines, a collaborative staff-awareness program, a 'no wrong door' approach, a cross-system low-tech disability travelcard, collaborative 'Try Before You Ride' and VR familiarisation, open-source beacon technology, and either adding people with ID to existing accessibility committees or creating dedicated ID reference groups with coordinated capacity-building and remuneration standards.
Values surfaced in the case: Market and efficiency values: a 'highly deregulated market' where operators 'compete for patrons rather than strategically plan and coordinate ... a poor service for all' (journal p. 7); Standards with 'very specific' compliance metrics (ramp widths, font sizes) where 'mere compliance ... will not make whole journeys accessible' (journal p. 8); a system that 'offer[s] greater mobility to passengers who have the skill and cognitive capacity to combine multiple modes'; PT policies 'that focus on commutes', so people with ID, 'frequently excluded from employment', are 'almost by default overlooked' (journal p. 3); a 'single problem, single answer' drift; integration 'achieved monolithically by the introduction of one app'. Community values: flexibility for variable need (predictability and consistency across a journey, low-pressure environments, keeping information on websites as well as apps because 'not all people have phones'), relational trust and confidence ('fear and lack of confidence have a strong influence on people's use of public transport'; unexpected changes 'trigger anxiety'), recognition and epistemic justice (lived expertise; 'too often, people with disability are asked to contribute without pay'), and interdependence (staff presence, 'no wrong door', paid versus volunteer assistance). Maps to flexibility for variable need, relational trust, and recognition or equitable access.
Ideal traveler per decision-makers: Strong. 'Public transport systems offer greater mobility to passengers who have the skill and cognitive capacity to combine multiple modes of transport on one trip ... and this potentially excludes passengers with ID' (journal p. 2). The mobility justice framing names 'white, masculine and enabled bodies as idealised performers of mobile subjectivities' (Sheller, quoted journal p. 3). 'Independence and spontaneity feature centrally in modern constructions of meaningful movement', which for people with ID reliant on pre-booked support 'limits mobility and spontaneity' (journal p. 3), and PT policy 'focus[es] on commutes' so non-commuters are 'overlooked by default'. The imagined traveler is an employed commuter, literate, smartphone-capable, able to chain modes independently and improvise around disruption. The paper cites Sheller's 'idealised performers' phrase but does not itself say 'ideal traveler'.
Actual travelers encountered: People with intellectual disability (the largest NDIS group), around 60 percent with severe communication limitations, who 'report unpredictable journeys' (delays, platform changes, varying staff communication styles), struggle 'with large amounts of information' and 'having to retain information to act on later', spend 'a high proportion of individual support packages on transport costs, mostly ... taxis and support staff', and for whom 'unexpected changes can trigger anxiety'. Also people without phones or unable to zoom in on timetables, people who 'dislike disclosing their disability', a growing ageing population acquiring cognitive disability, and transport staff under rising workloads. One focus-group participant contributed 'his lived expertise of ID'.
Gap between the two: Victoria is 'a world leader in accessible public transport' and the Standards dictate exacting physical metrics, yet 'mere compliance ... will not make whole journeys accessible' (journal p. 8), and cognitive access barriers 'have started to emerge on agendas only recently'. The network is designed for a traveler with 'the skill and cognitive capacity to combine multiple modes' (journal p. 2), while the privatised, splintered system forces passengers to 'adapt to different communication styles, fonts and delivery' across one journey (journal p. 7). Participation bodies 'tend to favour the most skilled and vocal' and 'often do not include people with ID' (journal pp. 11 to 12). Accessibility investment has 'targetted physical access' over communication access.
Quotable moment: "Public transport systems offer greater mobility to passengers who have the skill and cognitive capacity to combine multiple modes of transport on one trip ... and this potentially excludes passengers with ID." (journal p. 2). On participation: "Existing models for the participation of people with or without disability in government and corporate decision-making processes tend to favour the most skilled and vocal." (journal p. 11).
Cross-comparison note (our synthesis): The 'skill and cognitive capacity to combine multiple modes' line is a precise statement of the competent-user assumption our argument targets, and it maps almost directly onto an app-summoned AV: the rider is assumed to have a smartphone, to handle a dynamic pickup, and to improvise around disruption. The paper's point that individualised support 'reduce[s] incentives to make transport systems structurally accessible' is a useful frame for why AV accessibility features (a phone hail, an app) can look inclusive while shifting the burden onto the user. The 'performative research' method, a convening that produced concrete cross-industry commitments, is itself a small model of the participation our paper argues is skipped. The participation finding, that reference groups 'favour the most skilled and vocal' and exclude people with ID, is the same pattern Klaever and Bailey document. Caveats: a single one-day focus group of 16 practitioners, only one with lived experience of ID and no direct participation by people with ID; Melbourne's specific privatised governance; 2020, pre-AV; the study proposes an approach rather than evaluating outcomes.

Paper Title: Mindsets and actions: Shifts in equitable and sustainable development in U.S. cities
Study type / basis for inclusion: Primary fieldwork, but transport is one of several sectors. Contributes on the relational-trust value and on how efficiency framing crowds out equity in practice, not on a traveler.
Case setting: 23 primarily senior professionals working on sustainable and equitable urban development in US cities, interviewed August to September 2022. Sectors: built environment (11), transport and mobility (9), health and social care (8), housing (8), plus culture, parks, water, energy, and others. Organizations: local government (9), non-profit (9), private (1). States across all four Census regions (California, Florida, Kentucky, Massachusetts, New York, North Carolina, Ohio, Oregon, Pennsylvania, Tennessee, Washington), mostly with Democratic governors, five in Republican-governor states. Recruited through the authors' networks and Robert Wood Johnson Foundation grantees. The fieldwork predates the 2025 federal policy changes the discussion notes will disrupt this work.
Method(s), session by session: Semi-structured interviews with 23 professionals, August to September 2022; 49 invited (28 purposive, 21 snowball; final 11 purposive plus 12 snowball), targeting people with 'director' or 'manager' titles across sectors, geographies, and organization types. Recruitment by email. Interviews audio-recorded and transcribed. The lead author analysed transcripts in NVivo using reflexive thematic analysis (Braun and Clarke); a separate deductive content analysis identified 'specific approaches for operationalizing equity and sustainability'. A preliminary version fed a global sustainable and equitable development study (case-city selection). Findings grouped into four themes: distrust undermines dialogue; 'words matter' (framing and narrative); bottom-up efforts are transforming equitable development; and frameworks and approaches.
Tools and artifacts: A semi-structured interview guide; a demographic survey; NVivo; reflexive thematic analysis plus deductive content analysis. Practitioner artifacts documented: framing and narrative strategies (a 'targeted universalism' weightlifting analogy; a 'bootstraps' counter-narrative; 'narrative braiding'; 'it's an opportunity model. It's not a welfare and charity model'), redlining and homeownership data used 'to remove a sense of ideology or bias', a 'Flower Power framework' (base building, civic engagement, narrative change, policy advocacy, healing), a three-part equity framework ('normalize, organize, operationalize'), asset maps of nonprofits, community land trusts, land banks, and youth tactical-urbanism redesign of mobility infrastructure.
Underlying principle of the method: Social determinants of health; 'just sustainabilities' (Agyeman) integrating sustainability, equity, and justice; 'healthy urbanism' (Pineo) as inclusive plus equitable plus sustainable, where inclusive means processes and design that 'enable all members of society to conveniently participate in daily activities without feeling that they are disadvantaged by their personal characteristics or needs'. 'Just design and development must repair inequity and discrimination' and requires 'transformation of positionalities and power relationships through broad invitations to participate'. Framing and narrative as levers for 'cultural mindsets' (FrameWorks Institute). A critique that North American planning 'has been overly focused on the distributive and procedural components' (journal p. 5) and that 'equity has received lower prioritization ... compared to economic and environmental goals' (journal p. 5).
Provocation used to generate new ideas: The tactical-urbanism youth project is a design provocation: a youth-led redesign of 'mobility infrastructure on a road with high pedestrian fatalities' that 'elevated it' for the state agency and 'showed what was possible', moving from a small grant to 'a significant funding commitment' (journal p. 11). Framing analogies (the weightlifting and targeted-universalism story) are rhetorical provocations aimed at politicians. The interviews themselves are not provocation-based.
Who holds design authority: City governments, mayors, elected officials, and city staff hold final authority: a mayor 'allocated budget for the community land trust', and a new mayor adopting an advocacy group's recommendation let it 'completely reverse' a relationship with city staff. 'City processes and regulations were stacked against sustainable and equitable development solutions' (journal p. 11). Home builders' associations are named as an 'adversary' wanting 'changes that only benefit them individually'. CBOs 'had to work very hard to garner local government support for transformational solutions' and do repeated 'education' of city leaders ('Groundhog Day'). Scope: housing, zoning, parks, mobility infrastructure, and the framing of city plans.
What is being designed: Nothing by the study. Practitioners design equitable development plans and frameworks, community land trusts, anti-displacement packages, bus shelters (rural residents 'fighting' for shade), youth-redesigned mobility infrastructure on a high-fatality road, and above all city-plan narratives (shifting a city's story 'from healthcare to social determinants', to 'creating choices for people' and 'a vibrant urban community that's low stress').
Values surfaced in the case: Economic and efficiency values: 'Equity has received lower prioritization in urban plans and programs compared to economic and environmental goals' (journal p. 5); an SCRPG analysis where 'equity was not articulated, while sustainability and quality of life were prioritized' (journal p. 5); a chamber-of-commerce official who must frame equity as 'creating competitive urban places' and 'an opportunity model. It's not a welfare and charity model' to 'sell the idea' to politicians (journal p. 10); the 'bootstraps narrative' of success 'through sheer will and determination' that 'most public health narratives ... do little to change' (journal p. 13). Community values: relational trust (a whole theme: 'Distrust undermines dialogue'; 'what you need to do to counter that is to talk to people and build a relationship'; trust degraded by 'historical harms, undelivered promises, and a deficit of recognition'; feeling 'overlooked for many years'), recognition, and community power ('moving beyond procedural justice to a more fundamental power shift'). Also the emotional toll: 'very fresh and raw' after public meetings, 'Groundhog Day', 'five extra hours in a day ... to get to the same point'. Maps to relational trust, equitable access, and recognition.
Ideal traveler per decision-makers: Not a traveler study, and the mobility material is thin. The 'bootstraps narrative' is the implicit subject of much US policy: an individual whose 'success ... through sheer will and determination' is assumed 'rather than acknowledging that opportunities for success are severely constrained by race and class' (journal p. 13). Public health narratives focus on 'individual agency and behavior change' and reduce 'structural barriers to lifestyle choices' (journal p. 3). Rural residents outside a wealthy city had to 'fight' for bus shelters 'to provide shade' (journal p. 10), implying a default assumption of a traveler who does not wait outside. No 'ideal traveler' phrasing.
Actual travelers encountered: Low-income and racially minoritized residents who 'disproportionately face barriers to good health'; residents who felt 'overlooked for many years'; rural residents 'fighting' for bus shelters to provide shade; young people redesigning a high-pedestrian-fatality road; tenants with 'heartbreaking stories' of how affordable housing 'changed their lives'; CBO leaders doing unpaid, repeated explanatory work; and communities subject to 'down-zoning' that 'perpetuated that redlining ... we didn't realize it'.
Gap between the two: Cities 'now emphasize equitable planning and community engagement', but 'practitioners often lack the tools to implement just, equitable, and health-promoting policies effectively' (abstract); equity plans get 'conducted, yet significant changes on the ground did not occur' (Baltimore, journal p. 5); equity is prioritized below economic and environmental goals; and framing equity for politicians requires disguising it as 'opportunity' and 'competitiveness', 'not welfare' (journal p. 10). CBOs spearheading transformational solutions must repeatedly re-educate city leaders against processes 'stacked against' them, while trust is degraded by 'undelivered promises and a deficit of recognition'.
Quotable moment: "[people] have all kinds of terrible made-up ideas about what we do ... what you need to do to counter that is to talk to people and build a relationship ... they start seeing you as a human being that they can talk to." (journal p. 8, participant 9, affordable housing developer). And the framing bind: "we're not saying you have to give anything, we're talking about access to opportunity. It's not a welfare and charity model. It's an opportunity model." (journal p. 10, participant 8, chamber of commerce official).
Cross-comparison note (our synthesis): A contributor mainly on the relational-trust value and on how efficiency framing crowds out equity in practice. The finding that practitioners must repackage equity as 'opportunity' and 'competitiveness' to move politicians is a concrete instance of efficiency values setting the terms of debate, useful for our argument that community values enter only in translation. The trust theme, degraded by 'undelivered promises and a deficit of recognition' and rebuilt only by slow relationship work, supports our relational-trust claim and gives language for it. The youth tactical-urbanism redesign that 'showed what was possible' and unlocked state funding is a small positive model of community-led design changing an agency's mind, parallel to the 6 Wins EEJ case in Karner et al. Caveats: transport is one of several sectors and the mobility material is thin; 23 self-selected professionals recruited through a health-foundation network, skewing to Democratic-governor states and to people already doing equity work; no residents or travelers interviewed directly.

Paper Title: Implementing proximity planning under constraint: The case of Kiezblocks in Berlin
Study type / basis for inclusion: Primary fieldwork (practitioner-researcher). The authors ran the Pankow process; analysis draws on their own participation reports, traffic observations, and 30 Kiezblock projects citywide. A detailed co-production case and its ceiling. NOTE: this PDF is misfiled in the tracker under the Di Ruocco 'Mobilising equity' row.
Case setting: The Berlin-Pankow district (about 410,000 residents), where three Kiezblocks (Winsviertel, Boetzowkiez, Gruene Stadt) were developed through a structured participatory process and formally adopted by the district council between 2022 and 2023. Dense, comparatively young inner-city, with low car ownership (BZR 16 Prenzlauer Berg Sud: 285 cars per 1000 residents, density about 20,300 per square km, 22 percent foreign nationals). Berlin's traffic administration is 'historically fragmented between district-level and state-level competencies', and section 45 of the German Road Traffic Regulations (StVO) requires traffic measures to be 'justified by documented safety concerns or the protection of vulnerable users', with 'quality of life' or 'urban atmosphere' not legally sufficient (the StVO was amended mid-2025 but 'not yet been tested'). London Low Traffic Neighbourhoods and Barcelona Superblocks are used as secondary comparative reflections.
Method(s), session by session: Qualitative interpretive case study from a practitioner-researcher position, triangulating: (1) structured process documentation and an interim report (concept development, planning, political negotiations, administrative steps); (2) a comprehensive participation report covering public workshops, neighbourhood walks, citizen assemblies, and online feedback 'involving over 900 residents'; (3) stationary traffic observations and school-route diagnostics at conflict hotspots and around schools (peak hours, illegal parking, turning maneuvers, sightlines); (4) focus-group transcripts and thematic evaluations from parallel Berlin projects (Bergmannstrasse, Graefekiez, Wrangelkiez) 'capturing ... underrepresented voices such as elderly, mobility-impaired persons, and local businesses'; (5) a supplementary Berlin-wide meta-study on public acceptance, conflict, and narrative framing (STRATMO 2025). Analysis: process tracing plus hybrid deductive-inductive thematic coding, with an analytical lens on participation and legitimation (how formats were designed, who participated and who did not, how input was translated into legally viable proposals). Observation sites were chosen by a two-step rationale: sites repeatedly flagged in participatory mapping, and locations around schools. Statements are paraphrased and de-identified 'to avoid attributability in a contested local policy environment'.
Tools and artifacts: Four participatory formats: moderated neighbourhood walkshops (Kiezspaziergaenge); thematic workshops and planning roundtables (residents, civic groups, administrative staff, planners refining goals and reviewing traffic-calming scenarios); online feedback and map-based consultations (location-specific comments, conflict-zone prioritisation); and targeted engagement with local businesses on delivery logistics, access, and customer visibility, directly informing modal filters and loading zones. Plus tactile mapping with string models; digital participatory mapping producing hazard heatmaps; stationary traffic observations and video counts; photographic and micro-mapping documentation of intersections; GIS crash maps and heatmaps as 'a common planning reference for both civil society and administration'; the #Kiezblocks initiative's 19 pre-drafted conceptual layouts; and section 45 StVO as the legal-framing template for every measure.
Underlying principle of the method: Transformative and practice-oriented urban studies grounded in real-world experimentation and participatory planning (Finn; Silva). Proximity planning (the 15-minute city, Superblocks, Low Traffic Neighbourhoods) analysed 'not as a technocratic optimization tool, but as a politically contested process shaped by competing imaginaries' (abstract). Procedural justice and deliberative democracy: 'who speaks for the neighborhood', and how procedural design affects 'not only the quality of deliberation but also the substantive outcomes'. 'Institutionalized co-production': civil society initiates, the administration anchors it institutionally, and planners translate public input into implementation-ready concepts (journal p. 5). 'Legitimacy is not automatically created through participation or data. Rather, it must be continuously negotiated' (journal p. 6).
Provocation used to generate new ideas: Strong. The #Kiezblocks initiative had 'already drafted 19 conceptual layouts for traffic-calmed neighborhoods' (journal p. 4) as bottom-up provocations that became 'the starting point for formal planning and negotiation'. Walkshops 'grounded the process in everyday lived experience'; tactile string-model mapping and digital hazard heatmaps elicited 'everyday mobility experiences'. Parallel Berlin projects used 'temporary infrastructure (e.g. parklets, modal filters), small-scale surveys, and real-world testing formats to initiate debate and spatial reimagination' (journal p. 7). Residents' 'ambitious interventions such as area-wide modal filters, full street closures' functioned as provocations that planners then translated.
Who holds design authority: A 'civic-initiated, institutionally adopted' configuration (journal pp. 3 to 4). The #Kiezblocks campaign (NGO Changing Cities) and local groups drafted early concepts; the Pankow district administration 'took up these demands as a formal planning agenda', commissioned STRATMO (with gruppe F) using Berlin Senate district-investment funds, and 'explicitly invit[ed] civil society to take part in the design process'. Planning experts 'translated public input into implementation-ready concepts'; the district council formally adopts. But implementation 'hinged on scarce personnel, coordination hurdles, and approval from higher-level traffic authorities', and section 45 StVO means 'participatory demands, however well articulated, could not stand alone as justification' (journal p. 6). Scope: neighbourhood traffic calming (modal filters, one-way systems, curb extensions, school streets, street reclassifications).
What is being designed: Three neighbourhood-scale Kiezblock traffic-calming concepts: selective modal filters at cut-through links, one-way regulations, time-restricted 'school street' interventions during peak arrival and departure, redesigned crossings, curb extensions, and loading zones near retail. At the process level, an 'institutionalized co-production' procedural model that was adopted for future Berlin projects.
Values surfaced in the case: Technocratic and legal-formal values: proximity planning framed by discourse as 'a technocratic optimization tool'; section 45 StVO's demand for 'documented safety concerns', so 'general objectives such as improving quality of life, environmental conditions, or urban atmosphere are not, in themselves, legally sufficient grounds for road space reallocation' (journal p. 8); Berlin's 'historically fragmented' administration, 'staffing shortages', and 'limited resources'; the finding that 'push' measures 'generally meet stronger resistance than pull measures'. Community values: flexibility for variable need (residents' 'everyday mobility concerns', 'competing everyday needs', business 'delivery logistics, access needs'), relational trust ('legitimacy ... must be continuously negotiated'; 'transparent communication, inclusive design processes ... necessary but not sufficient'; civil-society 'frustration over slow timelines and procedural inertia'), and equitable access and representation ('organized, resourceful, and often middle-class actors were overrepresented in participatory forums, while lower-income, migrant, or mobility-constrained groups were under-engaged', journal p. 9). Maps to relational trust, flexibility for variable need, and equitable access or recognition.
Ideal traveler per decision-makers: Adjacent evidence rather than a named construct. Section 45 StVO frames the only legitimate subject of road-space reallocation as a 'vulnerable road user' whose safety is 'documented', which paradoxically means only measurable-hazard travelers count. The '15-minute city' or 'city of short distances' logic assumes a resident who can 'access daily necessities ... within a short walking or cycling distance', an able-bodied, proximate resident. Contestation came 'especially among car-owning residents in suburban areas', and 'mostly older residents questioned changes to parking or navigation', implying the status quo serves a car-owning traveler. No 'ideal traveler' phrasing.
Actual travelers encountered: Over 900 residents across the participation formats; the #Kiezblocks initiative and local groups (Netzwerk Fahrradfreundliches Pankow, AG Verkehr der Bremer Hoehe, Stadt fuer Menschen); parents reporting 'high levels of perceived danger at drop-off zones'; business owners worried about 'delivery access and visibility'; 'mostly older residents' worried about parking and navigation; and, named as under-engaged, 'lower-income, migrant, or mobility-constrained groups'. In the lower-turnout Gruene Stadt, few residents engaged and 'the specificity of proposals' suffered.
Gap between the two: Residents and civil society 'called for ambitious interventions such as area-wide modal filters, full street closures', but 'several of these proposals exceeded what the district could plausibly justify and enact' under section 45 StVO, so planners 'developed a differentiated, legally defensible alternative package', 'scaling back the most transformative ideas' (journal p. 6). Even after adoption, implementation stalled on 'scarce personnel, coordination hurdles, and approval from higher-level traffic authorities'. Participation 'skewed toward civically active residents, leaving gaps in demographic and experiential representation', so 'when participatory design does not actively engage marginalized constituencies, it can inadvertently reproduce or even exacerbate spatial and social inequalities' (journal p. 9). And 'data alone could not resolve disagreements over values or interests' (journal p. 6).
Quotable moment: "participatory demands, however well articulated, could not stand alone as justification. Instead, they had to be underpinned by empirical evidence of hazard or dysfunction." (journal p. 6). And: "legitimacy is not automatically created through participation or data. Rather, it must be continuously negotiated, between actors, institutions, and knowledge systems." (journal p. 6).
Cross-comparison note (our synthesis): An unusually detailed account of a genuine co-production process and its ceiling. The key finding for us: even a civic-initiated, administration-adopted process is bounded by a legal frame (section 45 StVO) that only recognises 'documented safety' hazards, so residents' broader quality-of-life demands must be re-justified in the regulator's terms or dropped, a concrete instance of community values entering only in translation into safety and efficiency metrics. The school-street compromise and 'island effects' negotiation show what 'responsiveness' looks like when authority stays with the administration. The representation finding (middle-class civic actors overrepresented; migrant, low-income, mobility-constrained groups under-engaged) matches Klaever, Bailey, and van Holstein. Positive: a co-production model was institutionalised for future projects. Caveats: the authors are the commissioned planners; statements are paraphrased and de-identified; the empirical window is concept development and adoption only (2022 to 2023, not implementation); and Pankow is 'a best-case under constraint', not representative of Berlin. This PDF (1-s2.0-S2667091726000014-main.pdf) is filed in the canonical tracker against the Di Ruocco 'Mobilising equity' row, whose participatory-method columns actually describe this Kiezblocks paper.

Paper Title: Mobilising equity. Emerging evidence for integrating vulnerable communities
Study type / basis for inclusion: Narrative literature review, not fieldwork and no design process. Contributes on the digitally-literate, solvent, urban user encoded by ICT mobility platforms, and on participation-beyond-consultation.
Case setting: Global scope (published in the Italian journal TeMA). Reviews evidence on transportation for six vulnerable groups: people with disabilities, economically disadvantaged people, the elderly, women and youth, ethnic minorities, and rural or remote residents. Central concern: smart-city and ICT mobility advances are 'predominantly focused on urban areas, often overlooking the critical need for integrating transportation systems with surrounding rural regions', and research over-focuses on the elderly 'while neglecting other vulnerable groups such as ethnic and gender minorities, women, young people'. About 16 percent of the global population faces restricted mobility.
Method(s), session by session: A single method: a narrative literature review (not systematic, no search protocol, databases, or inclusion counts reported), incorporating 'academic and grey literature, including policy documents and case studies'. Analysis organised around three dimensions: equity-focused policies (age, health, gender, economic status); community engagement frameworks that 'align mobility solutions with the lived experiences of vulnerable groups, fostering trust and sustainable adoption'; and technology adoption strategies bridging urban-rural divides. Section 3 identifies six target vulnerable groups from established literature (Hine and Mitchell; Lucas et al.; Van Wee and Geurs), tabulated with barriers, spatial context, and rationale (Table 1). Section 4 discusses across five sub-dimensions (policy frameworks, spatial planning and proximity, technological integration, infrastructure resilience, community engagement). Section 5 gives recommendations for policymakers, planners, and stakeholders. Central research question: how digital mobility solutions for reduced-mobility users can be integrated to enhance accessibility 'particularly in underserved urban and rural areas'.
Tools and artifacts: A three-dimension analytical framework; a six-group target taxonomy (Table 1); Litman and Lucas equity frameworks; the accessibility-activity participation model (Allen and Farber); a capabilities-based approach (Bantis and Haworth). Reviewed exemplars: Whim (Finland), Helsinki and Vienna MaaS, London contactless payment, Toronto and Barcelona fare programs, India's Common Service Centers as localised ICT hubs, Sao Paulo community-led BRT, Medellin community-driven transit, Barcelona co-designed inclusive transport (Chiscano and Darcy), and the DeepNAVI navigation system for visually impaired users.
Underlying principle of the method: Mobility poverty and transport-related social exclusion (Lucas; Kuttler and Moraglio). Social vulnerability as intersectional, extending beyond named 'vulnerable populations' to 'fragile individuals'. 'Community engagement bridges policy intent with user needs', and 'engagement must go beyond consultation, requiring active citizen participation in planning, monitoring, and evaluation processes'. Co-creation (Chiscano and Darcy); 'involving vulnerable citizens as active participants in shaping more accessible urban environments' (Mora et al.). The review warns that technology can 'introduce biases that restrict accessibility for vulnerable populations'.
Provocation used to generate new ideas: None. It is a review with no participant method, no prototypes, scenarios, or workshops. It reports others' co-creation and community-led exemplars (Barcelona, Medellin, Sao Paulo).
Who holds design authority: In the reviewed practice: cities, transport agencies, MaaS platform operators, and technology developers design digital mobility systems, 'often implemented as isolated solutions rather than being embedded into broader transportation and land-use strategies' (journal p. 103), and 'universal public transportation design often neglects vulnerable users' (journal p. 103). The review argues authority should shift via 'community involvement in the design and deployment phases' and transport 'co-designed with input from people with disabilities' (journal p. 104). The author holds review authority. Scope: digital mobility platforms, fare systems, land-use integration, paratransit, and station design, with recommendations addressed to policymakers.
What is being designed: Nothing. The paper produces a framework and recommendations: affordable and context-specific digital solutions, inclusive design principles, infrastructure readiness, integrated land-use policy, community involvement in design and deployment, and 'clear indicators for evaluating policy effectiveness'.
Values surfaced in the case: Efficiency and market values in the reviewed systems: MaaS and digital payment where 'affluent users benefit from seamless integration' while 'low-income populations often face financial barriers' (journal p. 99); 'subscription-based MaaS platforms' that 'financial barriers often prevent low-income populations from fully benefiting from' (journal p. 105); AI route optimisation and congestion prediction framed as efficiency; 'universal public transportation design' that 'often neglects vulnerable users, leading to unnecessary detours and collision risks' (journal p. 103). Community values: equitable access (the whole premise, that rural and peripheral and non-elderly vulnerable groups are 'underexplored' and 'excluded by design'), flexibility for variable need ('tailored to the unique challenges', 'context-specific'), and relational trust ('community engagement ... fosters trust and sustainable adoption'; 'engagement must go beyond consultation'). Maps to equitable access, flexibility for variable need, and relational trust.
Ideal traveler per decision-makers: Adjacent evidence. ICT-based mobility advances are 'predominantly focused on urban areas' (abstract), and the review identifies 'digital literacy gaps and interface design shortcomings, which often exclude older adults and visually impaired individuals' (journal p. 105) plus a 'digital divide' where 'access to affordable mobile devices and reliable internet connections is often restricted' (journal p. 105). With MaaS, 'affluent users benefit from seamless integration' (journal p. 99). The imagined user is urban, smartphone-owning, connected, and able to afford a subscription. No 'ideal traveler' phrasing.
Actual travelers encountered: All via the literature: people with mobility, sensory, or cognitive impairments; economically disadvantaged people 'disproportionately affected by high transport costs'; the elderly; women and youth facing 'safety concerns, caregiving responsibilities, and financial dependence'; ethnic minorities facing 'systemic discrimination and cultural exclusion'; rural and remote residents where transit is 'unreliable, sparse, or economically unfeasible' and who are 'confined to small, localized areas'; wheelchair users facing 'unnecessary detours and collision risks'; and immunocompromised people pushed 'to rely on private vehicles'.
Gap between the two: Smart-city and MaaS advances are 'predominantly focused on urban areas', 'often implemented as isolated solutions rather than being embedded into broader transportation and land-use strategies', and benefit 'affluent users' while excluding low-income and rural users via the digital divide. Research over-focuses on the elderly, 'neglecting other vulnerable groups such as ethnic and gender minorities, women, young people'. Engagement 'rarely goes beyond consultation'. Exemplars are 'presented in fragmented narratives, lacking systematic evaluation frameworks' (journal p. 98).
Quotable moment: "engagement must go beyond consultation, requiring active citizen participation in planning, monitoring, and evaluation processes." (journal p. 104). On the market skew: "while affluent users benefit from seamless integration, low-income populations often face financial barriers, limiting their accessibility and equity impact." (journal p. 99).
Cross-comparison note (our synthesis): A contributor that assembles, across many studies, the case that digital mobility platforms encode an urban, connected, solvent user, exactly the profile our argument attributes to app-summoned AVs. Its distinction between consultation and 'active citizen participation in planning, monitoring, and evaluation' is a compact version of the participation ladder our paper uses. Most useful for breadth (rural and non-elderly vulnerable groups) and for the MaaS-affluent-user finding. Caveats: a non-systematic narrative review with no methodology transparency, single Italy-based author, and a participation treatment that is brief and aspirational rather than evidenced. Note also that the canonical tracker's participatory-method columns for this paper actually describe a different study, the Rammert and Hausigke Kiezblocks paper, because of a title-to-PDF mapping error.

Paper Title: North Florida Stakeholder Perspectives: Gaps, Barriers, and Facilitators in the Transportation System
Study type / basis for inclusion: Primary fieldwork and a decision-maker paper. 13 interviews with Florida transportation stakeholders; contributes on how officials describe priorities and the fiscal-minimalism floor of service.
Case setting: North Florida, mainly Gainesville plus statewide framing. Florida has about 22.6 million residents (projected 31.4 million by 2050) and about 135 million annual visitors, and is deeply car-dependent (79 percent drive alone to work, 1.7 percent use transit, 2018 ACS). Mobility-vulnerable populations: people below the federal poverty threshold, people with disabilities, and older adults (65+ expected to grow 60 percent by 2045; 3 million drivers 65+, 90 percent using a personal vehicle). Gainesville is a University town in the Smart Cities Collaborative. Interviews were conducted by Zoom during COVID-19 (2021).
Method(s), session by session: Qualitative semi-structured interviews, N equals 13, with regional transit employees, city planners, state (FDOT) employees, industry (including AV operators), advocates (Gainesville Citizens for Alternative Transportation, Regional Mobility Group, AARP Florida, Pepper Institute on Aging), and specialty-population representatives (Florida Commission for the Transportation Disadvantaged, ADA Transit, VA). Purposive plus snowball sampling from existing networks and online public records; email and phone recruitment with a screening script. Eligibility: associated with Gainesville or Florida transportation services serving mobility-vulnerable populations, reliable internet and Zoom, English. Aimed for 15 for data saturation. The interview guide was built on a prior Jeghers et al. resident study and a strengths, weaknesses, opportunities, and threats (SWOT) frame (Barrella et al.): about 5 minutes welcome, 50 minutes of questions, 5 minutes close. Audio-recorded via Zoom; demographic questionnaire in Qualtrics; third-party transcription then team review; content analysis in NVivo 12 (identifying, coding, and counting SWOT perceptions); demographics in SPSS.
Tools and artifacts: A semi-structured interview guide; the SWOT framework; a Qualtrics demographic questionnaire; Zoom; NVivo 12; SPSS; reference tables of themes, quotes, and SWOT counts. Programs and artifacts discussed: the FDOT Safety Agency Resource, the Safe Mobility for Life Coalition (webinars), Target Zero, the 'Complete Streets' concept, travel-training programs, an AARP and Safe Mobility for Life partnership, website feedback forms and smartphone apps for feedback, a Walgreens transit-pass partnership, and Uber and Lyft used to 'complement our services'.
Underlying principle of the method: An occupational-therapy and community-mobility lens (all three authors are OT researchers), with 'mobility-vulnerable populations' framed by need (below poverty, disability, older adults). A stakeholder-perspectives method premised on the observation that 'community residents may value access and ease of transportation, whereas administrators and city officials may prioritize optimizing safe transportation in a city' (journal p. 1522). Data saturation; SWOT as an established structuring device; collaboration and 'shared goals' as the normative aim, with the Safe Mobility for Life Coalition offered as a model.
Provocation used to generate new ideas: Minimal. The SWOT prompts structure the elicitation. No prototypes, scenarios, or design workshops; this is a diagnostic interview study.
Who holds design authority: Federal and state priorities set funding: 'funding opportunities are often allocated based on federal and state priorities and are not long-term' (journal p. 1530), and 'once the funds were allocated, the ability to relocate the funds was often restricted, even if a higher priority need was identified'. City and county commissions 'are looking at what is the minimum that can be done to make it as safe as possible without having to spend real money' (P3). Politicians 'come and go. They have priorities, and they do not always match [the priorities of multiple stakeholders]' (P13). City officials 'prioritize student ridership frequency and funding compared to other populations' (journal p. 1527). Private operators, AV companies, and corporations (Walgreens, Uber, Lyft) are partners. Scope: transit routes, service times, bus design, sidewalks, 'Complete Streets', new-technology pilots, and funding allocation.
What is being designed: Nothing designed by the study. It is diagnostic (gaps plus SWOT). Stakeholder strategies discussed: educational resources, travel training, public awareness campaigns, feedback via surveys, apps, and community events, corporate partnerships for transit passes, and rideshare to 'complement' fixed-route transit.
Values surfaced in the case: Fiscal-minimalism and efficiency values: 'what is the minimum that can be done ... without having to spend real money' (P3); funding 'allocated based on federal and state priorities' for 'highways and roadways', short-term, and non-relocatable 'even if a higher priority need was identified'; smart mobility framed as improving 'efficiency, accessibility, and sustainability'; adjusting service to a '70 percent' ridership drop (P4); reducing costs so 'Uber or Lyft complement our services so we can reduce and use resources somewhere else' (P4).
