Community values: equitable access (the 'mobility-vulnerable populations' frame; the East Side 'is still hurting'; 'there is no point in having an accessible bus if a person with a wheelchair can't get to the bus stop'), flexibility for variable need (older adults with a cane and balance issues; 'lowering the bus so that it meets the sidewalk'; paratransit in rural areas), and relational trust ('Politicians come and go ... they do not always match'; 'It's not as though most people in Florida know about what we do'). Maps to equitable access, flexibility for variable need, and relational trust.
Ideal traveler per decision-makers: Adjacent evidence. Florida planning is car-dependent by default (79 percent drive alone; 'we don't have so many alternatives to driving', P8). 'Administrators and city officials may prioritize optimizing safe transportation in a city' rather than access and ease (journal p. 1522). In Gainesville, officials 'prioritize student ridership frequency and funding compared to other populations' (journal p. 1527). New technology ('autonomous ridesharing') is embraced as a system strength while 'much of the literature on smart cities focuses on technological advancements, less attention is given to how these innovations impact mobility-vulnerable populations' (journal p. 1521). The imagined traveler is a car driver, a University student commuter, or an app-using rideshare customer, and the 'minimum ... without spending real money' defines the floor of service for everyone else. No 'ideal traveler' phrasing.
Actual travelers encountered: Mostly via stakeholder accounts, with a few end users interviewed directly: residents below the poverty threshold with 'limited public transportation routes and longer service times'; older adults 'with a cane' who 'have a hard time getting up the steps'; wheelchair users and blind riders who 'can't get to the bus stop' or lack 'audible information'; residents in cul-de-sac subdivisions far from bus stops; Veterans whose service was furloughed during COVID-19; and East Side (higher-minority) Gainesville residents who are 'still hurting'.
Gap between the two: Stakeholders 'know about transportation inequities ... but feel there are constraints to making changes'. Funding is federal and state-priority-driven, historically for 'highways and roadways', short-term, and non-relocatable even when 'a higher priority need' appears. Commissions do 'the minimum ... without spending real money'. A University town skews service to students over minority-dense areas. Smart-mobility enthusiasm outpaces attention to how it lands for mobility-vulnerable populations, which stakeholders flag as a 'threat'. Paratransit is offered as an 'acceptable alternative' while being inaccessible, 'an affront to those with disabilities' (P6).
Quotable moment: "They [city and county commissions] are looking at what is the minimum that can be done to make it [transportation operations and infrastructure] as safe as possible without having to spend real money." (journal p. 1525, P3). And on misaligned priorities: "Politicians come and go. They have priorities, and they do not always match [the priorities of multiple stakeholders] because the East Side [area in Gainesville, FL with a higher percentage of minority population] is still hurting." (journal p. 1526, P13).
Cross-comparison note (our synthesis): A decision-maker paper whose value is the funding mechanism: officials describe a system where money is federal and state-priority-bound, historically road-oriented, short-term, and non-relocatable, so equity needs known to every stakeholder cannot be acted on, an institutional version of the arrives-without-participation problem. The 'minimum ... without spending real money' quote is a clean statement of fiscal minimalism as the operative value. Notably the same stakeholders list 'autonomous rideshare' as a system strength and its 'unknown impacts' on mobility-vulnerable populations as a threat, in the same breath, useful for our AV framing. The 'They have priorities' quote, restored to full form, shows the gap between political priorities and a minority neighbourhood's needs. Caveats: 13 self-selected stakeholders (only a few end users, no systematic resident sample), one mid-sized University town plus statewide framing, COVID-era, SWOT structuring, and the study's own aim is stakeholder alignment rather than a critique of who holds power. Note: the canonical tracker's quotable moment for this row was truncated to 'They have priorities', one of the CLAUDE.md known defects.

Paper Title: Towards Environmental Justice in Transportation Decision Making using Structured Public Involvement
Study type / basis for inclusion: Largely conceptual TRB conference paper, drawing on the authors' prior SPI case-study data rather than new fieldwork. Companion to Bailey et al. 2010; the clearest statement in the set that participation machinery itself stratifies citizens.
Case setting: US transportation Environmental Justice (EJ) practice under Executive Order 12898 (1994) and the USDOT's three EJ aims. Prior Structured Public Involvement deployments referenced: noise wall design, large context-sensitive bridge design, transit-oriented development (Louisville, Kentucky, 2002), transportation and land-use planning, and nuclear plant remediation. Process-satisfaction data drawn from open public meetings in Kentucky, Indiana, and Arizona between 2000 and 2009, total n of 1656.
Method(s), session by session: A cross-disciplinary literature review plus secondary analysis of the authors' own SPI process-performance datasets; no new fieldwork. The SPI protocol as described: planners, sponsors, and contractors first 'delineate a feasible option envelope' (technically, financially, legally, and ethically feasible), excluding infeasible options 'prior to the public evaluation phase'; the team builds geovisualizations and animations as elicitation methods; large groups evaluate via Audience Response Systems (anonymous electronic keypad polling), 'simultaneously, independently, anonymously, and rapidly'; each keypad is tracked so 'age, race, income, and even geographic location can be ... cross-tabbed with project data', enabling anonymous self-identification along EJ scales; the public then evaluates the process itself (satisfaction scored 1 'awful' to 10 'wonderful'). The authors propose four process-performance criteria, Quality, Inclusion, Clarity, and Efficiency (Table 1), drawing on TRB's 1999 evaluation document, FDOT's process-quality indicators, and public-administration, environmental-management, and group-systems literatures.
Tools and artifacts: Audience Response Systems (anonymous electronic polling keypads with demographic cross-tab); geovisualizations and animations; a 'feasible option envelope'; ratio-scale preference evaluation contrasted with 'forced choice, one-and-done voting'; the four-criterion performance-metric table; Rawls's procedural justice and access to justice; the Arnstein Ladder; 'Consensus with Dissent Noted' documents (as an anti-pattern); Checkland's soft-systems approach.
Underlying principle of the method: Rawlsian: 'absolute distributive justice ... is a worthy yet unattainable goal' (p. 5), so improve procedural justice across 'the entire population'. EJ's second aim (full and fair participation) is under-studied relative to the distributional aims, which 'give themselves more readily to quantitative and spatial measurement'. Working with targeted 'EJ populations' separately 'may actually compromise on the intent of the EJ directive by limiting who is allowed to be classified as EJ' (p. 7). 'Flatten the power distribution' by maximising participation and giving everyone 'the same quantity and quality of input methods', minimising 'special groups like advisory panels and consulting parties'. Consensus is rejected: 'the ideology of consensus ... is one of the most significant impediments'. View 'the public as more than lip-service partners, but as responsible, interested parties who have meaningful information' (p. 15).
Provocation used to generate new ideas: The SPI protocol uses geovisualizations and animations plus 'defined scenarios (alternative outcomes)' alongside 'open-ended (i.e. brainstorming or issue probing questions)' as elicitation devices, and ratio-scale preference evaluation instead of 'pick one'. No new provocation study; the paper describes SPI's device set.
Who holds design authority: 'The public involvement theorists work with the project sponsors and contractors to exclude infeasible options prior to the public evaluation phase' (p. 10), so the feasible envelope is set by professionals, and 'SPI does not mean public control'. The Executive Order and USDOT set EJ aims; FHWA guidelines 'do not specify the form, content or objectives'. NEPA 'consulting parties' and 'advisory panels' create 'tiered citizenship'. TRB's 1999 32 metrics were all 'proposed to be measured by the professionals charged with delivering the processes' (p. 11). Scope: transportation infrastructure design (bridges, noise walls, transit, transit-oriented development, corridors) plus the meta-question of how to evaluate public involvement.
What is being designed: The authors design a four-criterion evaluation framework (Quality, Inclusion, Clarity, Efficiency) for public-involvement processes, and argue for stakeholder-driven rather than professional-driven metrics. SPI itself is the method being advocated.
Values surfaced in the case: Engineering and expert-authority values: 'the widespread and commonly expressed view among professionals that the public is not technically qualified to advise them' (p. 9); 'selective competency requirements for participation' (Kyem); large-group processes imagined as 'improvisational theater or karaoke night' (p. 8); the impulse 'to discourage attendance or to control who participates'; TRB's own 32 metrics 'measured by the professionals'; agencies' 'opaque risk-averse behavior' (p. 15). Efficiency is one of the four criteria, defined as 'dollars spent on public involvement, time taken and demanded, in relationship to performance achieved', with a call for 'a ratio of cost-effectiveness'. Community values: procedural justice and relational trust ('Populations that have experienced less effectiveness over time are less likely to participate'; 'civic detachment'; the public as more than 'lip-service partners'), equitable access ('flatten the power distribution'; open meetings where 'any interested party from an EJ community can ... contribute ... anonymously and on an equal footing'), and flexibility for variable need ('many of the issues surrounding project trade-offs are not susceptible to cost-benefit analysis ... they must rely on ethical and other judgments that emerge from the value systems of the subject populations', p. 6). Maps to relational trust and procedural justice, equitable access, and flexibility for variable need.
Ideal traveler per decision-makers: Not a traveler study, and the mobility content is thin. The nearest analogue: professionals imagine a public that is unqualified, a nuisance, and best minimised ('karaoke night', 'not technically qualified'), and EJ practice imagines a bounded, expert-defined 'EJ population' versus 'not', a 'forced choice' that excludes residents who are 'near EJ or even don't know we're in EJ' (p. 7). The level-of-service aside, that residents could 'define what the true level of service is on their roads, and what would count as improvement prior to developing plans' (p. 5), implies that level-of-service is currently set without them. No 'ideal traveler' phrasing.
Actual travelers encountered: Referenced from prior SPI projects: participants in transit design, bridge design, transit-oriented development (Louisville), noise-wall design, and nuclear-plant remediation; about 1656 participants across 2000 to 2009 who rated SPI process satisfaction highly and 'distinguish between their judgments about the distributive justice implications ... and the procedural justice implications' (p. 12). 'Disenfranchised' residents who have learned that participation is not efficacious, and residents who are 'near EJ' or 'don't know we're in EJ' and fall outside the census-driven category.
Gap between the two: EJ's participation aim is 'less systematic' and less researched than its distributional aims; 'public involvement evaluation is almost absent' and 'transportation lags other fields' (p. 11). Mandates 'do not specify the form, content or objectives' and there are 'no formal process performance metrics'. Practice produces 'tiered citizenship' and 'four classes of citizens', with 'different types of engagement for each'. Targeted 'EJ population' work is a 'forced choice' that can exclude the near-EJ. Consensus ideology and the view that the public 'is not technically qualified' push practitioners toward small, controllable groups. Evaluation, when done, is 'by the professionals or their clients, using informal criteria or anecdotal observation' (p. 11).
Quotable moment: "the execution of transportation projects yields four classes of citizens: advisory panels, consulting parties, and EJ populations, and everyone else ('the public')." (p. 7). And on the expert frame: SPI "does not mean public control; it means gathering large group input in a structured way using advanced analytic methods that allow designers access to these preferences." (p. 10).
Cross-comparison note (our synthesis): The clearest articulation in the set of how participation machinery itself stratifies citizens: 'four classes of citizens', with 'different types of engagement for each', so procedural injustice is built into the process design. The level-of-service aside, that residents could set what counts as 'improvement' before plans exist, is a compact statement of our claim that infrastructure values are fixed upstream. Two limits worth carrying: SPI keeps the 'feasible option envelope' with professionals ('does not mean public control'), and the paper's own evidence is the authors' self-collected process-satisfaction data. Companion to the Bailey et al. 2010 row; use whichever quote fits the section.

Paper Title: The dignity experience of people with disability when using trains and buses in an Australian city
Study type / basis for inclusion: Primary fieldwork. 26 interviews with disabled public transport users; strong on the medical-model non-disabled default and on smartphone-app solutions built without consultation.
Case setting: An unnamed Australian city in South East Queensland, focused on trains and buses (the macro system also has ferries, light rail, taxis, ride-share, and e-scooters). Australia is a UNCRPD signatory; more than 30 percent of disabled Australians report difficulty using public transport; the Disability Standards for Accessible Public Transport (2002) required 100 percent of bus stops to be compliant by 31 December 2022, and 'most states are well behind'. Data collected January to March 2021 with COVID-19 considerations.
Method(s), session by session: Qualitative design: semi-structured in-depth interviews plus Framework Analysis (Ritchie and Spencer). 26 interviews, 25 minutes to 1 hour 10 minutes (average 38), January to March 2021. Recruitment: an introductory email and flier to people who had consented to research contact via an Australian public-sector organisation, plus an advert in that organisation's public-transport-user newsletter. Eligibility: self-identified visible or invisible impairment, public transport experience, aged 18 plus, able to consent; participants chose their own terminology. 75 people expressed interest and completed a demographic intake survey; 30 were purposively selected; 26 were interviewed (13 female, 12 male, 1 non-binary; median age bracket 40 to 49; 21 with a physical impairment, 9 with chronic pain or illness; 16 regular users, 6 sometimes, 4 rarely). Framework Analysis in five steps (familiarisation; thematic framework; indexing; charting; mapping and interpretation), combining inductive coding with deductive inclusion of aims and a priori literature.
Tools and artifacts: A semi-structured interview guide; an online demographic intake survey for purposive sampling; a Framework Analysis matrix. System artifacts discussed: journey-planner apps, digital signage, audible and visual announcements, ticketing products and tap-on and tap-off validators, mobile boarding ramps ('boards'), bus route-number signage ('great big white signs' versus 'itty bitty little slim line' signs), icons, journey and route maps, and low-floor buses. Universal Design as the guiding principle.
Underlying principle of the method: Dignity as the frame, 'characterised equally by the absence of discrimination, shame, and humiliation, as ... by positive experiences of acceptance and inclusion'. A social and relational model of disability, disability as 'a mismatch between impairment and environment', set against 'the pervasive nature of the medical model' which 'constructs disability as an individual problem' so 'considerations for accessibility and inclusion are often omitted from transport planning' (journal p. 2376). UNCRPD rights (Articles 3, 9, 20); Universal Design; 'ecosystems of respect' and 'systemic empathy'; a whole-journey lens (wayfinding plus wayfaring).
Provocation used to generate new ideas: None. Retrospective interview elicitation of dignity experiences. No prototypes, scenarios, or design activities.
Who holds design authority: Transport planners and agencies design precincts, conveyances, signage, ticketing, and journey-planner apps, and 'most transport planning occurs without engaging marginalised populations, particularly people with disability' (journal p. 2390). Frontline staff are 'street-level bureaucrats' who 'must deal with policy and practice gaps'. Compliance runs on voluntary standards: the ADA 'relies on voluntary compliances and allows agencies to opt out of providing accommodations if they would be financially burdensome' (journal p. 2391). Smartphone technology is 'typically developed without consultation from people with diverse impairments'. The paper calls for 'policy changes and embedded mandates for including people with diverse impairments in planning and development'. Scope: PT infrastructure, conveyances, information systems, ticketing, and staff practice, plus the policy and standards frame.
What is being designed: Nothing designed by the study. Recommendations: Universal Design in new build and retrofit; accessible, multi-modal, real-time, plain-language, lived-experience-informed information 'beyond the journey planner'; co-designed staff training 'that extends beyond box-ticking diversity and inclusion training'; 'inclusion of people with disability during solution design phases'; and embedded policy mandates for participation.
Values surfaced in the case: Engineering, economic, and compliance values: 'The legacy of the medical model of disability in transport planning and economic prioritisation makes it difficult for Universal Design to be achieved' (journal p. 2390); accessibility 'omitted from transport planning ... because disability stems from an individual deficit' (journal p. 2376); compliance regimes where 'broad based standards are assessed as having been met, but the individual intricacies of meeting those standards for people with impairments are not universally met' (journal p. 2391); the ADA lets agencies 'opt out ... if ... financially burdensome'; 'over-reliance on smart phone accessible technology, typically developed without consultation'; retrofitting 'costly'; and the aesthetic-over-function swap of 'great big white signs' for 'look at me, I'm sexy' slimline signs. Community values: dignity ('dignity is independence... by allowing us to be more independent, you're giving us dignity'; wheelchair use made a participant 'feel human'), relational trust ('the most significant barriers to dignity came not from access but from the treatment you receive'; being 'compelled to unnecessarily prove and justify their needs'), flexibility for variable need (participants with different impairments finding 'the same products ... inaccessible but for different reasons', and doing 'extra sense-making over and above what people without disability may need to do'), and recognition ('really involved in decisions that might affect them'). Maps to relational trust and recognition, flexibility for variable need, and equitable access.
Ideal traveler per decision-makers: Strong. Information 'should be informed by lived experience of visible and invisible impairment, rather than on non-disabled and medical model assumptions about how people (usually those with visible impairments) interact with transport systems' (journal p. 2393). 'Over-reliance on smart phone accessible technology, typically developed without consultation from people with diverse impairments, can further increase the gaps for marginalised populations who may not have or use smart phones' (journal p. 2393). The medical model treats disability as an individual deficit, so planning 'omits' accessibility. The imagined traveler is non-disabled, or at most has a single visible impairment, owns and uses a smartphone, moves at pace ('everyone's always in a rush behind me'), and does not need to pre-plan the whole journey chain. No 'ideal traveler' phrasing.
Actual travelers encountered: 26 people with diverse visible and invisible impairments: wheelchair users 'left on trains because they could not independently disembark' who 'felt entirely undignified and vulnerable'; a bus rider whose high step-off means 'I've got to always hold on to the sides ... people are staring at me; I'm taking too long because everyone's always in a rush behind me' (P007); a Deaf participant who reads 'people's body language' and 'panicking' to work out why a train has stopped; a low-vision participant who has 'hailed trucks ... hailed wrong buses'; participants with cognitive impairment charged higher fares for forgetting to 'tap off'; and 73 percent who do 'comprehensive pre-planning and sense-making' and feel indignity 'about the need to do extra sense-making over and above what people without disability may need to do'.
Gap between the two: A dignified system 'looks like one that is universally designed without gaps', but 'that is not the current reality'. 'Most transport planning occurs without engaging marginalised populations, particularly people with disability'. The medical model omits accessibility from planning; compliance standards are 'assessed as having been met' while 'diverse needs are not well understood nor resourced'; the ADA lets agencies 'opt out ... if ... financially burdensome'; smartphone-first solutions are 'typically developed without consultation'. Even where Universal Design elements exist (low-floor buses, mobile ramps), 'broader system constraints ... continue to present and reinforce barriers', and 'if any part of a journey was inaccessible, participants were vulnerable to indignity'.
Quotable moment: "over-reliance on smart phone accessible technology, typically developed without consultation from people with diverse impairments, can further increase the gaps for marginalised populations who may not have or use smart phones." (journal p. 2393). And a participant: "people with disabilities... need to feel like they are included and need to feel like they're really involved in decisions that might affect them." (journal p. 2382, P014).
Cross-comparison note (our synthesis): Direct evidence for two of our claims at once. First, the smartphone-app finding, that digital solutions are 'developed without consultation' and assume a phone-owning user, is precisely the AV-hailing assumption our argument targets, stated by disabled riders about existing systems. Second, 'most transport planning occurs without engaging marginalised populations' plus the 'really involved in decisions that might affect them' quote is the participation deficit, from the rider side. The dignity frame gives us a concrete community value ('dignity is independence') that efficiency and compliance planning forecloses when 'any part of a journey' fails. The line that transport infrastructure is 'more immutable than the societal values that existed when they were built' is a compact statement of the path-dependence our other rows document. Caveats: 26 interviews in one Australian city, buses and trains only (no ferries, light rail, taxis, or AVs), recruited via a public-sector research panel and PT-user newsletter (so over-representing engaged riders), a single time window, and a descriptive study with no design or participatory component of its own.

Paper Title: Travelling in the margins: Impacts of transport poverty on travel attitudes and behaviours
Study type / basis for inclusion: Primary fieldwork; a contributing paper on lived travel experience, not a design or planning process. Its value: it exposes the average, rational, predictable traveler that behaviour-change theory and travel surveys assume, and shows who sits outside it.
Case setting: Rexdale, an inner-suburb northwest of Toronto (five social planning neighbourhoods, a high concentration of low-income, unemployed, and racially diverse residents, several designated 'Priority Neighbourhood Areas' or 'Neighbourhood Improvement Areas' with low neighbourhood equity scores). High-rise towers, no nearby subway, congested surface bus routes, transit commute mode share 20 to 24 percent (versus 26 percent citywide). The Finch West LRT is under construction and delayed. TTC ridership is below pre-pandemic levels with reduced reliability, more slow zones, and some violent-crime incidents. Data collected October to November 2023.
Method(s), session by session: Qualitative, cross-sectional with retrospective recall. Four focus group discussions with 30 participants (about 90 minutes each), plus 20 follow-up semi-structured one-on-one interviews (40 to 60 minutes). Recruited via the Rexdale Community Hub and its North Etobicoke Resident Council mailing list. Eligibility: precarious finances and/or chronic health or mobility issues limiting TTC conventional-service use (now or in the past five years); resident five years or more; primarily biking, transit, or walking. Sessions moved to Zoom because 'many residents requested online participation due to caregiving responsibilities, commuting barriers, health concerns, and work schedules'. Participants were not asked directly about attitudes or intentions, but about 'experiences and feelings of socio-economic and travel barriers'. Digitally recorded, transcribed verbatim, and analysed with reflexive thematic analysis (Braun and Clarke), blended inductive and deductive coding, analytical memos, and interviewer field notes. The sample skews young, racialized, and non-car-owning (1 of 20 interviewees owned a car).
Tools and artifacts: Focus-group and interview guides focused on experiences rather than attitudes; a proposed conceptual framework integrating transport poverty with the Theory of Planned Behaviour, the Theory of Cognitive Dissonance, Habit Theory, and Mele's proximal and distal intention framework (Figs. 1 to 5); reflexive thematic analysis; pseudonyms; Zoom.
Underlying principle of the method: Social-psychological theories of travel attitude and behaviour (Theory of Planned Behaviour, Theory of Cognitive Dissonance, Habit Theory), extended with 'transport poverty' (Lucas) as 'actual behavioural control' and with intersectionality (Crenshaw) at 'the intersections of race, gender, poverty and transportation quality'. Also Social Practice Theory (stuff, skills, images) and Motility (access, competence, appropriation). The stance that 'whether social inequities influence that attitude-forming information is crucial from a transportation justice perspective', and that 'transportation should be considered as a social policy issue'.
Provocation used to generate new ideas: None. The study deliberately did not ask about attitudes or intentions directly, and used retrospective elicitation of experiences. No prototypes, scenarios, or design activities.
Who holds design authority: The TTC, Metrolinx, and the City of Toronto, with provincial and federal funders, design and fund routes, schedules, infrastructure, and marketing. The Finch West LRT 'aimed to better serve the equity-deserving population ... has been delayed several times with no clear end date in sight', and subway Line 3 serving 'the poorly accessible area of Scarborough' was 'permanently closed in 2023 ... without any definitive plans' (journal p. 15). The TTC 'promotes itself as relaxed, affordable, and entertaining', appealing 'to the cognitive aspect of attitude'. 'Transportation planning often neglects the barriers these people experience' (journal p. 4). Residents are research participants, not co-designers. Scope: transit routes, schedules, reliability, infrastructure delivery, operator training, and harassment-reporting mechanisms.
What is being designed: Nothing designed by the study. It proposes a conceptual framework and policy implications: planners should 'appreciate the affective and behavioural components of attitudes' not just the cognitive; timely completion and maintenance of equity-serving transit projects; addressing intersectional 'compounded vulnerability ... in their planning processes'; and educating transit operators, fare inspectors, and special constables 'about racial justice' with 'robust mechanisms for reporting and addressing racial harassment'.
Values surfaced in the case: Efficiency and rational-actor values embedded in method and practice: travel-behaviour research premised on 'a rational decision-making process' (TPB and TCD); a push for 'cost-effective, sustainable interventions'; 'exogenous interventions in the form of promotional offers' (free travelcards) that fail long-term; 'raising awareness' and 'targeted programs' as the behaviour-change toolkit; the TTC's marketing appeal to 'the cognitive aspect of attitude' only; a funding logic where 'slower travel [compensates] for the lack of federal and provincial funding for network maintenance'; and travel surveys that 'may not accurately capture' ad-hoc, dynamically adapted travel. Community values: equitable access (transport poverty as 'transport-related social exclusion'; 'the absence of feasible alternatives often compels them to continue using it despite ... persistent racial harassment'; 'So many times I decide to stay back'), relational trust (racism from operators and passengers, 'the drivers ignore me ... because of my background'; police who 'did not believe his complaints'; 'I think I don't want anybody into trouble'), and flexibility for variable need ('daily travel behaviours ... are often ad-hoc and dynamically adapted'; 'I just start walking ... And wherever I catch a bus, I enter the bus'). Maps to equitable access and relational trust, plus flexibility for variable need.
Ideal traveler per decision-makers: Strong and methodological. Travel-behaviour theory 'assume[s] a rational decision-making process' (journal p. 3), and the TPB 'does not shed light on how people develop and execute their travel plans' or account for 'resources, opportunities, and abilities' (journal p. 4). 'Perceived control could be a reliable indicator of actual control if individuals possess sufficient information about the behaviour and the context remains relatively stable' (journal p. 3), conditions transport poverty removes. Travel surveys 'may not accurately capture' behaviour that is 'less predictable due to the obstacles they face' (journal p. 15). Behaviour-change interventions target motivation on the assumption that resources are not the constraint. The TTC's marketing addresses a traveler who chooses transit on cognitive grounds. The assumed traveler is a rational chooser with a stable context, adequate resources and information, a predictable routine, and no experience of harassment. No 'ideal traveler' phrasing.
Actual travelers encountered: 30 mostly young, racialized, non-car-owning Rexdale residents in precarious finances and/or with health or mobility conditions: Blake (25), whom 'white people ... wouldn't want ... to sit next to'; Dylan (27), whom 'the drivers ignore ... because of my background. Racial background'; Hayden (22), who checks her purse and 'So many times I decide to stay back'; Enzo (30), called a 'black monkey' while biking, disbelieved by police, who 'refused to go to work' for a time; women who feel 'scared to take cabs at night too' (Laxmi, 65); Ruby, for whom night buses are 'kind of really hard' and TTC arrival times keep 'changing'; and people whose travel is 'ad-hoc and dynamically adapted' ('I just start walking ... And wherever I catch a bus, I enter the bus').
Gap between the two: Travel-behaviour theory and surveys assume a rational chooser with a stable context and predictable routine; the residents interviewed adapt 'ad-hoc and dynamically', so surveys 'may not accurately capture' their behaviour and 'cost-effective' interventions aimed at motivation miss a resource-and-safety constraint. Transit affordability 'is not adequate to retain transit customers'; people 'lean towards car-oriented travel as they gain financial stability' because 'driving feels safer' and 'racism, sexism in transit occur more frequently ... than driving-related fatalities' (journal p. 15). Equity-serving infrastructure (Finch West LRT, Line 3) is 'delayed' or 'permanently closed ... without any definitive plans'. The TTC markets to the cognitive attitude while the affective and behavioural components, shaped by 'repeated exposure to racism, harassment, and poor quality of transportation coupled with poverty', drive actual behaviour.
Quotable moment: "the drivers ignore me. I do have to walk more. I understand that maybe he can ignore me because of my background. Racial background." (journal p. 9, Dylan, 27). And on affordability constraining travel: "At times umm I want to go out, ... and I'm looking at my purse, there is no money. So many times I decide to stay back." (journal p. 9, Hayden, 22).
Cross-comparison note (our synthesis): A contributor that exposes the average-user assumption at the level of research method: the Theory of Planned Behaviour and travel surveys are built for 'a rational decision-making process' with 'sufficient information' and a 'stable' context, and the residents interviewed, whose travel is 'ad-hoc and dynamically adapted' under harassment and scarcity, sit outside that model, so they are hard to survey and easy for 'cost-effective' interventions to miss. This is the same erasure our argument attributes to AV demand models. The finding that people move toward cars 'as they gain financial stability' because 'driving feels safer' than an unreliable transit system where 'racism, sexism ... occur more frequently ... than driving-related fatalities' is a direct challenge to efficiency-framed mode-shift goals. The delayed Finch West LRT and closed Line 3 are concrete instances of equity infrastructure that arrives late or not at all. Caveats: not a design or participation study, so the ideal-traveler material is inferred from the methods it critiques; 50 participants in one Toronto inner-suburb recruited through a single community hub's mailing list, skewing young and online-responsive; Zoom-only; cross-sectional with retrospective recall.

Paper Title: Transit Equity in the Face of the COVID-19 Pandemic: A Study of Six Ontario Transit Authorities
Study type / basis for inclusion: Primary fieldwork and a decision-maker paper (SSRN working paper, circa 2021). 11 interviews with transit officials and municipal leaders across six Ontario bus systems. Strong on decision-makers who saw the equity harm but could not act on it.
Case setting: Six Ontario bus-based transit authorities: Brampton, Brantford, Burlington, Kingston, London, and Windsor (municipality sizes about 98,000 to 594,000; 33 to 450 buses; 2019 ridership 1.9 million to 31.9 million). The first pandemic year, 2020 to early 2021. Ridership dropped 80 to 90 percent immediately and recovered to 40 to 50 percent a year on; fare revenue collapsed (London forecast 46 percent farebox recovery and got 29.6 percent; Windsor's fares, about half of expenditure, 'initially disappeared completely'). Same provincial jurisdiction, same provincial decisions and funding (the Safe Restart Agreement put 1 billion dollars federal plus 1 billion dollars provincial into Ontario transit). Windsor's mayor unilaterally shut down all Transit Windsor for four weeks under an Emergency Measures Bylaw.
Method(s), session by session: A comparative case study. Semi-structured interviews with 11 transit decision-makers across the six authorities, over video link, in December 2020 (about nine months into the pandemic). Interviewees were asked about the pandemic's impact, their authority's response, the major problems ahead, and how transit can survive; 'interviewees were not asked specifically about transit equity until near the end', to test whether equity, transit poverty, or disadvantaged groups came up unprompted. Interviewees could edit their transcripts. Three research questions: the pandemic's impact on service; the extent transit users and marginalized groups were consulted; and the extent decision-makers took equity into account. Secondary data: municipal websites, publications, announcements, and news reports on service, safety, and consultation.
Tools and artifacts: A semi-structured interview guide with a deliberate 'is equity mentioned unprompted?' design; a comparative case framework of six similar-but-different bus authorities; horizontal versus vertical equity (Carleton and Porter) as the analytic lens; tables of transit-authority data, riders' concerns (service coverage, buses in service, social distancing, health-guideline violations), safety measures (cleaning, rear-door boarding, limited capacity, plexiglass, shutdown), operating budgets, and Safe Restart funding. Transit advisory committees; Windsor's Emergency Measures Bylaw.
Underlying principle of the method: Transit equity as 'level of service, affordability, and accessibility' for 'those most reliant on public transit', plus a procedural dimension: 'a lack of transit equity may also be evident in the context of transit planning and decision-making with disadvantaged groups unable to participate effectively ... even in contexts when public participation is encouraged or required' (p. 4). Verbich et al.: asking agencies 'the objectives they use ... provides important information about the prevalence of transit equity in transit planning'. Vertical equity, distributing more to those with greater need.
Provocation used to generate new ideas: None. A diagnostic interview study; the only device is the unprompted-equity interview design.
Who holds design authority: Transit authority management and municipal councils set 'levels of service, service coverage, transit routes'; in emergencies the Windsor mayor had 'sole authority' and shut the whole system 'unilaterally' under the Emergency Measures Bylaw, without consulting 'transit groups and users' (p. 18). Transit advisory committees 'cannot make binding decisions ... limited to providing recommendations and advice' (p. 20). The province (the transportation minister) and the federal government were 'central influences' via guidelines and Safe Restart funding; local medical officers of health set the health rules. The six authorities 'worked collaboratively' to set 'best practices'. A January 2021 motion to give Windsor's full council control over transit in emergencies 'was supported by three city councillors but opposed by the mayor and the remaining seven'. Scope: service levels, route retention or cuts, boarding rules, capacity, and funding appeals.
What is being designed: Nothing designed by the study. It documents authorities' pandemic measures: route cuts (keeping 'basic grid routes ... while eliminating some of the less-used routes'), frequency reductions ('half of a service' for the same fare), rear-door boarding (which meant free rides and lost fare revenue), reduced capacity, cleaning cycles, plexiglass, multilingual service-change communications (Brampton), and spare-operator pools. Phase Three Safe Restart funding 'could be used to finance experiments with on-demand transit and regional transit initiatives'.
Values surfaced in the case: Service-continuity and fiscal-survival values: 'The transit systems were forced to prioritize the maintenance of existing levels of service ... with only a limited capacity to introduce measures to advance transit equity' (abstract); 'decision-making could not always wait for consultations'; authorities 'focusing primarily on trying to respond quickly to changing health and safety guidance ... and to reassure passengers that public transit is safe'; a 'successful public transit network requires a broad range of riders', so service must 'attract all socio-economic classes'; route cuts that keep 'the major routes that are most frequently used' while 'eliminating some of the less-used routes' (p. 25). Community values: equitable access (officials 'all realised that transit is an essential service for many of their riders'; the ODSP and Ontario Works quote on 733 to 1169 dollars a month leaving 'very little ... for taxi service'; a 4 dollar trip becoming '30 in taxi fares'), relational trust ('funding ... to build trust in public transit'; the Windsor shutdown 'left those reliant on public transit excluded from society'), and flexibility for variable need (seniors and people on disability support who 'could not work from home and nor could they decide to drive'). Maps to equitable access, relational trust, and flexibility for variable need.
Ideal traveler per decision-makers: Adjacent evidence. The 'less-used routes' are cut while 'the major routes that are most frequently used' are kept, so the protected design population is the peak commuter. A 'successful public transit network requires a broad range of riders' and service must 'attract all socio-economic classes' (p. 27), an explicit choice-rider framing where retaining the discretionary rider is a system goal alongside serving the reliant rider. The pandemic surfaced that many riders 'have no other mobility options' and 'whose income is too low to drive' but 'live too far from work or school to walk or cycle' (CUTA, p. 30), a population the normal model treats as a given rather than a design target. No 'ideal traveler' phrasing.
Actual travelers encountered: Via officials and news: 2,000 to 3,000 Windsor riders 'left scrambling to get to work or make other essential trips' when the system shut, for whom 'a trip that may have cost them 4 dollars ... could end up costing 30 in taxi fares'; seniors complaining about reduced Windsor service; people on ODSP (733 dollars a month) or Ontario Works (1169 a month) with 'very little ... for taxi service to go to a pharmacy ... or to work'; a 'frequent low-income rider who had to resort to using taxi services ... which left them in a financial crisis'; front-line food-service workers who 'could not work from home'; and new immigrants, seniors, and social-service recipients 'most likely to live in areas underserved by public transit'.
Gap between the two: Officials 'were aware of transit equity and did know that transit service cuts disproportionately affected the most vulnerable', 'proposed measures to mitigate', and 'raised transit equity in their appeals ... for more funding', but 'were ... limited in their ability to address transit equity' and 'forced to prioritize the maintenance of existing levels of service' (abstract). Consultation collapsed: 'less regularized consultation with transit users and groups than occurs in normal times', and 'the primary way they heard from the public was through complaints' (p. 20). Windsor's mayor shut the whole system without consulting anyone, and the advisory committee's recommendation to make transit an essential service and give council emergency control was voted down (p. 19). Route cuts protected the busiest routes, concentrating harm on the 'less-used' routes that serve those with fewest alternatives.
Quotable moment: "The transit systems were forced to prioritize the maintenance of existing levels of service during the pandemic with only a limited capacity to introduce measures to advance transit equity." (abstract, p. 2). And an official on the disability-support reality: "by the time you cover your housing costs and your food that leaves very little for them to be able to use on taxi service to go to a pharmacy to get their medication, or get to a grocery store, or to work." (p. 26).
Cross-comparison note (our synthesis): A clean case of decision-makers who understood the equity harm, named it, and could not act on it, because the operative constraint was fiscal survival and service continuity, not a lack of awareness. That distinction matters for our argument: the gap here is not ignorance but a structure that makes 'maintain existing service' the only feasible move. The Windsor shutdown (unilateral mayoral authority, no consultation, advisory committee overruled) is a compact example of infrastructure decisions that arrive without participation, and the 'less-used routes' cut logic shows the peak commuter as the protected default. The 'broad range of riders' and 'attract all socio-economic classes' framing is a useful instance of choice-rider retention as a stated system value. Caveats: 11 self-selected officials, no riders or advocates interviewed directly (rider voice is via officials and news); six mid-sized Ontario bus systems only, no rail or large metros; a single crisis window (December 2020); an unpublished SSRN working paper with no stated year on the PDF.

Paper Title: Bike Share Equity for Underrepresented Groups: Analyzing Barriers to System Usage in Baltimore, Maryland
Study type / basis for inclusion: Primary quantitative fieldwork (intercept and member surveys, Chi-square and regression), not a design or participatory process. Contributes on the narrow demographic band bike share serves and its registration assumptions.
Case setting: Baltimore Bike Share (BBS), launched in 2016 to support the city's 'network of sustainable transportation options' and 'almost immediately accused of ... transit apartheid'. The first 20 docks opened in the downtown and Inner Harbor area (October 2016); expansion was delayed by supply-chain and maintenance backlog and a docking-lock design flaw that caused theft; the system shut down in September 2017 to redesign locks, reopened in October 2017, and reached 39 stations by August 2018. Study population: residents within a quarter-mile walk of BBS stations.
Method(s), session by session: Three components. (1) An intercept survey of non-users: instrument adapted from NACTO's Bike Share Intercept Survey Toolkit, 17 barrier statements (9 about riding a bike, 8 about accessing and using BBS) rated on Likert agreement, conducted on 6 weekdays and 5 weekend days in April to May 2018, with administrators spending 3 hours near 8 docking stations of varied land use and soliciting 'diverse race, gender, and age'. Eligibility: Baltimore resident, 18 plus, knows how to ride a bike, has heard of but never used BBS. n equals 109. (2) A member survey emailed 16 April 2018, tourist trips excluded, n equals 245 (about 8 percent response), demographics only. (3) Both compared against ACS 2010 to 2015 five-year estimates averaged for the service area. Analysis: Chi-square tests of independence between barriers and 'sociodemographic communities of interest' (female, low income, not white, less educated, unemployed, Hispanic), with barrier responses collapsed to dichotomous variables, then multivariate OLS linear-probability regression (STATA) for effect sizes on the six barriers that varied.
Tools and artifacts: The NACTO Bike Share Intercept Survey Toolkit (adapted); a 17-item barrier questionnaire (Appendix A); dichotomised sociodemographic-community variables; Chi-square and OLS regression; an ACS service-area comparison; and the BBS docking network and its credit or debit card plus internet registration flow as objects of study.
Underlying principle of the method: Transportation equity, specifically 'vertical equity' (Litman), 'the appropriate and fair distribution of costs and benefits among groups that differ by income or social class' (p. 2). 'Bike share equity is generally conceptualized as addressing barriers to accessing bike share ... for targeted populations'. 'Adequate access, or equity of opportunity' is the operative goal, 'even if less agreement on the need for equity of outcome exists' (p. 1). 'Having ridership that reflects the demographics of a community is often a goal' (p. 1). Barriers are treated as 'amenable to change through transportation practices and policies'.
Provocation used to generate new ideas: None. A survey and statistical study. It recommends provocation-type outreach devices (a bike-share ambassador program, organized community rides, 'opportunities to test bike share bikes at community events') but did not run them.
Who holds design authority: The City of Baltimore and the bike-share operator design the system: docking-station siting (downtown and Inner Harbor first), the lock hardware (a 'design flaw' caused theft and a shutdown), the 'credit or debit card to sign up' requirement that 'allows for efficient billing ... and ... serves as collateral' but 'poses problems for those who are unbanked' (p. 3), bike design (no cargo or child capacity), and pricing (annual membership 'about the same as a monthly transit pass'). NACTO sets the survey standard. The researchers hold analytic authority. Scope: bike-share hardware, the station network, registration and payment, pricing, and cycling infrastructure in the service area.
What is being designed: Nothing designed by the study. Recommendations: targeted community outreach (a grassroots bike-share ambassador program, organized community rides, test-ride events, targeted marketing), bicycle designs that 'incorporate gear to make it easier ... to transport items and to ride with children', and cycling-infrastructure upgrades (separated bike lanes, road diets, traffic calming) in bike-share service areas.
Values surfaced in the case: Efficiency and market values in system design: the credit or debit card requirement chosen because it 'allows for efficient billing of users and equally serves as collateral' (p. 3); docking stations sited first in 'the downtown and Inner Harbor area'; 'bike share operators may be limited in their ability to serve underrepresented areas' (p. 2); membership priced 'about the same as a monthly transit pass'. 'Equity of opportunity' preferred over 'equity of outcome'. Community values: equitable access (members are 'predominately male, white, highly educated, high-income earners, employed, and non-Hispanic', statistically different from the service-area population), flexibility for variable need ('notwhite' associated with a roughly 36-point increase in concern about 'the ability to carry a child or cargo'; 'lower income people of color are more likely to have children at home'), relational trust and safety (women more concerned about 'being a victim of crime or harassment'; 'concerns among socioeconomically underrepresented groups about potential interactions with police'; the 'transit apartheid' accusation), and belonging (bicycles 'associated with drug dealers and perceived as symbols of gentrification'). Maps to equitable access, flexibility for variable need, and relational trust.
Ideal traveler per decision-makers: Strong for the target population. Bike-share systems 'serve a narrow demographic band', and users are 'predominately white, non-Hispanic, male, highly educated, employed, and high-income earners' (p. 1). The design assumes a rider with a credit or debit card, internet access to register, no children or cargo to carry, tolerance for short rental time limits, and a downtown or Inner-Harbor destination; the bike itself has no cargo or child capacity. The 'transit apartheid' critique names the assumed rider as the affluent white professional. No 'ideal traveler' phrasing.
Actual travelers encountered: 109 non-user Baltimore residents proportionately reflecting the service-area population; women reporting concern about 'being a victim of crime or harassment', comfort, hygiene, knowing how to use the system, and overall interest; 'not white' respondents (74 percent Black) concerned about carrying 'a child or cargo'; and, from the reviewed literature, unbanked residents (African Americans and Hispanics 'overrepresented'), non-English speakers, immigrants 'less likely to know how to ride bikes or understand rules of the road', people for whom bikes signal 'not successful' or 'gentrification', and residents facing a 'spatial mismatch between low-income communities and access to jobs'. In this sample, internet-access and no-card barriers were reported by fewer than 10 to 14 percent, and low income and less education were 'not found to be more or less likely' to perceive the barriers, which the authors flag against interviewer and social-desirability bias.
Gap between the two: Bike-share membership is 'statistically different' from the service-area population, skewed white, male, high-income, and educated, but the system serves that band by design: cards for 'efficient billing' and 'collateral', downtown-first docks, bikes with no cargo capacity, and short rental limits. The equity goal is set as 'equity of opportunity' (access), with 'less agreement on the need for equity of outcome', so a system can be judged equitable while its ridership stays narrow. Operators are 'limited in their ability to serve underrepresented areas'. Majority safety concern about riding on Baltimore's streets is held 'independent of socioeconomic condition', yet infrastructure is not in the system's control.
Quotable moment: "bike share users are predominately white, non-Hispanic, male, highly educated, employed, and high-income earners." (p. 1). And on the payment design: requiring "a credit or debit card to sign up allows for efficient billing of users and equally serves as collateral ... but poses problems for those who are unbanked, the majority of whom are low-income individuals." (p. 3).
Cross-comparison note (our synthesis): A contributor that documents, quantitatively, how a shared-mobility system settles on a narrow, affluent, white, banked, internet-equipped rider, the same profile our argument attributes to app-summoned AVs, and does so through concrete design choices (a card requirement for 'efficient billing' and 'collateral', downtown-first docks, no cargo capacity) rather than stated intent. Framing the equity goal as 'equity of opportunity' not 'equity of outcome' is a useful instance of how an efficiency-compatible definition of equity lets a system pass. Caveats: a quantitative barrier study, not a design or participation study, so the ideal-traveler material is mostly from the reviewed literature plus the membership skew; small samples (109 non-users, 245 members, about 8 percent member response), one city, 2018 data, and the study's own finding that low-income and card and internet barriers were weaker than expected, which it attributes partly to intercept-survey bias.

Paper Title: Bridging the gap: Do community needs assessments enhance public participation in transportation planning?
Study type / basis for inclusion: Secondary comparative analysis of 24 California community needs assessments, not the authors' own fieldwork. A strong contributor: shows a dedicated, funded, grassroots engagement program still reproducing the participation deficit.
Case setting: California's Clean Mobility Options Voucher Pilot Program, part of California Climate Investments, administered by the Shared-Use Mobility Center (the authors' employer). The California Air Resources Board funded 24 Community Transportation Needs Assessments (CTNAs); the first round launched in June 2020 with about 1.15 million dollars, vouchers up to 50,000 dollars, roughly nine-month projects in 2020 to 2021, awarded first-come first-served, open only to 'eligible disadvantaged communities' plus low-income tribal and affordable-housing communities. Awardees were public agencies, nonprofits, private consultants, and American Indian tribes. 'The program did not include an official mechanism by which final CTNA reports ... would influence transportation plans or funding decisions'; a completed CTNA let awardees apply for a Mobility Voucher for zero-emission microtransit, scooter, bike, or carshare.
Method(s), session by session: Content analysis of CTNA application materials (to identify each study's target population), final reports (methods, recommendations, and their specificity), awardee exit surveys (31 questions), and the awardees' own community survey responses (to check whether the intended community was reached). Comparison of five CTNA project areas against their region's long-range transportation plan public-participation process. Analysis of recommendation types and cited mobility barriers. Not fieldwork with residents; a document and data analysis of a completed program.
Tools and artifacts: CTNA applications, final reports, exit surveys, and community-survey microdata; a comparison table of engagement methods (CTNA versus long-range plan); Arnstein's ladder and 'citizen power' as a reference; CalEnviroScreen (which defines 'disadvantaged'); the observation that 'underrepresented' has 'no such criteria' and is left to awardees. The CMO Mobility Voucher as a downstream funding artifact.
Underlying principle of the method: Public participation as 'citizen power' (Arnstein; Slotterback and Lauria) that 'gives residents real power' and 'build[s] social capital and trust', set against a skeptical frame: traditional participation 'advantage[s] people with the resources (time, knowledge, ability)', has a 'representation gap' (participants 'older, white, and relatively affluent'), 'tends to attract residents seeking an avenue to oppose', and transportation projects have 'concentrated costs and diffused benefits'. The alternative-to-participation argument: 'the role of local participation could shift from the public meeting or community study to the ballot box', and 'Moving decisions from the local to the state level could ... better democratize planning investments'.
Provocation used to generate new ideas: The CTNAs used, and the paper catalogues, provocation-type methods: surveys, focus groups, interviews, 'photovoice journals', 'walk and bike safety audits', 'collaborative mapping', 'demonstration events', and a 'virtual reality component'. The paper itself runs no provocation; it evaluates.
Who holds design authority: CARB designed the CTNA program and left 'underrepresented' undefined 'so as to enable state agencies to be as inclusive as it wants'. Awardees designed their own study methods. But 'the program did not include an official mechanism by which final CTNA reports ... would influence transportation plans or funding decisions', and awardees 'would need to use additional resources to take their recommendations to the relevant authority, like their city council'. MPOs and state agencies hold plan authority; the Bipartisan Infrastructure Law mandates public involvement but agencies 'may choose the simplest procedures to check legislatively-mandated boxes' (journal p. 7). Scope: needs-assessment design, survey methods, and recommendations, within the broader participatory-planning apparatus.
What is being designed: Nothing designed by the study. The CTNAs produced recommendations (most cited barriers: high costs 88 percent, access 79 percent, safety 63 percent); recommendations skewed to 'zero emission shared vehicles' (75 percent) over active transportation (58 percent), partly because 74 percent of awardees 'planned to use their CTNA report to apply for the CMO mobility voucher program, which offers funds restricted to clean mobility fleet purchases ... and not street improvements' (journal p. 7). The paper recommends folding 'targeted outreach ... into existing long-range planning practices, rather than create additional studies', reviewing existing studies first to avoid survey fatigue, and requiring independent needs assessments only 'under distinct circumstances ... such as ... when a novel transportation technology is introduced'.
Values surfaced in the case: Administrative box-checking and efficiency values: agencies 'may choose the simplest procedures to check legislatively-mandated boxes'; 'the process is costly'; 'money that could be used to fund mobility interventions or reduce carbon emissions directly is instead directed towards additional studies' (opportunity cost); 'if recommendations are generally predictable, then perhaps data-driven approaches ... offer a far less resource-intensive process'; CTNA funding 'restricted to clean mobility fleet purchases ... and not street improvements'; and the 'concentrated costs and diffused benefits' logic that predicts who shows up. Community values: relational trust ('build social capital and trust'; residents 'less likely to contribute if their previous experiences ... did not lead to any tangible outcomes'), recognition and equitable access (CTNAs 'intended to include historically underrepresented groups' but 'many target population groups underrepresented in survey responses'; focus-group participants 'appeared to be primarily white and older'), and flexibility for variable need (language barriers; people 'physically isolated from broader society'). Maps to relational trust and equitable access, plus flexibility for variable need.
Ideal traveler per decision-makers: Adjacent evidence. The representation gap names the participant and beneficiary as 'older, white, and relatively affluent', and the paper's illustrative example is a bike lane opposed by drivers and business owners whose 'concentrated costs' they feel while the 'broad and hypothetical' beneficiaries do not turn out. Federal surveys, 'the US Census and travel behavior surveys like the National Household Travel Survey', 'historically under-count low-income groups, racial/ethnic minorities, and immigrants' (journal p. 6), so the data that feeds planning already encodes a narrower population. CTNA recommendations tilt to 'zero emission shared vehicles' because the downstream money funds fleets, implying an assumed user who wants a shared clean vehicle. No 'ideal traveler' phrasing.
Actual travelers encountered: Via the CTNA target lists and surveys: low-income (92 percent of assessments), Latino/a (83 percent), non-English speakers (75 percent, including a Mixteco and a Hmong outreach that got no responses), carless (58 percent), no driver's license (54 percent), immigrants (54 percent), no internet (50 percent), unemployed, tribal residents, farm workers 'waiting upwards of two hours at a regular food distribution event', students, older adults, undocumented, single parents, and homeless people. Survey samples ranged from nearly 3,000 to 12 (median 168); one had 8 usable responses; several assessments 'did not ask whether respondents were farm workers' despite targeting them.
Gap between the two: CTNAs were 'intended to include historically underrepresented groups', but the authors 'found many target population groups underrepresented in survey responses', awardees 'tended not to ask pertinent demographic questions', and where tracked, focus-group participants 'appeared to be primarily white and older' (the same representation gap as traditional planning and federal surveys). Recommendations 'tend to overlap with existing long-range transportation plans', so 'the value of additional community studies can be questioned if their findings could be more readily identified without ... costly outreach'. And with 'no official mechanism' to feed findings into plans, a study 'might rigorously identify transportation gaps and propose solutions, but if those solutions are not approved by the powers that be, they may never take root'. The Sacramento 'blueprinting' co-development 'ultimately led to very little change in the regional transportation system and land use patterns, and on net the region increased its greenhouse gas emissions'.
Quotable moment: "a community-based study might rigorously identify transportation gaps and propose solutions, but if those solutions are not approved by the powers that be, they may never take root." (journal p. 7). And on the representation gap: "if the people who attend a meeting to discuss a new public transit route never envision themselves using it, but constitute a minority among a broader potential transit-riding population, their voices may have outsized influence." (journal p. 2).
Cross-comparison note (our synthesis): The clearest documentation in the set that a dedicated, funded, grassroots-run engagement program still reproduced the participation deficit (white, older, affluent respondents; targeted groups undercounted) and, critically, had 'no official mechanism' to feed its findings into plans, so participation and authority stayed disconnected. That is the structural version of our claim. Two specifics worth carrying: the recommendation to reserve extra needs assessments for 'when a novel transportation technology is introduced' is a direct hook for AV deployment, and the finding that CTNA recommendations tilted toward 'zero emission shared vehicles' because that is what the downstream money funds shows how the funding envelope shapes the 'community-identified' need. Caveats: a document and data analysis of one California program, not fieldwork; the authors' employer co-administers the program (disclosed); 'we are unable to ascertain whether the community studies led to any changes in local transportation systems'; small and uneven survey samples across awardees. Note: papers/Community Needs Assessments in Transportation Planning.pdf is a renamed duplicate of this paper, not a separate study.

Paper Title: Race, Space, and Struggles for Mobility: Transportation Impacts on African Americans in Oakland and the East Bay
Study type / basis for inclusion: Historical and legal case analysis of the Darensburg v. MTC lawsuit and its context, not fieldwork (two of three authors were involved in the case). The strongest historical case in the set for race-neutral technical analysis setting the ideal traveler as an affluent suburban commuter.
Case setting: Oakland and the East Bay, San Francisco Bay Area, from post-Civil-War settlement through 2005. Two geographies: mostly-White suburban South Alameda and Contra Costa Counties, and the inner East Bay's historically African American West, North, and East Oakland and South Berkeley. AC Transit (bus, serving low-income people of color) versus BART (rail, 'oriented toward suburban commuting'). The Metropolitan Transportation Commission (MTC), the region's MPO, was created in 1970. In Darensburg et al. v. MTC (2005), minority bus riders alleged MTC's rail-favoring practices violated Title VI; the District Court and Ninth Circuit ruled for MTC. Subsidy per trip: about 3 dollars for bus riders versus 6 to 14 dollars for rail riders; bus service 'stagnant' while rail 'more than doubled'; about 80 percent of Oakland bus riders were low-income people of color.
Method(s), session by session: A three-part historical analysis using an environmental racism framework. Part I sets out the framework (race-neutral processes 'layering onto a segregated metropolitan geography ... reproduce, and reinforce racial barriers'). Part II traces historical forces to about 1970 (Jim Crow, New Deal and wartime planning, urban renewal, freeway encroachment, transit divestment, the 'white noose'). Part III covers 1970 to 2005 across three 'distributional impacts of transportation': participation and representation, infrastructure impacts, and service disparities. Sources: MTC and ABAG documents, Public Advocates litigation materials, historian Robert Self, prior scholarship, court records, and author-produced GIS maps. Not the authors' own fieldwork with riders; Sanchez was an expert witness and Marcantonio the plaintiffs' attorney in Darensburg (disclosed).
Tools and artifacts: The environmental racism framework (Pulido); MTC's own transportation forecasting model and its 1998, 2001, and 2005 RTP equity analyses; the Lifeline Transportation gap study; the Regional Transit Expansion Program (RTEP); Title VI and Executive Order 12898; the Darensburg trial record; author-produced GIS maps of the East Bay; ridership demographic tables.
Underlying principle of the method: Environmental racism and environmental justice: past overt discrimination 'leave[s] a cumulative physical imprint on the metropolitan landscape', and 'current decisions ... while they may be made on race-neutral (e.g. technical or market based) bases, inexorably perpetuate past discriminatory outcomes'. Rejects the 'post-racial' and 'color-blind' view (Judge Noonan: 'a Bay Area board bent on racist goals is a specter that only desperate litigation could entertain'). Three distributional impacts: participation and representation, localized burdens, and mobility benefits (the authors extend the framework to the third). Distinguishes investments that meet low-income communities' needs (local bus) from those that 'while potentially beneficial ... may fail to meet their needs, while actually impacting them much more' (commuter rail, via displacement and diverted resources).
Provocation used to generate new ideas: None. Historical and legal analysis.
Who holds design authority: MTC, whose 'Fourteen of its sixteen voting members are appointed' with a structure 'biased toward suburban representation' (suburban Napa County had the same one commissioner as Alameda County's 1.5 million-plus residents; 'only two of MTC's 16 voting members are minorities'). MTC set funding rules: RTEP 'directed 94 percent of some 13 billion dollars funds to rail expansion', 'projects to expand local (non-commuter) bus services were not eligible ... at all', and congestion-relief requirements were 'applied more rigorously to bus proposals while it was assumed rail projects brought such relief'. MTC 'actively filled capital maintenance shortfalls ... primarily benefiting rail systems, while leaving unfunded operating shortfalls resulting in bus service cuts'. Courts upheld this as 'justified by MTC's need to balance competing interests'. Scope: regional transportation funding allocation, rail versus bus, and the RTP.
What is being designed: Nothing designed by the study. The infrastructure at issue: BART rail expansion (station expansions, new lines), AC Transit bus service levels, and freeway alignments (the Cypress Freeway rebuilt 'completely around the community' after NEPA-enabled opposition, 'adding an extra mile ... and 500 million dollars'; the Fruitvale BART parking structure cancelled and replaced by a community-developed housing, retail, and services project).
Values surfaced in the case: Efficiency and technical-neutrality values: MTC's equity analysis 'used a transportation forecasting model' that 'grouped all public transit systems together, making it impossible to understand whether BART or bus riders benefited', 'assumed that bus service will not be cut', and 'determined travel paths by finding the one best path in terms of minimum travel time without taking into account the prices', so it 'assumed most people would take BART' though it is more expensive; congestion relief was 'assumed' for rail ('[t]he degree to which [congestion reduction] happens ... who knows'); rail projects were 'more expensive per new rider than similar bus projects' but funded, 'their congestion impacts ... never verified'; and regional planning's 'increasingly technical character ... creates barriers to participation by the public and minorities'. Larry Dahms, former BART general manager and MTC executive director, framed the goal as bringing 'the middle class back into transit'. Community values: participation and representation ('the exclusion of some communities from participation ... can itself contribute to an unequal distribution'), equitable access ('divestments in mobility can trap certain populations'), and relational trust ('The time I spent [working with MTC] was worse than a waste of time'). Maps to equitable access, relational trust, and participation.
Ideal traveler per decision-makers: Strong. 'New regional transportation policies ... favored the mobility needs of more affluent suburbanites over those of African American East Bay bus riders' (abstract). BART 'was not designed to' serve the urban core but 'to connect suburban professionals to downtown office jobs', and the stated aim was to bring 'the middle class back into transit'. MTC's model 'assumed most people would take BART' via 'the one best path in terms of minimum travel time'. The subsidy structure (6 to 14 dollars per trip rail versus about 3 per trip bus) and RTEP (94 percent to rail, local bus ineligible) encode the rail commuter as the investment priority. The ideal traveler is a suburban middle-class professional commuting by rail to a downtown office job; Judge Noonan's 'color-blind' framing treats the 'racially neutral criteria and technical analyses' as proof of no racialized consequence. No 'ideal traveler' phrasing.
Actual travelers encountered: Via the case and demographics: Oakland AC Transit bus riders, about 80 percent low-income people of color, facing 'stagnant' service, cuts, and fare hikes; low-income workers for whom 'the cost [of BART] is prohibitive'; communities 'isolated not only with respect to their local travel needs but also in their access to high-opportunity communities' because there is no 'direct bus service from Oakland to suburban job centers'; West Oakland residents 'not represented on OCCUR'; and advocates who joined MTC's equity analysis and left 'fatigued and disappointed'. The Los Angeles Bus Riders' Union (Labor/Community Strategy Center v. LA MTA, settled 1996) is a parallel.
Gap between the two: MTC distributed 'the benefits and burdens of new transit investment onto an already racialized geography', so 'race-neutral policies that promoted rail expansion at the expense of bus service had the effect of reproducing existing racial inequities' (journal p. 2). When advocates 'urged MTC to make more detailed analyses' and 'redistribute funding', 'MTC refused', ran an aggregated model that 'concluded the RTP was fair', and when a federal 'corrective action' made it invite advocates in, the analysis 'as in 1998, concluded the RTP was fair on similar grounds' (journal p. 19). The Lifeline gap study identified 2.1 billion dollars in needed transit for low-income communities; the 2001 RTP 'allocated no funding to Lifeline', the 2005 RTP 'just 10 percent'. Courts held the disparities 'justified'. And advisory-committee members concluded consultation was 'worse than a waste of time' while it let MTC 'say they consulted the community'.
Quotable moment: "'The time I spent [working with MTC] was worse than a waste of time,' reflects Reverend Andre Shumake ... 'Not only did they not accept many suggestions and recommendations from our diverse group, but now MTC can say they consulted the community about environmental justice.'" (journal p. 20). And on the model: it "determined travel paths by finding the 'one best path' in terms of minimum travel time without taking into account the prices" (journal p. 19, note 9).
Cross-comparison note (our synthesis): The strongest historical case in the set for our claim that 'racially neutral criteria and technical analyses' set the ideal traveler as an affluent suburban commuter and reproduce inequity without anyone stating intent. Concrete mechanisms transferable to AV planning: an equity model that aggregates modes so the disparity is invisible; a 'minimum travel time' path assumption that erases price; congestion benefits 'assumed' for the favored mode and 'never verified'; and a funding rule that makes the disfavored service 'not eligible ... at all'. The Shumake quote is a precise statement of consultation used as legitimation, and the Cypress Freeway and Fruitvale BART reversals show what community-forced redesign looks like when a legal lever (NEPA or Title VI) exists. Caveats: 2013, pre-AV; a historical and legal analysis, not fieldwork, with two of three authors participants in the litigation (disclosed); one region and one lawsuit the courts ultimately decided against the plaintiffs.

Paper Title: Inclusive planning: African policy inventory and South African mobility case study on the exclusion of persons with disabilities
Study type / basis for inclusion: A 29-country desktop policy inventory (no stakeholder contact, flagged as the main limitation) plus secondary analysis of the South African National Household Travel Survey. Not fieldwork; a contributor on the historical male, middle-class, private-car ideal and on policy that omits people with disabilities.
Case setting: 29 sub-Saharan African countries (11 Francophone, 18 Anglophone) for the policy inventory; South Africa as the mobility case study. Between 10 and 20 percent of the African population has a disability (5 to 10 percent school enrolment for disabled minors), with underreporting attributed to stigma. South Africa's 2011 Census put disability at 7.5 percent (highest among low-income and no-schooling groups, and among Black Africans at 7.8 percent). Anchored to the UNCRPD (2006) and SDG 11.2 ('access to safe, affordable, accessible and sustainable transport systems for all ... with special attention to the needs of those in vulnerable situations'). Funded by UKAid's Research for Community Access Partnership; feeds a Masters in Transport Leadership capacity-building programme.
Method(s), session by session: Two parts. (1) A desktop study, June to July 2020, by three trained researchers: collate two segments per country (constitutional and policy frameworks for people with disabilities; transport-sector-specific provisions per disability type), rate documents against an international best-practice benchmark (NACTO), accumulate and normalise scores 0 to 10 with a linear function, and produce heat maps in Excel. 'No contact was made with stakeholders in the various countries ... identified as the main limitation of this study' (journal p. 5); document availability online was used as a proxy for inclusiveness; the researchers' own experience in 12 of the 29 countries was used to validate. (2) Secondary analysis of the SANHTS raw data (collected January to March 2013, 51,341 households, 157,273 respondents, weighted to the population) comparing weekly trip rates of people with disabilities against able-bodied adults. Ethics approval; 'Participant consent was not required as only secondary data sources were used'.
Tools and artifacts: A disability-inclusion checklist (vision impairment, hearing impairment, mobility aids, other); a NACTO best-practice benchmark; a linear normalisation function; Excel heat maps; the SANHTS microdata; the UNCRPD and SDG 11.2 as normative anchors; Universal Design principles.
Underlying principle of the method: Universal Design plus the SDGs and the UNCRPD, the last of which 'recognized ... the need for PWDs to have the opportunity to be actively involved in decision-making processes about policies and programmes' (journal p. 2). A transport-justice frame (Martens) that 'tends to overlook how people are differently embodied'.
