'A lack of understanding of the needs of people with disabilities leads to isolation ... measured through trip frequencies'; and, on implementation, 'the devil is in the details'.
Provocation used to generate new ideas: None. Document analysis and secondary survey analysis.
Who holds design authority: National governments (constitutions and People with Disabilities Acts, with Ghana's 'the most inclusive'), transport ministries, and 'municipalities [that] play a crucial role'. 'Accessibility is not yet a systematic concern in the planning or implementation of urban transport infrastructure', and 'one of the implementation obstacles is the misconception that the application of universal design (UD) standards would be more costly'. The paper recommends including 'community leaders, nongovernmental organizations (NGOs), lobby groups ... in ongoing transport infrastructure implementation projects' in a 'custodial role', plus 'infrastructure audit capacity ... based on UD practices before opening to the public', while noting it 'did not investigate their potential role'. Scope: transport policy, infrastructure standards, and municipal implementation.
What is being designed: Nothing designed by the study. It produces a policy inventory (heat maps ranking 29 countries), a South African trip-rate analysis, and recommendations: translate inclusive policy into practice via municipal human-resource capacity and infrastructure audits; address road-safety and personal-security burdens on vulnerable road users; make constitutions 'people-centric'; and 'changing the way impacts are assessed ... will go a long way towards changing funding streams that are currently biased towards unsustainable, motorized, and private modes used by able-bodied individuals'.
Values surfaced in the case: Efficiency, capacity, and cost values: 'the misconception that the application of universal design (UD) standards would be more costly'; funding streams 'currently biased towards unsustainable, motorized, and private modes used by able-bodied individuals'; and the historical (1970s) focus on 'enhancing road capacity where drivers were predominantly male, middle-class workers, using private motor vehicles' (journal p. 2). Institutional omission: 'many African countries omit, or only superficially include, people with disabilities in their transport policy framework'. Community values: equitable access (people with disabilities 'live less integrated, more isolated lives'; SDG 11.2's 'transport ... for all'), participation and recognition (the UNCRPD's 'actively involved in decision-making', the recommendation to give NGOs a 'custodial role', and the study's own failure to consult stakeholders), and flexibility for variable need (a checklist across vision, hearing, mobility, and intellectual disability; 'the highest prevalence of disability ... among those with lower income'). Maps to equitable access, participation and recognition, and flexibility for variable need.
Ideal traveler per decision-makers: A strong historical statement: 'In the 1970s, the focus was enhancing road capacity where drivers were predominantly male, middle-class workers, using private motor vehicles' (journal p. 2), and funding streams remain 'biased towards ... motorized, and private modes used by able-bodied individuals' (journal p. 10). Policy frameworks 'omit, or only superficially include, people with disabilities', so the implicit subject of transport planning is an able-bodied private-car driver, and 'written information continues to be the most common form of communication', assuming a literate traveler. No 'ideal traveler' phrasing.
Actual travelers encountered: Via the SANHTS, with no direct fieldwork: in South Africa, '4.5 percent of the population did not travel at all in the 7 days before the interview, as disability or age prevented them ... or due to a lack of appropriate travel services'; people with disabilities' weekly trip rates are 'between 27.2 percent and 65.8 percent' of able-bodied adults' (mobility impairment minus 52.9 percent, self-care minus 27.2 percent, communication minus 65.8 percent); and people using a walking frame or stick, crutches, or wheelchairs. The authors cite their own earlier 'focus group interviews in Tshwane' (a separate study) with similar findings. Underreporting means many disabled people are not in the data at all.
Gap between the two: SDG 11.2 promises 'transport ... for all' and the UNCRPD requires people with disabilities be 'actively involved in decision-making', but 'many African countries omit, or only superficially include, people with disabilities in their transport policy framework', and even where 'inclusive policy frameworks exist, such as in Ghana, the translation ... into practice' is lacking. The measured result in the SANHTS is a 27 to 66 percent reduction in trip-making and 4.5 percent not travelling at all. Universal Design is blocked partly by 'the misconception that ... UD standards would be more costly'. And the study itself, in a paper about inclusive planning, 'made no contact ... with stakeholders' and 'did not investigate' the role of community leaders and NGOs.
Quotable moment: "In the 1970s, the focus was enhancing road capacity where drivers were predominantly male, middle-class workers, using private motor vehicles." (journal p. 2). And: "many African countries omit, or only superficially include, people with disabilities in their transport policy framework." (abstract, journal p. 1).
Cross-comparison note (our synthesis): A contributor whose single most useful line is the explicit statement that mid-20th-century transport planning was built for 'male, middle-class workers, using private motor vehicles', and that funding streams are still 'biased towards ... private modes used by able-bodied individuals', a direct articulation of the ideal-traveler default our argument names. The SANHTS trip-rate finding quantifies the cost. Also useful: the recommendation that impact-assessment methods be changed to redirect funding, and the observation that 'the misconception that UD standards would be more costly' is itself a barrier. Notably self-undermining for our purposes: a paper arguing for disability-inclusive planning that 'made no contact with stakeholders' and 'did not investigate' NGO and community-leader roles, a small illustration of how even equity research can proceed without the people it is about. Caveats: a desktop policy inventory using document availability as a proxy, plus secondary survey analysis, not fieldwork; 2013 SANHTS data; Africa-wide with a single-country (South Africa) mobility case.

Paper Title: The equity-environmental sustainability nexus in autonomous vehicles: An integrated framework for policy and planning
Study type / basis for inclusion: Conceptual and interpretive literature review plus a proposed framework, not fieldwork and no empirical case. The most on-topic paper in the set: explicitly about equitable, sustainable AV deployment, naming the induced-VMT, digital-divide, and affluent-first risks our argument targets.
Case setting: Autonomous passenger transport in urban contexts (freight and logistics excluded). No specific city; draws on the global AV policy debate and pilot literature. Bahrain-based authors (Bahrain Polytechnic, University of Bahrain). Part of a 'Sustainable Transport' special issue.
Method(s), session by session: A 'conceptual and interpretive approach rather than a systematic or integrative review' (journal p. 4). Steps: (1) critically review the AV literature on environmental and social-equity impacts, identifying 'specific research voids' in AV policy, community impacts, behavioral acceptance, and integrated assessment methods; (2) thematic synthesis 'across these strands to identify recurring gaps, tensions, and integration challenges'; (3) develop a conceptual framework (Fig. 1) with three core components (policy levers; equity dimensions; sustainability dimensions) linked by feedback loops and grounded in AV system design; (4) derive five 'key principles for integrated planning' (proactive and anticipatory planning; meaningful community engagement; adaptive governance; interdisciplinary collaboration; data-driven decision-making with integrated metrics); (5) an application pathway (Fig. 2) for iterative policy adaptation. No primary data.
Tools and artifacts: The three-component conceptual framework (Fig. 1); the application pathway (Fig. 2); the three-pillar sustainability model (Elkington); four policy levers (regulation, incentives, infrastructure investment, urban planning); equity dimensions (guaranteed accessibility, affordability, inclusive interfaces, community participation in decision-making, fair distribution of benefits and burdens); mobility justice as a keyword; and a cited synthesis of 74 AV studies (Parekh et al.).
Underlying principle of the method: 'Environmental degradation disproportionately affects marginalized communities, and conversely, social inequities can hinder the adoption and effectiveness of sustainable solutions', so the two must be optimised together. 'Technological advancement, while powerful, is not inherently benevolent', and 'without explicit ethical guidelines and robust governance, AVs could exacerbate existing societal problems' (journal p. 6). A shift from 'reactive rather than proactive' AV governance. 'Meaningful community engagement' and 'co-creation of AV solutions ... that reflect community values' as a framework pillar; 'planning processes must ... be community-centric, involving residents in the design and implementation of AV services'.
Provocation used to generate new ideas: The framework proposes 'pilot programs and impact assessments' to 'provide real-world evidence, enabling refinement and scaling', and calls for 'simulation models that can test different AV deployment scenarios'. No provocation is run by the authors; the paper is conceptual.
Who holds design authority: 'Governments and planners' hold the 'policy levers' (regulation, incentives, infrastructure investment, urban planning). The paper argues authority over AV deployment should be shared: 'meaningful participation of marginalized communities in AV planning and governance is essential', and 'community engagement should be a cornerstone of local AV planning'. It diagnoses the status quo: 'existing policies often focus on singular aspects, such as safety or technological regulation', a 'reactive rather than proactive approach' (journal p. 3). Technology choices (automation level, propulsion, service model) 'both shape and are shaped by policy'. Scope: AV regulation, pricing, infrastructure, land use, service model, and ethical decision-making frameworks.
What is being designed: The authors design a conceptual framework and an application pathway. Concrete proposals: 'mandate equitable access to AV services', 'tiered pricing structures, public-private partnerships, and targeted subsidies', 'subsidies for low-income users of AV services', HOV lanes adapted for shared AVs, 'AV paratransit services (on-demand, shared AVs)', zoning that 'encourage[s] shared AV services over private ownership', repurposing parking for 'housing, green spaces, or other community assets', 'performance-based regulations that incentivize positive social and environmental outcomes', and workforce retraining for displaced drivers.
Values surfaced in the case: Efficiency and technological-optimism values, named critically: AVs 'promise ... advancing environmental sustainability through efficiency gains', via 'optimized traffic flow, reduced congestion, increased vehicle utilization'; 'optimizing AV routes for maximum environmental efficiency might inadvertently bypass certain low-demand areas, impacting equitable access' (journal p. 6); 'a policy promoting widespread private AV ownership for individual convenience might improve personal mobility ... but could drastically increase VMT'; and a 'siloed approach' that optimises 'AV technology for environmental performance ... without adequately considering the distributional justice of these benefits'. Community values: equitable access ('guaranteed accessibility ... for all groups, including individuals with disabilities, the elderly, and low-income communities'; 'both physical and digital access'), relational trust ('building trust and acceptance'; 'transparent decision-making, and accountability mechanisms'), participation and recognition ('co-creation of AV solutions that ... reflect community values'; 'community-centric' planning), and flexibility for variable need ('inclusive interfaces'; 'context-specific solutions'). Maps to equitable access, relational trust, participation, and flexibility for variable need.
Ideal traveler per decision-makers: Strong and directly about AVs. 'The cost of AV services, especially in early deployment phases, could render them inaccessible to low-income individuals, creating a new form of transportation exclusion' (journal p. 3); 'the digital divide poses a barrier, as access to and proficiency with smartphone applications and digital platforms may be necessary to utilize AV services, potentially marginalizing those without such access'; and 'the spatial distribution of AV services could also be inequitable, with services initially concentrated in affluent urban areas'. On induced demand, AVs could become 'significantly cheaper, more convenient, and productive (e.g., allowing occupants to work or relax)'. The implicit AV rider the technology is optimised for is an affluent, urban, smartphone-owning individual who values a productive private commute. No 'ideal traveler' phrasing, but the 'affluent communities ... while burdening marginalized ones' framing is explicit.
Actual travelers encountered: None encountered (no fieldwork). From the literature, the populations at risk: 'low-income individuals, elderly, disabled, rural residents'; 'professional drivers' facing 'job displacement'; 'those without such access' to smartphones and digital platforms; 'underserved communities with limited or no access to these advanced mobility options'; and jaywalkers and pedestrians whose 'behavioral variability' AV planning must integrate.
Gap between the two: There is 'a significant void in comprehensive policy frameworks that explicitly integrate social equity and environmental sustainability considerations into AV deployment planning'; 'existing policies often focus on singular aspects, such as safety or technological regulation', producing 'a reactive rather than proactive approach' (journal p. 3). Research and policy 'treat these two critical dimensions in isolation'. 'The potential for AVs to either widen or narrow existing transportation disparities for marginalized groups ... remains a critical, yet under-researched area', with 'empirical evidence and prescriptive solutions ... often lacking'. And 'research often overlooks how perceptions of equity (or inequity) in AV deployment influence public acceptance'. The framework itself is untested: 'conceptual and interpretive', with no empirical validation.
Quotable moment: "the digital divide poses a barrier, as access to and proficiency with smartphone applications and digital platforms may be necessary to utilize AV services, potentially marginalizing those without such access." (journal p. 3). And: "technological advancement, while powerful, is not inherently benevolent. Without explicit ethical guidelines and robust governance, AVs could exacerbate existing societal problems." (journal p. 6).
Cross-comparison note (our synthesis): The most directly aligned paper in the set: it is our paper's premise, argued from the AV-policy literature. It independently names the three failure modes our argument leans on: affluent-area-first deployment, the smartphone and digital-divide access barrier, and induced VMT from a 'cheaper, more convenient, and productive' private ride. It also foregrounds 'meaningful community engagement' and 'co-creation ... that reflect community values' as a required framework pillar, and diagnoses current AV governance as 'reactive rather than proactive'. Useful as a citation for the state of the field and for the specific access mechanisms. Where it diverges from our framing: it treats equity and sustainability as co-optimisable via better frameworks and 'synergies' (for example 'shared electric AVs that reduce both emissions and transportation costs for low-income users'), a more technocratic, framework-driven remedy than our participation-first argument, and it offers no case, no fieldwork, and no evidence the framework changes outcomes. Caveats: a conceptual and interpretive review, self-described as 'not a systematic or integrative review'; no empirical validation; Bahrain-based authors writing at a global scale; 2026, still ahead of most large AV deployments.

Paper Title: From transportation equity to transportation justice: Within, through, and beyond the state
Study type / basis for inclusion: Theoretical and policy synthesis (author manuscript version, so pagination differs from the published article), not fieldwork. The clearest theoretical statement in the set of the state-centric equity versus society-centric justice split our argument runs on.
Case setting: US transportation planning. Central case example: the Fresno County Council of Governments participatory budgeting and equity advocacy in California's San Joaquin Valley (Karner et al. 2014). Other examples: the LA Bus Riders Union Title VI case (Labor and Community Strategy Center v. LACMTA); the Bay Area 6 Wins and EEJ alternative scenario (Marcantonio and Karner 2014); Buford Highway pedestrian improvements in Atlanta. Frames drawn from environmental justice movement scholarship.
Method(s), session by session: A literature synthesis. Steps: synthesize the transportation planning and environmental justice literature; review transportation equity and justice 'in practice'; place 'a sample of common planning activities on a continuum' from most state-centric to most society-centric (Table 1), scoring each by 'definition of justice, recognition of knowledge, and examples from the literature and practice'; and derive implications for scholars, practitioners, and advocates. No primary data. The paper argues for a 'shift in focus from transportation equity to transportation justice'.
Tools and artifacts: Table 1 (the state-to-society-centric continuum of planning activities); Schlosberg's tripartite justice (distribution, procedure, recognition); Martens's 'sufficientarianism' and 'ladder of justice standards' (from strict legal compliance to 'restorative equalization'); the capabilities approach (Sen, Nussbaum); 'inside' versus 'outside' society-centric strategies; performance-based planning; Title VI disparate-impact litigation; participatory budgeting; and scenario planning.
Underlying principle of the method: 'Transportation justice describes a normative condition in which no person or group is disadvantaged by a lack of access to the opportunities they need to lead a meaningful and dignified life', requiring 'transforming the structures and processes'. Justice also requires that 'residents and other stakeholders should be able to actively participate in and influence the decisions that affect their lives' and 'a recognition of diverse forms of knowledge in decision making' (Schlosberg). Environmental justice scholarship's state-centric critique: 'the state works to bolster rather than constrain racialized attacks on vulnerable communities'. The society-centric alternative: social movements 'working with and on behalf of disadvantaged populations ... sometimes in collaboration but often in conflict with public-sector planners'. Distinguishes reform (equity, state actors) from transformation (justice, activists).
Provocation used to generate new ideas: The society-centric case examples include provocation-type moves (the 6 Wins EEJ alternative scenario 'modeled alongside the agency's preferred alternative'; community-led analysis 'in partnership with academic researchers'). The paper itself is a synthesis.
Who holds design authority: 'Transportation policies, plans, and projects all flow through state institutions because of the substantial cost of infrastructure and the need to assess ... performance', and 'the impetus for such efforts stems from the formal authority of the state to regulate and finance transportation improvements'. 'In almost all cases in practice, the agency itself is responsible for undertaking this type of performance analysis on data that it generates' (manuscript p. 9). Formal EJ law 'emphasizes an agency-led performance analysis process, from data collection and analysis to the determination of disproportionate impacts and the selection of alternatives and mitigations' (manuscript p. 10). 'Public involvement is also solicited, but it is often pro forma, and its results are unlikely to affect ultimate decisions'. Society-centric approaches shift agency toward 'community-based organizations'. Scope: the whole transportation-planning apparatus.
What is being designed: Nothing designed by the study. It designs a conceptual continuum (Table 1) and a research and practice agenda: 'state-centric strategies such as developing new equity-oriented tools, metrics, and planning processes are necessary, but not sufficient'; planners must 'develop new ways of engaging with environmental justice and related social movements'; and approaches 'which emphasize the agency and power of community-based organizations and acknowledging and addressing structural factors ... will be crucial'.
Values surfaced in the case: State, efficiency, and technical values: 'transportation planners around the world more commonly focus on technical fixes and quantitative equity analyses ... often relying upon large-scale simulation models of future land use and travel behavior' (manuscript p. 3); 'performance-based planning can provide false certainty for less common or more novel metrics (such as non-auto travel or collision rates) ... because the travel demand models used to evaluate outcomes were built to assess ... vehicle delays or congestion levels' (manuscript p. 9); 'strict legal compliance ... is easy to achieve as long as an agency conducts some equity-related analysis'; and 'low justice standards simply seek to not make existing conditions worse'. Community values: participation and recognition ('stakeholders should be able to actively participate in and influence the decisions'; 'recognition of diverse forms of knowledge'), equitable access ('no person or group is disadvantaged by a lack of access'; 'restorative equalization'), and relational trust ('building trust by using neutral facilitators'; the risk that a public process lets an agency claim it consulted the community). Maps to participation and recognition, equitable access, and relational trust.
Ideal traveler per decision-makers: Adjacent and methodological. Travel demand models 'were built to assess ... more traditional measures such as vehicle delays or congestion levels', so they give 'false certainty' on 'non-auto travel or collision rates' (manuscript p. 9), meaning the modelled subject is a car commuter contributing to delay. Equity analysis is 'imbued with substantial subjectivity' and 'determining whether the results demonstrate evidence of (in)equity is often left until the analysis is conducted'. US EJ practice fixes attention 'on people of color and low-income people', while European practice identifies 'individuals and locations at risk of low participation'. The implicit traveler in the state-centric model is a car user whose congestion the model was built to measure. No 'ideal traveler' phrasing.
Actual travelers encountered: Via cited case examples, with no direct fieldwork: LA bus riders in the BRU case ('two separate and unequal' systems); San Joaquin Valley frontline communities engaged through Fresno County participatory budgeting; Bay Area low-income communities of color behind the EEJ scenario; Buford Highway pedestrians; and, in general, 'people of color, low-income people, people with disabilities, older adults, and youth ... at risk of various forms of transportation injustice'.
Gap between the two: 'Most research and planning practice related to transportation equity has relied upon state-sponsored analytical methods', which 'mainly reform, rather than transform, the transportation system and leave unchanged the power positions and well-being of disadvantaged populations'. 'Public involvement ... is often pro forma, and its results are unlikely to affect ultimate decisions'. 'In almost all cases in practice, the agency itself is responsible' for the analysis 'on data that it generates'. Justice (transformation, participation, recognition) is what activists pursue; equity (reform, distribution) is what state actors do; 'state-centric strategies ... are necessary, but not sufficient'. The society-centric alternative has its own limits (financial fragility, 'mission creep', professionalisation from 'outside agitators' to 'advisory committees', and NIMBY tendencies).
Quotable moment: "Public involvement is also solicited, but it is often pro forma, and its results are unlikely to affect ultimate decisions." (manuscript p. 3). And: "state-centric strategies such as developing new equity-oriented tools, metrics, and planning processes are necessary, but not sufficient to achieve transportation justice." (manuscript p. 4).
Cross-comparison note (our synthesis): The clearest theoretical statement in the set of the split our argument runs on: 'equity' as state-centric reform (better tools, metrics, distribution) versus 'justice' as transformation that requires participation, recognition of diverse knowledge, and a shift of agency to community-based organizations. Directly useful: the observation that travel demand models 'were built to assess ... vehicle delays or congestion levels' so they under-serve non-auto and safety metrics is a precise version of our claim that the modelling apparatus encodes the car commuter, and 'the agency itself is responsible for undertaking this ... analysis on data that it generates' names the closed loop. The Fresno and Bay Area cases are cited as partial society-centric wins. Caveats: a theoretical synthesis, not fieldwork; US-focused; the author's manuscript version, so page numbers do not match the published Journal of Planning Literature article; the society-centric alternative is presented with its own significant limits.

Paper Title: The promise of Universal Basic Mobility
Study type / basis for inclusion: Literature review of Universal Basic Mobility, synthesising social-policy formation, US transportation-policy history, and mobility-justice theory, plus a table of US pilots. Not fieldwork. Contributor on the mode-supply default and on travel speed as the planner's proxy for mobility.
Case setting: US transportation policy. UBM pilots tabulated (Table 1): Oakland, California (West Oakland, two cohorts, 300 dollars on prepaid debit plus a community partner), Pittsburgh (2022 to 2023, free transit pass, EV carshare, and e-bike access, 50 people), Los Angeles (South LA, two cohorts, 1,800 dollars a year on prepaid debit), plus Stockton and Bakersfield. Historical: the McCone Commission after the 1965 Watts uprising blamed 'inadequate and costly transportation for the isolation of residents in South Central Los Angeles' and recommended transit; the Job Access and Reverse Commute program; Obama- and Biden-era equity initiatives.
Method(s), session by session: 'A thorough examination of literature' across three bodies: (1) frameworks of past and current social policy formation (basic needs versus capabilities; universal versus means-tested; supply-side versus demand-side); (2) empirical evidence on previous US transportation policy for the transportation-insecure; and (3) theories of transportation and mobility justice. The review synthesises three 'essential elements' of UBM (mobility as essential to well-being; targeting resources to the transportation-insecure; combining supply and demand components) and proposes a definition. It compiles a table of US UBM pilots. US-focused 'to manage the scope'.
Tools and artifacts: A comparison table of US UBM pilots (eligibility, benefit, cohort size); the basic needs approach (Doyal and Gough); the capabilities approach (Sen, Nussbaum); 'targeted universalism' (powell et al.); 'transportation insecurity' (Murphy et al.); mobility justice (Sheller, Untokening Collective); the 'mobility wallet' concept; and universal basic income as an analogue.
Underlying principle of the method: Mobility justice (Sheller; Untokening) and the capabilities approach: 'mobility is about people having freedom of movement, or, the capability to move in ways and to places that best suits oneself'. Against 'the traditional notion of mobility as just the ability to move between different activity sites, which transportation planners and engineers most often boil down to travel speed' (journal p. 356). Transportation has historically been 'excluded ... from basic needs frameworks' as a 'derived demand'. 'Targeted universalism': not 'everyone with the same mobility resources' but targeting 'those suffering from transportation insecurity'. Mobility justice 'asks planners and policymakers to repair past harm ... and so centre voices of those experiencing ... transportation disparities'.
Provocation used to generate new ideas: None. A literature review and typology.
Who holds design authority: Local US jurisdictions design and run UBM pilots (LA DOT, the City of Pittsburgh, the City of Oakland), setting the benefit form, cohort size, eligibility, and duration. Federal history: the McCone Commission recommended transit; JARC; presidential initiatives. The paper argues design should 'look beyond specific modes to people and their needs' and 'centre voices of those experiencing ... transportation disparities'. It critiques current pilots for 'misalignment between current program goals and the basic premise of UBM'. Scope: transportation subsidy programs, service provision, and program eligibility and delivery.
What is being designed: Nothing designed by the study. It proposes a definition and a set of 'essential elements' for UBM and a critique and redirect of existing pilots. Its conceptual product: UBM as 'the guaranteed provision of resources, subsidy and service, that allows individuals who disproportionately suffer from transportation insecurity to get to where they need and want to go in a way that best suits them and those who depend on them'.
Values surfaced in the case: Efficiency and mode-supply values: US transportation policy's 'myopic focus on mode, rather than people's ability to move around and reach destinations'; 'the provision of public transit alone has largely kept such travellers at a disadvantage'; planners and engineers who 'boil down' mobility 'to travel speed'; and transportation framed as 'a derived demand'. Means-tested-benefit values: benefits 'typically are low, sometimes time-limited, and often include behavioural expectations ... intended to disincentivize lengthy stays'; 'social constructions of deservedness'; and a 'dominant U.S. model ... one that prioritises minimal government intervention and a reliance on the private market'. Community values: equitable access (transportation insecurity; 'targeted universalism'; the transportation-insecure 'live in poverty, do not own cars, live in urban areas, are younger, have less education, and are people of colour'), flexibility for variable need ('the service side of UBM cannot take a one-size-fits-all approach'; 'in a way that best suits them'), and participation and recognition ('centre voices of those experiencing ... transportation disparities'). Maps to equitable access, flexibility for variable need, and participation.
Ideal traveler per decision-makers: Adjacent and clean. Transportation planning 'most often boil[s] down [mobility] to travel speed' and treats transportation as 'a derived demand', so the implicit subject is a trip-maker whose value is measured in minutes saved. US transportation policy 'has largely relied on supply-side interventions, namely, public transit' (journal p. 357), assuming a rider who can reach and use fixed-route transit, which 'do[es] not work as well in dispersed environments such as suburbs, where a majority of low-income and people of colour in the U.S. now live'. The assumed traveler is a car owner whose speed is optimised or a dense-urban transit rider; the carless suburban low-income person is outside both. Means-tested framing further assumes an undeserving claimant needing 'behavioural expectations'. No 'ideal traveler' phrasing.
Actual travelers encountered: None directly (a review). The transportation-insecure per Murphy et al.: people who 'live in poverty, do not own cars, live in urban areas, are younger, have less education, and are people of colour', plus 'those who are prohibited from driving due to age, immigration status, or ability'. UBM pilot participants in Oakland, Pittsburgh, Los Angeles, Stockton, and Bakersfield (an Oakland mid-program survey reported '40 percent of respondents' reducing personal-vehicle use). And the South Central Los Angeles residents identified by the McCone Commission in 1965.
Gap between the two: US transportation policy for the transportation-insecure has been 'piecemeal, largely focused on interventions specific to a single mode (most often public transit), a single neighbourhood, and/or demonstration projects that operate for limited periods', and 'these approaches have not adequately addressed the needs ... [and] have had little effect on mitigating poverty'. Current UBM pilots show 'misalignment between current program goals and the basic premise of UBM', so they 'are poised to repeat the same mistakes'. Means-tested benefits are 'low, sometimes time-limited', with 'behavioural expectations'. And planning still treats mobility as travel speed and a derived demand rather than 'a basic need'.
Quotable moment: Mobility justice goes "beyond the traditional notion of mobility as just 'the ability to move between different activity sites', which transportation planners and engineers most often boil down to travel speed." (journal p. 356). And: "a myopic focus on mode, rather than people's ability to move around and reach destinations, has insufficiently addressed transportation disparities." (journal p. 358).
Cross-comparison note (our synthesis): A contributor whose most useful line is that transportation planning 'boil[s] down' mobility 'to travel speed' and treats it as 'a derived demand', a compact statement of the efficiency frame our argument critiques. UBM is offered as the corrective: mode-agnostic, targeted, resources plus service, 'in a way that best suits them', close to our 'flexibility for variable need' and to a Mobility as Social Service framing. The pilot table (Oakland, Pittsburgh, Los Angeles) is a concrete inventory of what is being tried, and the paper's own critique, that the pilots are 'poised to repeat the same mistakes' because they stay mode-focused, is a useful caution against reading UBM as already solving the participation problem, since the paper never claims the pilots co-designed anything with participants. Caveats: a literature review, no fieldwork; US-only; the pilots are small and short; the paper is definitional and does not evaluate outcomes.

Paper Title: Enhancing Equity in Public Transportation Using Geographic Information Systems and Spatial Optimization
Study type / basis for inclusion: Quantitative GIS and spatial-optimization modeling study (Maximal Covering Location Problem plus a bi-objective model), one worked application to a single city. No fieldwork and no participation. Contributor: a clean, self-aware specimen of the coverage-maximisation frame our argument critiques, and of design authority held entirely by the analyst and the transit agency.
Case setting: City of Hilliard, Ohio, a suburb near downtown Columbus served by the Central Ohio Transit Authority (COTA). 9,646 parcels on the base map. A desk study built on census, socioeconomic, and land-use data layers; no residents were contacted.
Method(s), session by session: No sessions. Analytical pipeline: (1) identify origin-based transport-disadvantaged parcels from socioeconomic and demographic data (young under 14, old 65 and over, household income below 15,000 dollars a year, zero-vehicle households, disabled people); (2) identify destination-based demand parcels from land-use data (employment, shopping, amenities, education, public services); (3) discretise the road network into candidate bus-stop points (914 origin-based, 163 destination-based) using Polygon Intersection with Network Point Set (PINPS); (4) run the Maximal Covering Location Problem for p = 2 to 50 stops against a 400 metre suitable-access standard; (5) build a bi-objective MCLP combining origin- and destination-based coverage via the weighting method, varying weight w from 0 to 1; (6) read the tradeoff curves and select coverage levels, treating 70 to 80 percent as 'efficient given demand and limited conditions'.
Tools and artifacts: GIS; the Maximal Covering Location Problem (Church and ReVelle 1974); PINPS network discretisation; the weighting method for multi-objective optimization; Pareto (tradeoff) curves; census and land-use data layers; a 400 metre access-standard buffer. No participatory or design artifacts.
Underlying principle of the method: Distributive equity as the fair spatial distribution of service: 'equity in public transportation is concerned with the fair distribution of public transportation service' (p. 2), and public investment 'ought to favor the transport disadvantaged' (Hodge 1995, cited p. 3). Operationalised as coverage maximisation: 'the most efficient and feasible way is to adjust the location of facilities such as service stop locations or service routes' (p. 3). Equity is rendered as a quantity: 'This improved level of access for the transport disadvantaged exemplifies evidence of enhanced levels of equity' (p. 4). Need is inferred from census categories, never asked.
Provocation used to generate new ideas: None. A modeling study.
Who holds design authority: The analyst and the transit agency (COTA). 'any combination of weights can be selected based on the planning strategy of the decision makers, and associated preferences' (p. 25); the model determines 'how many new service stops are required and where they should be located' (p. 4). Residents of the transport-disadvantaged parcels are data inputs (demand points), not participants. Scope: bus-stop siting and route coverage inside a fixed-route system.
What is being designed: Locations for new bus stops added to COTA's existing fixed route in Hilliard: 22 to 26 stops for origin-based coverage, 28 to 36 for destination-based coverage, and a consolidated bi-objective set of 36 stops. The service model itself (fixed route) is held constant.
Values surfaced in the case: Efficiency and cost-recovery values, stated plainly: adjusted stop locations giving 'higher ridership as well as better access ... would contribute to increasing revenues of the public transportation operator and likely decrease the need for governmental subsidy' (p. 3 to 4); coverage of '70% to 80% is efficient given demand and limited conditions, such as planning budget' (p. 16); 'Decision makers are usually interested in the general pattern of tradeoff curve, not in specific gap points' (p. 20). Distributive-equity values: service 'should favor the transport disadvantaged'; mobility and accessibility as 'basic needs for all members of a community' (p. 3). Against our three community values it addresses equitable access only in the thin sense of proximity to a stop; relational trust and flexibility for variable need are absent; and the future-research suggestion is to add 'maximization of current regular demand, which is located in mostly densely populated or commuting areas' (p. 25), pulling back toward the commuter. Maps to equitable access (thin), efficiency, and cost recovery.
Ideal traveler per decision-makers: Strong and explicit for a technical paper. The paper names the status quo it reacts against: recent transit investment's 'beneficiaries are mainly commuters, which are mostly the able-bodied and employed' (Denmark 1998, quoted p. 3). Its own modelled subject is a parcel: a person is 'suitably covered' when within 400 metres of a stop, regardless of trip purpose, schedule, fare, transfers, or any disability beyond the census flag. Access is defined purely as 'a person's proximity to service and cost' (p. 4), and value is measured as coverage percentage. No 'ideal traveler' phrasing.
Actual travelers encountered: None. The 'transport disadvantaged' appear only as census aggregates, 'the young, the old, low income earners, those with no vehicle and the disabled' (p. 3), rendered as origin-based demand parcels (Figure 1). The one field contact the paper mentions is with the road data, not people: for an uncovered area in southwestern Hilliard, 'some field work by the author found that this absence of roads is an error in the data layer' (p. 16).
Gap between the two: The paper concedes its equity is theoretical: the coverage figures are 'theoretical statistical findings' and 'The most suitable combination of coverage would be based on specific planning goals' (p. 23). It notes that existing paratransit and community transport 'are not integrated services into fixed-routes but separate complementary services' (p. 6) and that 'service quality can only be meaningful when people have access' (p. 4), yet it never checks whether a modelled stop is one a rider would or could actually use. The 400 metre standard is acknowledged as contestable: if some demand areas 'are actually too far away ... this will raise another issue of the justification of suitable access standard of 400 meters. Otherwise, this demand area will be permanently excluded from bus service coverage' (p. 16).
Quotable moment: "If adjusted public transportation facility locations provided higher ridership as well as better access, it would contribute to increasing revenues of the public transportation operator and likely decrease the need for governmental subsidy." (p. 3 to 4). And: "most convex-shaped MCLP tradeoff results consider that coverage of 70% to 80% is efficient given demand and limited conditions, such as planning budget" (p. 16).
Cross-comparison note (our synthesis): A pure-modeling contributor useful precisely as a specimen of the frame our argument critiques. It defines equity as a coverage percentage, infers need from census categories rather than asking anyone, holds the fixed-route service model constant, and states openly that the payoff of better siting is 'increasing revenues of the public transportation operator and likely decrease[d] ... governmental subsidy'. Design authority sits entirely with the analyst and COTA; residents are demand points. Set against the fieldwork rows, it shows what stands in for participation when participation is absent: a 400 metre buffer and a weight slider. The honest touches (equity numbers called 'theoretical', the 400 metre standard flagged as contestable, the one permanently uncovered neighbourhood) make it a fair rather than a straw example. Caveats: 2020, single city, no fieldwork or participation by design; the 'ideal traveler per decision-makers' cell here is inferred from how the model defines a covered person, not from any stated persona.

Paper Title: Inclusive Mobility: Dismantling transportation injustice at the intersection of race and disability
Study type / basis for inclusion: Viewpoint / conceptual article (not fieldwork): a historical synthesis plus a conceptual framework (Fig. 1) arguing for an intersectional (race by disability) lens on transportation injustice. Included as a contributor above all for one thing: it names the transit planner's 'ideal rider' explicitly.
Case setting: US public transportation, focused on two overlapping populations, Black people and disabled people. Running example: Baltimore, Maryland (the 'Black Butterfly' versus 'white L' transit-stop disparity; the cancelled Red Line). Authors at the University of Michigan and Johns Hopkins. The copy read is a ClinicalKey page-print, so pagination is the 6-page PDF's, and the journal cites the article as 101848.
Method(s), session by session: No sessions. A three-part argument: (1) describe transportation history for Black people and for disabled people in the US (slavery and segregation, redlining, highway clearance, 'white flight'; ableist exclusion, the 1978 Gang of 19, section 504, the ADA and its 'voluntary compliance' gap); (2) articulate the public-health impact of transportation injustice; (3) advocate an intersectional lens and community-led planning. Presents a conceptual framework (Fig. 1) to guide future research. No primary data collection.
Tools and artifacts: Intersectionality theory (Crenshaw); mobility justice (Sheller; Cidell) and Crip Mobility Justice (Hamraie); the five A's of access (available, affordable, adjacent, accommodating, acceptable); 'catalytic forecasting'; the conceptual framework Fig. 1; American Community Survey disability-by-race data (Table 1); FTA public-involvement and Title VI guidance.
Underlying principle of the method: Mobility justice and Crip Mobility Justice: 'Dismantling transportation injustice requires that everyone has access to transportation that allows for a meaningful, dignified, and fulfilling life' (p. 3). Intersectionality: people 'do not live single issue lives' (Lorde, quoted p. 4). Explicitly participatory in its prescription: 'Characterizing, measuring, and dismantling transportation injustice must include leadership by those who are most impacted' and 'Public systems must empower voices that have been sidelined' (p. 4); 'community-led planning and policy-making that center the voices of marginalized groups' (p. 4 to 5).
Provocation used to generate new ideas: None run. As protest history it cites the Gang of 19 blocking buses ('We Will Ride!') and the #WheresMyRide campaign as disruptive claims on the system.
Who holds design authority: Transit agencies and government. 'When cities developed and invested in public transportation systems, people with disabilities were not included as planners or thought of as potential users' (p. 2). ADA implementation was left to agencies via 'voluntary compliance and freedom to deny accommodations if financially burdensome' (p. 2). On the cancelled Red Line, Maryland's administration 'did not seek input from the Department of Transportation, Baltimore citizens, or community groups on this decision' (p. 2). The paper argues authority should shift: 'share power so community voices are part of decision-making', and involve 'potential users at all stages of the transportation lifecycle (design, advisory boards, procurement, and implementation)' (p. 5). Scope: transit service design, stop siting, paratransit eligibility and provision, and the FTA grant and Title VI process.
What is being designed: Nothing built by the paper. It designs a research framework (Fig. 1) and a set of prescriptions: collect disability data 'in all locations where demographic information is collected'; use catalytic forecasting to site stops and set frequency; make Title VI disparate-impact review apply to 'all changes (not only major changes)'; make public engagement 'accessible, offer flexible opportunities for feedback, and share power'.
Values surfaced in the case: The efficiency and cost-burden frame appears as the mechanism of exclusion: ADA accommodations can be denied 'if financially burdensome' (p. 2); the 'segregated demand-response system is challenging for transportation systems to operate due to financial and structural reasons', so paratransit is 'often less efficient, reliable, and flexible than comparable fixed-route' service, and labor shortages drive 'major scale backs to paratransit coverage areas and denial of trip requests' (p. 3), with 41 percent of Chicago paratransit pickups late (p. 3). Even the reform tool is sold on efficiency: catalytic forecasting 'increasing overall efficiency and equity of movement in cities' (p. 4). Community values named: equitable access (as a 'fundamental human right'), relational trust (the Red Line cancellation with no consultation; racial profiling in paratransit eligibility assessments, p. 3), flexibility for variable need ('availability, quality, quantity, and flexibility' of service to the disability community, p. 3; Crip Mobility Justice's 'greater flexibility in multi-model transit systems'), and participation and recognition ('share power'; 'leadership by those who are most impacted'). Maps to equitable access, relational trust, flexibility for variable need, and participation and recognition.
Ideal traveler per decision-makers: The strongest single statement in the whole set. 'Public transit systems frequently design their services with a specific "ideal rider" in mind, usually an economically secure, able-bodied, white male commuter. This bias can exclude and disadvantage individuals who don't match this profile, by failing to meet their needs' (p. 1, drawing on Lubitow et al. 2017). Historically reinforced: disabled people 'were not included as planners or thought of as potential users' (p. 2). A direct, citable articulation of the decision-makers' imagined traveler.
Actual travelers encountered: None met by the authors. Reported via campaign testimony: Tierra Fletcher (the article spells it 'Flecther'), 'a Black, disabled woman being stranded by the paratransit system' in Baltimore, whose booked ride was pushed to 2:00 AM (quoted p. 3, from the #WheresMyRide campaign). Population-level: 'nearly two-thirds of people with disabilities report problems using public transportation' and '70 % of disabled adults reduce daily travel because of inaccessible transportation' (p. 2); Black residents of the 'Black Butterfly' neighborhoods that 'host the fewest public transportation stops, greatest need of transportation investment, and highest disease prevalence' (p. 2).
Gap between the two: The imagined 'economically secure, able-bodied, white male commuter' against riders for whom the fixed-route system was never accessible and the paratransit fallback is 'less efficient, reliable, and flexible', scaled back, and subject to racial profiling at the eligibility gate. The ADA's promise is undercut by 'voluntary compliance' and a cost-burden exemption. Major infrastructure decisions (the Red Line) are made without consulting the affected public-transit-dependent population. And the evidence base itself has a gap: 'what is known about transportation experiences for Black, disabled people is limited' because disability data is not collected everywhere demographic data is.
Quotable moment: "Public transit systems frequently design their services with a specific 'ideal rider' in mind, usually an economically secure, able-bodied, white male commuter. This bias can exclude and disadvantage individuals who don't match this profile, by failing to meet their needs." (p. 1). And, Tierra Fletcher via the #WheresMyRide campaign: "They said we're not going to be able to pick you up until 2:00 AM in the morning. This was at 8:55. I'm in an area where it's darkly lit. Anything can happen to me. So, then that caused me to have a panic attack." (p. 3).
Cross-comparison note (our synthesis): The single most quotable source in the set for the decision-makers' side of our ideal-traveler comparison: it states outright that transit 'design[s] their services with a specific "ideal rider" in mind, usually an economically secure, able-bodied, white male commuter'. The rest of the paper is consistent with our argument: infrastructure decisions made about communities rather than with them (redlining, highway clearance, the Red Line cancellation 'without input'), a cost-burden logic that lets agencies deny accommodations, and a prescription that is participation-first (share power, leadership by the most impacted, users involved 'at all stages of the transportation lifecycle'). The intersectional (race by disability) framing sharpens the point: exclusion compounds. Caveats: a viewpoint article, no fieldwork or new data; the one lived-experience account is second-hand campaign testimony (attributed); US-only; ClinicalKey page-print, so page numbers are the 6-page PDF's.

Paper Title: Inclusive and Accessible Transportation for All: Strategies for Integrating Equity in Transportation Research
Study type / basis for inclusion: Narrative literature review of how equity is 'conceptualized, measured, and operationalized' in transportation planning, cataloguing the assessment methods and tools. Not fieldwork. Contributor: a clean inventory of the technocratic equity toolbox our argument contrasts with participation, and of 'groups of concern' defined by analysts from demographic data.
Case setting: US-centred transportation research and planning literature (the paper notes as a limitation that 'only one geographic location is considered'). Authors at North Carolina A&T State University and the University of Tennessee at Knoxville. Illustrative examples drawn from San Francisco (SFCTA travel demand microsimulation, congestion pricing), Perth, Paris, and Melbourne.
Method(s), session by session: No sessions. A synthesis: (1) set out the concept of equity, split into horizontal equity ('the equal treatment of similar groups') and vertical equity ('prioritizing disadvantaged populations'); (2) review measurement, cost-benefit analysis, population-group identification, and distributive principles; (3) catalogue measuring tools, indicators, and models (accessibility, affordability, service quality, equity models); (4) review planning and policy instruments (congestion pricing, TOD, Vision Zero); (5) list 'factors for developing equity' (demographic analysis, socioeconomic considerations, transport and land-use integration); (6) conclusions and future research. Includes a summary comparison table of methods and data sources. No primary data.
Tools and artifacts: Accessibility indices and Lorenz-curve measures; affordability metrics (Location Affordability Index, Housing + Transportation Affordability Index, Transportation Cost Index); cost-benefit analysis; travel demand models (activity-based, tour-based microsimulation, SF-CHAMP and RPM-9); the Environmental Justice framework and the Capability Approach; Rawlsian and Walzerian 'spheres of justice' distributive models; 'Justice Tests' for transit investment (Nazari and Donovan); surveys and user feedback for service quality; GIS mapping of minority and low-income areas near proposed projects.
Underlying principle of the method: Distributive equity operationalised through two lenses, horizontal ('fair distribution among individuals or groups with similar needs') and vertical ('resource allocation based on diverse needs and abilities, particularly for marginalized groups'). Justice-based models 'move beyond traditional cost-benefit or demand-based analyses by explicitly asking whether transportation resources and opportunities are distributed fairly', prioritising 'improving accessibility for those who are worst off, thus operationalizing "Rawlsian principles of justice"' (p. 19). The remedy the review proposes is methodological: 'clearer and more consistent frameworks, improved data collection, and more inclusive, community-driven decision-making processes' (abstract).
Provocation used to generate new ideas: None. A review.
Who holds design authority: 'Transit agencies and researchers employ different models and design approaches to evaluate the degree and methodology of equity integration' (p. 18). Authority over both assessment and design sits with agencies and analysts: the San Francisco County Transportation Authority runs the microsimulation that 'identif[ies] groups of concern'; planners perform 'demographic analysis' to 'identify equitable and effective solutions'. The only nod to shifting authority is the conclusion's call for 'Inclusive decision-making processes that involve underrepresented communities' so 'their voices are considered', and for 'involving community stakeholders'. Scope: transit service and network planning, fare and pricing policy, TOD, and project appraisal.
What is being designed: Nothing built. The paper synthesises an assessment apparatus and recommends its standardisation: 'standardized methods for incorporating equity considerations into transportation project appraisals', 'clearer, more actionable frameworks and metrics', better data collection, and 'progressive redistribution strategies in policies like congestion pricing'.
Values surfaced in the case: Efficiency and effectiveness as the inherited frame, stated up front: conventional transportation research 'focused on improving the physical components of transportation networks and developing measures to improve their efficiency and effectiveness' (p. 1). The tools carry it forward: service-quality improvement is valued because it 'can lead to increased ridership, shorter travel times, and improved overall satisfaction' (p. 18); land-use integration culminates 'in more efficient and accessible mobility systems' (p. 23); models are praised for 'a more precise assessment of transportation policy consequences' (p. 19). Community values, mostly as aspiration: equitable access (vertical equity; 'those who are worst off'; Universal Design for facilities), participation (the abstract's and conclusion's 'community-driven decision-making'; 'their voices are considered'), and flexibility for variable need (vertical equity's 'diverse needs and abilities'; the caveat that dense-urban fixes 'may not be appropriate for low-density suburban or rural areas'). The review concedes its own tools' blind spots: 'surveys and feedback ... often capture only a snapshot' and 'the impact of service quality on accessibility outcomes for individuals with disabilities ... may not be adequately addressed' (p. 18 to 19). Maps to equitable access, participation, and flexibility for variable need, with efficiency as the baseline value.
Ideal traveler per decision-makers: Implicit and methodological. Equity models 'group people based on socioeconomic status', and the SFCTA microsimulation 'identif[ies] groups of concern based on income, car availability, household composition, and gender', then 'assesses equity using mobility and accessibility metrics such as travel time and job access' (p. 19). The default modelled subject is a commuter whose worth is measured in travel time and job access; the 'disadvantaged' traveler enters only as a demographic subgroup the model flags. Demographic analysis of 'age, race, gender, English proficiency, and household composition' is what stands in for knowing who the travelers are (p. 23). No 'ideal traveler' phrasing.
Actual travelers encountered: None. Populations appear only as analytic categories: 'low-income populations', 'individuals with disabilities', 'marginalized groups', 'underserved populations', and the model-defined 'groups of concern'. The paper itself notes that 'comprehensive data on the transportation needs and patterns of disadvantaged groups are insufficient' (p. 24).
Gap between the two: The review documents the gap in its own domain: equity is inconsistently defined and operationalised, 'practical methods for assessing these objectives are lacking', data on disadvantaged groups' needs is 'insufficient', and 'current evaluations often capture only snapshots of user experiences and may not fully reflect the long-term or nuanced impacts' (p. 24). Its fix is more and better method (standardised frameworks, richer data, advanced modelling), with 'inclusive decision-making' named last and least developed. It does not examine whether the modelled 'groups of concern' recognise themselves in the analysis, or whether any of the tools involve the affected public in defining what counts as equitable.
Quotable moment: "This conventional perspective has focused on improving the physical components of transportation networks and developing measures to improve their efficiency and effectiveness." (p. 1). And: "while surveys and feedback are useful, they often capture only a snapshot of the user experience and may not fully reflect the long-term or nuanced impacts of service quality on different population groups." (p. 19).
Cross-comparison note (our synthesis): A contributor useful as a catalogue of the equity-assessment toolbox that our argument sets against participation: accessibility indices, affordability indices, cost-benefit analysis, travel demand microsimulation, Rawlsian 'Justice Tests'. In every tool the affected population is a data category ('groups of concern', demographic subgroups), and the paper's own worked example (SFCTA) shows equity being 'considered at every level' by the agency's own model. It names the inherited value plainly, transportation research built to improve 'efficiency and effectiveness', and concedes its tools miss the 'nuanced' and the disability-specific. Its remedy is more method plus a late, thin call for 'community-driven decision-making'. Set against the fieldwork rows, it is a clean picture of the analyst-centred alternative. Caveats: a narrative review, no fieldwork or new data, US-focused and self-limited to 'one geographic location'; MDPI Logistics, 2025; the 'ideal traveler' reading here is inferred from how the models segment riders, not stated.

Paper Title: Integrating equity in transportation scenario planning: A systematic review
Study type / basis for inclusion: PRISMA-style systematic literature review of how equity has been 'envisioned, planned, and evaluated' in transportation scenario planning; sources are academic papers, agency reports, and materials from the TRB 2nd Conference on Scenario Planning in Transportation (September 2022). Not fieldwork. Contributor: shows how 'participation' and 'equity' get slotted into a mainstream long-range planning tool, and what still gets left out.
Case setting: US state DOT and MPO long-range transportation planning. Scenario-planning practice examples: the California Regional Blueprint Planning Program (2006), Denver Regional Council of Governments (2012), Oregon DOT, Washington State DOT (SR 167), Delaware Valley RPC, and the COVID-19 transit scenario exercise by Shaheen and Wong (2021). Lead author at Oak Ridge National Laboratory; co-authors at Alberta, UMass Amherst, MassDOT, and Arizona. The copy read is a double-spaced manuscript with no visible publication venue or date.
Method(s), session by session: No sessions run by the authors. Review method: keyword search of four academic databases plus grey literature and TRB conference slide decks; PRISMA inclusion and exclusion screening; then analysis along three axes, (1) which scenario-planning steps equity enters (defining missions and goals; creating scenarios; evaluating policies), (2) how equity analysis has evolved over time (Figure 3), and (3) the circumstances under which equity is and is not considered (a four-study paired comparison, Table 3). Output: five policy recommendations and a phase-by-phase guideline.
Tools and artifacts: The FHWA scenario-planning method and guidebooks (2011 to 2017); the two-axis driving-forces scenario matrix (typically four futures); horizontal versus vertical equity (Litman; Bills and Walker); equity indicators (accessibility, affordability, job-training access, mobility, land use, sustainability); person-level versus zonal metrics; GIS-based scenario platforms; robustness analysis (worst-case mitigation); 'justice indicators'; qualitative tools (focus groups, expert panels, interactive exercises and games at public meetings); Table 4 (equity analyses that can be run on standard scenario-planning outputs).
Underlying principle of the method: Scenario planning as a mindset shift from forecasting one future to preparing for 'numerous futures', so agencies can 'face uncertainties with flexibility and nimbleness'. Equity is layered on as horizontal ('benefits and costs being distributed equally across all groups or spaces') and vertical ('disadvantaged groups should receive a greater share of resources'). The review's normative anchor is Karner et al. (2020): 'This focus on community participation to build justice-oriented outcomes ... can be furthered by training community leaders and members of local communities about the scenario planning process ... and how to conduct data analysis' so 'people can understand how ... their participation can affect long-term plans' (p. 21).
Provocation used to generate new ideas: The scenario matrix itself is a structured provocation: 'Forces are often designed to be extreme to include lower probability but high consequence futures' (p. 9), and agencies use 'interactive exercises, and games at public meetings and workshops' (p. 21) to develop and test scenarios. The review reports these; it does not run one.
Who holds design authority: Agencies. 'The formation of scenarios depends on the identified goals and missions of the performing agency' (p. 8), and scenario creation is 'mostly based on the agency's goals or the staff members' experiences' (p. 9). Three modes of scenario-composition input are catalogued: '1) small-scale within-agency discussions, 2) focus groups with experts, and 3) collective inputs from residents' (p. 9), with the within-agency and expert-panel modes described as the common ones. The review argues authority should extend outward via 'advanced community participation techniques' and community training. Scope: long-range transportation plans, the policies tested within them, and the evaluation metrics, not vehicle or service design.
What is being designed: Nothing built. The paper designs a set of recommendations and a phased guideline for embedding equity in scenario planning: clarify the equity definition, add demographic trends (aging) as driving forces, build 'quantifiable equity metrics', run 'robustness analysis' to minimize 'the likelihood of the worst-case situations for underserved populations' (p. 19), integrate vertical-equity analysis, and use 'advanced community participation techniques'.
Values surfaced in the case: The review states the divide directly: 'studies that did not consider equity tended to emphasize system efficiency, economic growth, and/or technological aspects', while 'equity considerations were more commonly observed when the experiences of transportation system users played a significant role' (p. 18). Emerging-technology scenarios (driverless cars, connected infrastructure) after 2019 'sparked more scenario planning conversations', but 'equity was not thoroughly examined in these emerging scenario planning exercises' (p. 16); EV subsidies flow disproportionately to 'higher-income households who make up a larger share of the electric vehicle market' (p. 21). Community values: participation ('collective inputs from residents'; 'advanced community participation techniques'; training community members 'how to conduct data analysis'), flexibility for variable need (vertical equity's 'differing needs'; 'a wide participant base ... based on demographic characteristics'; the 'flexible guideline'), and equitable access (horizontal and vertical equity; 'advancing the policy benefits for all people'). Relational trust is largely absent as a named value. Maps to participation, flexibility for variable need, and equitable access, with efficiency, growth, and technology as the frame equity is set against.
Ideal traveler per decision-makers: Implicit and structural. When equity is not deliberately added, scenario planning 'often involves an examination of various outputs such as emissions, mobility, and accessibility' that 'do not directly represent equity impacts' (p. 19 to 20), and its default subject is the system-level trip-maker whose congestion, emissions, and travel time are the outputs. The 'equity indicators' used historically did not include 'the analysis of the distribution of benefits and costs by demographic groups, such as low-income populations' (p. 8). The distinction the review draws, growth and technology framings versus 'the experiences of transportation system users', is essentially our decision-maker versus lived-experience split. No 'ideal traveler' phrasing.
Actual travelers encountered: None by the authors. Reported: residents giving 'collective inputs' in some agencies' scenario workshops; workshop participants in the Shaheen and Wong (2021) COVID exercise who produced 'a traveler's bill of rights, mobility-for-all strategies, targeted service for underserved populations'; and TRB conference discussion of 'how the pandemic affected minority, low-income, and essential employees in particular' (p. 17). Population categories: 'underserved populations', 'aging populations', 'low-income populations'.
Gap between the two: 'Only 15% of MPOs reported employing a scenario planning approach in a 2013 FHWA survey' (p. 15), and within that minority equity is inconsistently handled: equity is considered 'primarily in three steps', but 'the policy impact on the equitable distribution of transportation system was infrequently evaluated' even when equity was a stated goal (p. 8). 'Many studies have investigated horizontal equity indicators, but relatively few have addressed vertical equity' (p. 14). Emerging-tech scenarios skip equity almost entirely (p. 16). Community input, where it happens, is mostly 'focus groups, interactive exercises, and games at public meetings', and the review's own recommendation is that 'more advanced community participation approaches should be explored' and that residents be trained to run the analysis themselves, an acknowledgement that current participation is shallow.
Quotable moment: "it appears that equity considerations were more commonly observed when the experiences of transportation system users played a significant role in scenario planning. Conversely, studies that did not consider equity tended to emphasize system efficiency, economic growth, and/or technological aspects." (p. 18). And: "equity was not thoroughly examined in these emerging scenario planning exercises." (p. 16).
Cross-comparison note (our synthesis): A contributor that maps our decision-maker versus lived-experience split onto an existing planning tool. Its cleanest finding for us: scenario exercises framed around 'system efficiency, economic growth, and/or technological aspects' leave equity out, while those framed around 'the experiences of transportation system users' include it, and the newer AV and connected-infrastructure scenarios sit almost entirely in the first camp ('equity was not thoroughly examined in these emerging scenario planning exercises'). It also shows how thin 'participation' usually is inside this tool: mostly within-agency and expert panels, with resident input a third and less common mode. Its own strongest recommendation, train community members to run the vertical-equity analysis themselves (per Karner et al. 2020), is close to our participation-first argument. Caveats: a systematic review with no fieldwork; a manuscript with no visible publication venue or date (references run to 2023); US agency practice only; scoped to long-range plans, not to service or vehicle design; the 'ideal traveler' reading is inferred from what scenario outputs measure by default.

Paper Title: Beyond research delays: science funding disruptions limit community participation in climate and infrastructure planning
Study type / basis for inclusion: A 'Perspective' essay (npj Urban Sustainability) reflecting on the authors' own US federal grant being paused, and what that did to a community-engaged environmental-justice transportation and climate project. Not a study with findings. Thin contributor: it names the techno-rational planning frame precisely and gives a compact technical-versus-lived example.
Case setting: A multi-phase mixed-methods project based in California, USA: semi-structured interviews with environmental-justice community-based organizations plus a comparative quantitative and spatial analysis of climate vulnerability and risk, 'in partnership with local planners, policymakers, and engineers'. Federal funding was paused four months into the work and 'only released after legal intervention', about six months later. Authors at USC and UC Davis.
Method(s), session by session: No sessions completed as designed (the essay is about the disruption). Planned method: (1) qualitative semi-structured interviews with EJ community-based organizations 'to understand the needs and efficacy of current climate response strategies'; (2) a quantitative and spatial analysis of vulnerability and risk; (3) a paired examination of 'whether the perceptions of risks in vulnerable communities align with existing secondary data tools', to test 'whether gaps exist among research, practice, and community perspectives'. During the funding suspension 'data collection was halted, research staff had to be reassigned or furloughed, and collaborations with local community-based organizations were interrupted'.
Tools and artifacts: Semi-structured interviews; spatial vulnerability dashboards; the US Climate Vulnerability Index and California's CalEnviroScreen (both described as relying on 'perspectives from community-based organizations to identify relevant indicators'); cost-benefit analysis (named as the standard method for 'the value of transportation investments'); the concept of 'epistemic justice'.
Underlying principle of the method: 'Centering community perspectives is one approach that can improve methodologies and address environmental injustice'; this is framed as 'a form of epistemic justice, where decision makers value the knowledge that communities possess as legitimate forms of data, on par with quantitative sources of data'. Community knowledge 'illuminates intersectional forms of vulnerability that are challenging to measure or identify with solely quantitative data'. 'Analyzing transportation and climate justice requires an approach that goes beyond the constraints of road infrastructure, transit services, and specific transportation policies'.
Provocation used to generate new ideas: None. A reflective essay.
Who holds design authority: The essay's own frame: 'Transportation is a field dominated by techno-rational planning, where quantitative metrics are privileged in the forecasting, design, and evaluation of facilities and services'. Regulatory air monitoring 'is rarely performed at a scale that can account for these hazards from an environmental justice perspective'. The project's aim was to widen authority by 'providing equitable opportunities for vulnerable, urban communities to provide input on climate infrastructure, including transportation'. The disruption's first-named short-term harm is 'exclusion of community members from data decision-making'. Scope: transportation and climate infrastructure planning, risk assessment, and the data tools used in 'state policy and funding decisions'.
What is being designed: Nothing built. The intended product was 'improving risk assessment approaches by promoting policy-actionable metrics for decision-making aimed at reducing environmental injustices', and better 'methods for collecting community-level data'. The essay closes with three recommendations centred on restoring federal research funding and collaborating with state and city partners.
Values surfaced in the case: Efficiency and cost-recovery values, named as the default and criticised: techno-rational planning privileges 'Levels of service, vehicle miles traveled, frequency and efficiency, value of travel time, and crash outcomes'; from 'a utilitarian perspective', these measures 'can help identify whether transportation investments and air quality impacts are economically efficient, effective in providing value to system users, ... and provide an efficient use of resources for government investment', and 'Cost-benefit analyses ... are common methods'. But 'such a techno-rational, quantitative approach reduces inputs and effects of these investments to a dollar amount, which rarely captures the full distribution of benefits and burdens' and 'misses both the experiences of those users and the communities through which such a system operates'. Community values: participation and recognition ('epistemic justice'; community knowledge 'on par with quantitative sources of data'), equitable access, and relational trust (global partners 'no longer trusting U.S.-led climate interventions'; community collaborations 'interrupted'). Maps to participation and recognition, with equitable access and relational trust secondary, set against a named efficiency and cost-benefit frame.
Ideal traveler per decision-makers: Adjacent and sharply drawn in one example. 'A technical analysis might reveal that a walking route to a transit stop has no pedestrian crashes and low traffic volume, demonstrating that it is a safe route to walk. However, community knowledge might reveal that the street lacks lighting to illuminate the path at night and has limited visibility into surrounding homes and businesses, creating a place where people feel unsafe walking, regardless of what official statistics indicate' (p. 1 to 2). The implicit subject of the technical analysis is a daytime pedestrian whose safety is fully captured by crash counts and traffic volume. Air monitoring similarly 'look[s] at certain hazardous air pollutants but only in one area with a limited scope'. No 'ideal traveler' phrasing.
Actual travelers encountered: None reported (the fieldwork was interrupted). The intended participants were 'environmental justice community-based organizations' and residents of 'vulnerable urban communities ... across California'; the essay names asthma and 'trouble breathing' as the 'health experiences that may be tied to poor air quality' community members can report, and 'people feel unsafe walking' at night on a street a technical analysis calls safe.
Gap between the two: The essay's whole argument is this gap: 'a technical analysis' vs 'community knowledge' on the same walking route; regulatory monitoring 'rarely performed at a scale that can account for these hazards from an environmental justice perspective' vs residents' 'visual experiences of air pollutants as well as health experiences'; 'quantifying certain kinds of air pollutants in limited areas for regulatory ... purposes limits the incorporation of residents' lived experiences in regulatory decision-making and governance'. The project meant to test whether that gap exists and was stopped before it could.
Quotable moment: "a technical analysis might reveal that a walking route to a transit stop has no pedestrian crashes and low traffic volume, demonstrating that it is a safe route to walk. However, community knowledge might reveal that the street lacks lighting ... creating a place where people feel unsafe walking, regardless of what official statistics indicate." (p. 1 to 2). And: "such a techno-rational, quantitative approach reduces inputs and effects of these investments to a dollar amount, which rarely captures the full distribution of benefits and burdens." (p. 2).
Cross-comparison note (our synthesis): A thin contributor whose value is two lines.
