First, the compact statement of the frame our argument critiques: 'Transportation is a field dominated by techno-rational planning, where quantitative metrics are privileged in the forecasting, design, and evaluation of facilities and services. Levels of service, vehicle miles traveled, frequency and efficiency, value of travel time, and crash outcomes ...'. Second, the lit-street example, a technical model calls a route safe while residents will not walk it after dark, which is exactly our decision-maker-versus-lived-experience split rendered in one sentence. The essay frames the fix as 'epistemic justice', community knowledge treated as legitimate data, which aligns with our participation-first argument. Caveats: not a study, no findings; the essay is largely about US science-funding politics in 2026; California-specific; the project it describes was disrupted, so there is no fieldwork to draw on.

Paper Title: Implementation science frameworks for active and sustainable transportation interventions with a focus on equity: A scoping review
Study type / basis for inclusion: PRISMA-ScR scoping review (Transportation Research Interdisciplinary Perspectives 38, article 102020) of peer-reviewed studies that used implementation science theories, models, or frameworks for active and sustainable transportation interventions, categorised against an implementation science taxonomy. Not fieldwork. Thin contributor: it names the 'pathway of actors' who hold design authority and finds that equity, and community participation, are the exception rather than the rule.
Case setting: Global peer-reviewed literature. Six databases searched from inception to 4 June 2025; 8,892 records, 26 studies included, spanning walking and cycling programs, School Streets, bus rapid transit, Mobility-as-a-Service, pedestrian barrier-removal plans, and transit integration, in the USA, UK, England, Newcastle, Klang Valley, Amman, and elsewhere. Authors at York, Dalhousie, Memorial, Saskatchewan, and Monash. Note: lead author 'McCullogh' is a different person from Sarah Rebolloso McCullough of the Performative Equity row.
Method(s), session by session: No sessions. Review method: librarian-assisted search of six databases; two-reviewer independent screening at title, abstract, and full-text, conflicts resolved by consensus or a third reviewer; thematic analysis and narrative synthesis (Popay et al.); frameworks categorised using Nilsen's implementation science taxonomy; barriers and facilitators extracted and organised into cross-cutting themes; equity content extracted separately (Table 4). The authors substitute 'interest-holders' for 'stakeholders' 'to refrain from reproducing colonial language'.
Tools and artifacts: Implementation science frameworks (CFIR, RE-AIM, ELASTIC, PTSIL, the Octopus Framework, process and determinant models); Nilsen's taxonomy of theories, models, and frameworks; the transportation-equity definition from Williams et al. (2023); a barriers-and-facilitators synthesis; Table 4 mapping equity constructs and indicators across the included frameworks (accessibility, affordability, mobility of vulnerable groups, transparency in decision-making, public participation).
Underlying principle of the method: Implementation science: the systematic study of 'barriers and facilitators' to moving an intervention into practice, 'particularly useful in the context of built environment' change. Transportation equity is adopted from Williams et al. (2023) as encompassing 'the fair distribution of transportation resources, inclusive participation in decision-making processes, and recognition of the prevailing injustices that shape different levels of need and power within transportation systems'. The review's stance: 'equity be embedded throughout the implementation process, including meaningful engagement with communities', and frameworks should be 'tailored to the context and flexible enough to adapt to local settings'.
Provocation used to generate new ideas: None. A review.
Who holds design authority: Named directly: 'Active and sustainable transportation interventions are implemented through a pathway of actors responsible for funding, design, planning, and construction'. Across the included studies the actors are municipal staff, transportation agencies, school leaders and administration, university administration, and 'sustainable transportation councils'; 'senior management support' and 'the support of school principals and/or school administration' are repeatedly cited as make-or-break facilitators. Community participation appears as a facilitator that 'powers [residents] as active agents' but also as a cost: 'the time needed to design participatory strategies, education, and mobilize participants may be too long for project owners as they may face time and budgetary constraints' (quoted, p. 1316). One included study warns that 'Often in developing countries, technocrats implement western ideologies, which may not result in changes that are suitable for developing nations'. Scope: active-transport infrastructure, transit service and integration, School Streets, and MaaS, not policy design.
What is being designed: Nothing built by the review. It produces a categorisation of the frameworks in use and a recommendation set: embed equity throughout implementation, engage communities meaningfully, tailor frameworks to context, and use flexible rather than rigid models.
Values surfaced in the case: Efficiency, cost, and feasibility recur as the dominant decision criteria in the included studies: 'funding was identified as a facilitator and as a barrier'; interventions are favoured when they are 'feasible to run and maintain' and 'did not take a substantial amount of work, time, or funds to initiate'; 'because of the financial constraints that transportation agencies are facing, it is crucial to incorporate livability principles into the agency's existing processes'; 'the viability of the projects is based on demands, financial capability, and stability'. Community values: participation and recognition (a named cross-cutting theme; participation can 'foster trust, ownership, and learning'; 'public engagement is required for developing successful sustainable transportation infrastructure'), relational trust (the 'trust, ownership' finding; 'checking-in with the community'), equitable access (Table 4's accessibility, affordability, and 'mobility of vulnerable groups' constructs), and flexibility for variable need (the review's call for 'context-specific' and 'flexible' frameworks; MaaS and paratransit as flexible modes). Crucially, '17 of 26 included studies did not address equity'. Maps to participation and recognition, relational trust, equitable access, and flexibility for variable need, with cost and feasibility as the working value.
Ideal traveler per decision-makers: Implicit. When equity is not built into the implementation framework (the majority case), the intervention's success is judged on uptake, feasibility, and cost, so the implied beneficiary is whoever a low-cost, quick-to-start program happens to reach. Several included studies 'employed the language of accessibility ... often used to refer to physical access to infrastructure, such as wide sidewalks, shading devices, and lighting ... for able-bodied' users, rather than to equity. The frameworks themselves, in their pre-2022 versions, 'do not have any equity- or accessibility-focused constructs'. No 'ideal traveler' phrasing.
Actual travelers encountered: None met by the review authors. Via the 26 included studies: residents in socio-economically deprived neighbourhoods (walking programs); school leaders, parents, and pupils (School Streets); persons with disabilities (pedestrian barrier-removal plans); older adults; and, in Wan and Titheridge's China framework, 'People without urban or local citizenship (Hukou)' and 'Disadvantaged families/households'. These appear as study populations and framework 'target groups', not as voices.
Gap between the two: 'The majority of included studies (n = 17) did not address equity, a notable gap', and 'attention to transportation equity is limited'. Where accessibility language is used it often means physical infrastructure 'for able-bodied' users, not equity. Community engagement is identified as both facilitator and barrier, and is treated by 'project owners' as a time-and-budget cost that 'may be too long'. Older versions of the core frameworks (CFIR pre-2022) carry no equity constructs at all. The review's recommendation, embed equity and meaningful community engagement throughout implementation, is a statement of what is currently missing.
Quotable moment: "Active and sustainable transportation interventions are implemented through a pathway of actors responsible for funding, design, planning, and construction." (abstract). And: "the time needed to design participatory strategies, education, and mobilize participants may be too long for project owners as they may face time and budgetary constraints." (quoted in the review, p. 1316).
Cross-comparison note (our synthesis): A thin contributor that is useful in two ways. It names the 'pathway of actors responsible for funding, design, planning, and construction', a clean statement of where design authority sits for the kind of infrastructure our argument is about. And its headline finding, that 17 of 26 implementation studies did not address equity at all and that community engagement is widely treated as a time-and-budget cost 'too long for project owners', is direct evidence that participation is the exception, not the default, in how transport interventions get built. Table 4 also shows that when equity does enter a framework it usually enters as an indicator list (accessibility, affordability, 'mobility of vulnerable groups'), not as shared authority. Caveats: a scoping review, no fieldwork; only 26 studies, heterogeneous (many about walking and cycling programs rather than transit or vehicle design); global scope with no single setting; the 'ideal traveler' cell is inferred.

Paper Title: Mobility Injustice by Design
Study type / basis for inclusion: Scholarly monograph (Routledge, Changing Mobilities series, DOI 10.4324/9781003459729). The source read is a publisher preview: front matter, preface, and roughly the first seven pages of Chapter 1 only. Chapters on Design, Injustice, Unhoused, Disabilities, Aging, and the Conclusion were not available. Thin contributor: it frames mobility injustice as an outcome of design decisions and supplies a sharp signal-timing example of the encoded ideal traveler.
Case setting: Cities and urban public space, three realms of practice: people living unhoused, disabled people, and aged people. Empirical base named in the preface: the 'Exclusionary Design, social exclusion in public spaces' research project (Copenhagen, 2021 to 2024, Velux Foundation), which included PhD fieldwork on 'how unhoused people experience social exclusion on the streets of Copenhagen', a steering group of Copenhagen NGOs and the municipality, and a public exhibition ('Den Udstodende By', October 2024); plus fieldwork in Japan (Bevica Foundation) and engagement with the Universal Design Hub. Author: Ole B. Jensen, Professor of Urban Theory, Aalborg University, Denmark.
Method(s), session by session: Not visible in the preview beyond description. The book is 'a theoretically informed framework, allowing us to "see" mobility injustices more clearly'. The preface names: a systematic literature search across mobilities, aging, homelessness, and disability (by a student assistant); primary data from the Exclusionary Design project (interviews, with all interviewee identities concealed and fictitious names, empirical statements set in italics); secondary data sources; and commissioned sketches illustrating 'mobile situations'. The stated method question comes from situational mobilities research: 'how does it feel to move/be moved?'
Tools and artifacts: Mobility justice (Sheller 2018); design justice (Costanza-Chock 2020); design ethics (Wakkary 2021); critical disability studies; Universal Design (via the Bevica Foundation's 'Leave no one behind'); post-phenomenology; the 'right to the city' (Lefebvre) and 'right to roam' (UN Universal Declaration of Human Rights, Article 13); the concept of the 'mobile with' (assisted, relational mobility); illustrative sketches.
Underlying principle of the method: Mobility is 'made' and therefore contestable: 'the "artificial" nature of mobilities and the fact that it is designed ("made") means that it can be different and that it can be challenged and changed'. The autonomous mobile subject is a fiction: mobility is 'relationally dependent on others', so 'the figure of the autonomous mobile subject is fictional', yet 'the trope is powerful and has found its way into foundational policy documents'. The governing question, borrowed from Hendren (2020): 'Who is the built world built for?' Design carries values: 'How are values inscribed into "made" and designed spaces, artifacts, and technologies?'
Provocation used to generate new ideas: The book positions art and design as provocateurs: it 'reflects on the potential for those in the arts and design to provoke public engagement in these timely issues', and the Exclusionary Design project's findings were disseminated through a public exhibition. No provocation exercise is described in the preview.
Who holds design authority: Designers, planners, and city authorities, whose choices 'of materials, design of spaces, and implementation of technologies afford or hinder particular mobilities'. Exclusion happens 'either intentionally to facilitate immobility or social exclusion, or because of a lack of awareness of the aggregated consequences'. Cities 'are still mainly built for the able-bodied citizens, nested in middle-class values, and for "ordinary" citizens'. Scope: urban space, street furniture, pavements, crossings, vehicles, infrastructures, and the technologies (including digital) that mediate access.
What is being designed: Nothing built by the book. Its product is a conceptual framework for 'learning to see' the normativity of design, and an agenda for 'commoning the values and normativity of design' and mobilizing 'a design ethics' toward mobility justice.
Values surfaced in the case: Efficiency and vehicle-throughput values, shown operating against slow bodies: pedestrian crossings where 'the "green period" that is designed into the system has its priority to make cars circulate the city as seamlessly as possible, with the result that slow-walking citizens cannot cross roads quickly enough'; hostile benches 'angled so horizontally placed bodies will fall off simply due to gravity'; 'pointy metal spikes' under bridges; 'digital technology requirements [that] favor some citizens' mobility relative to others'. 'Middle-class values' and design for the 'ordinary' citizen are named explicitly. Community values: equitable access (the 'right to roam' as a human right; 'Leave no one behind'), recognition (disabled, unhoused, and aged people 'not thought of' in design), and relational trust and flexibility for variable need (the 'mobile with', mobility as 'relationally dependent on others' and mediated by care). Maps to equitable access and recognition, with efficiency and middle-class 'ordinariness' as the frame.
Ideal traveler per decision-makers: Strong for the material available. The pedestrian signal's 'green period' is timed to 'make cars circulate the city as seamlessly as possible', so a slow walker 'cannot cross roads quickly enough' and over time 'stop[s] doing so completely', the crossing encodes an able-bodied, car-paced body as its design subject. More broadly, 'cities are still mainly built for the able-bodied citizens, nested in middle-class values, and for "ordinary" citizens (e.g., not people in homelessness)', against Hendren's question 'Who is the built world built for?' The autonomous, self-moving subject 'is a key figure in much of politics and mobilities thinking' but 'biased'.
Actual travelers encountered: Described, not quoted, in the preview: unhoused people and street sleepers 'on city streets around the world', met by hostile benches and anti-homeless spikes; senior citizens 'struggling to walk the rumbling stone pavements' and unable to cross at lights; wheelchair users facing 'high curbs, lack of ramps, and artifacts such as cafe chairs or advertisement signs on the sidewalks'. The Exclusionary Design project's Copenhagen fieldwork with unhoused people is the primary empirical source, with participant identities concealed. Global scale figures: an estimated 1.3 billion people with a significant disability (WHO 2023), around 895,000 people in homelessness in Europe (Feantsa 2023).
Gap between the two: The book's thesis is the gap: 'millions of citizens have their "right to roam" curbed by design and planning decisions', while the widespread cultural belief holds that 'design is in the service of "the good"'. Design is 'working counter' to that belief. The autonomous mobile subject that policy assumes is a fiction, yet the built environment keeps being made for the 'able-bodied', 'middle-class', 'ordinary' citizen, so unhoused, disabled, and aged people 'experience mobility injustice' by the aggregated, often unnoticed, consequences of ordinary design choices.
Quotable moment: "The 'green period' that is designed into the system has its priority to make cars circulate the city as seamlessly as possible, with the result that slow-walking citizens cannot cross roads quickly enough." (p. 3). And: "cities are still mainly built for the able-bodied citizens, nested in middle-class values, and for 'ordinary' citizens." (p. 4).
Cross-comparison note (our synthesis): A thin contributor (read from a preview only) that gives the argument a book-length theoretical anchor and one very usable example. The claim that mobility is 'made' and therefore contestable, and that design decisions exclude 'either intentionally ... or because of a lack of awareness of the aggregated consequences', is close to our framing of infrastructure that arrives carrying values without anyone deciding to impose them. The pedestrian 'green period' timed for car throughput is a compact, citable instance of the decision-makers' ideal traveler encoded into a device. Jensen's 'Who is the built world built for?' (via Hendren) is our ideal-traveler question in five words. Caveats: only the front matter, preface, and opening of Chapter 1 were available, so the method, the injustice framework, and all three case chapters (unhoused, disabilities, aging) are unread; the empirical base is Copenhagen and Japan, not the US; a monograph, not a study with reported findings; page numbers are the preview PDF's.
